en: Then, having heard the beginning of the latter half and the third quarter recited by the wise Sūta,
those best of sages asked for the fourth quarter. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 3.1.1)
This third quarter has been traversed by you through our connection;
now proclaim in detail the fourth quarter, the withdrawal (saṃhāra).
All the previous Manvantaras, along with those that follow,
as well as the current interval of the present Manu and these Seven Sages, [have been described].
Tell us everything in full detail and in proper sequence regarding the origin of that great-souled one, including all his various components.
Sūta said:
O best of sages, I shall relate all of this to you exactly as it is, including this fourth quarter along with its dissolution.
O twice-born ones, listen to this creation of the high-souled Manu Vaivasvata, the present one, in detail and in its proper sequence.
Listen as I describe in brief the seven future Manvantaras, along with the dissolution of the worlds.
These seven Manvantaras, along with their respective progeny, have indeed been correctly described in brief; now hear from me about those that are yet to come.
I shall now proclaim, in brief, the future history of the future Sāvarṇi Manu, the son of Vivasvat; listen to that.
And seven great sages are likewise recorded here as those yet to come:
Kauśika, Gālava, and Jāmadagnya of the Bhṛgu lineage.
Dvaipāyana, Vasiṣṭha, Kṛpa Śāradvata,
the radiant Ātreya, and the sage Śṛṅga Kāśyapa.
Bharadvāja, as well as the highly illustrious Aśvatthāman, the son of Droṇa—these seven high-souled ones will be the future supreme ṛṣis;
and there will be three groups [of attendants]: the Sutapas, the Amitābhas, and the Sukhas.
The host of those gods is recorded as consisting of twenty members each;
I shall now declare their names by name—listen with concentrated minds.
Ṛtu, Tapas, Śukra, Kṛti, Nemi, Prabhākara, Prabhāsa, Māsakṛt, Dharma, Tejoraśmi, Kratu, and Virāṭ.
Arciṣmān, Dyotana, Bhānu, Yaśas, Kīrtti, Budha, and Dhṛti.
These twenty are indeed proclaimed by their names as the Sutapas:
Prabhu, Vibhu, Vibhāsa, Jetṛ, Hantṛ, Rihā, and Ṛtu.
Sumati, Pramati, Dīpti, Samākhyāta, Mahas, Mahān, Dehin, Muni, Iṇa, Poṣṭṛ, Sama, Satya, and Viśruta.
Thus, these twenty Amitābhas have been proclaimed:
Dāma, Dānī, Ṛta, Soma, Vitta, Vaidya, Yama, and Nidhi.

The person, the oblation, the offering, the gift, the giver, austerity, tranquility, the fixed place, the ordinance, and the restraint—these constitute the twenty. (Bṛhad-yogiyājñavalkya-purāṇa 3.1.19)
For these are declared to be happy in their similarity to Sāvarṇi;
they are the sons of the high-souled Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci.
In that interval, sixty gods will belong to the present [Manu];
furthermore, there will be exactly nine sons of Sāvarṇa Manu.
Virajas, Ārvarīvan, Nirmoka, and others as well;
I shall indeed describe nine others among the future Sāvarṇi Manvantaras.
And there will be other Sāvarṇa Manus, the sons of Brahmā;
they are Merusāvarṇi and the others—those four who possess divine vision.
For these sons of Dakṣa’s granddaughter, the daughters of Kriyā,
were endowed with great ascetic power and possessed of great majesty upon the summit of Mount Meru.
Generated by Brahmā and others, as well as by the wise Dakṣa himself, they have gone to Maharloka; having passed away, they will become the future [progenitors] residing on Mount Meru.
Those of great power were born previously in the Cākṣuṣa interval;
they indeed became Manus in the future intervals yet to come.
The sons of Manu who were the grandsons of Dakṣa Prācetasa are five by name, known as the Sāvarṇas; four of them were born of the supreme ṛṣis.
Sāvarṇi was the son of Saṃjñā, and likewise Vaivasvata;
the eldest son of Saṃjñā was named Mūrti, the lord Vaivasvata.
When the Vaivasvata interval arrived, the auspicious birth of those two took place.
These fourteen Manus have been celebrated, who increase one's fame.
In the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and the Purāṇas, they are all described as sovereign lords;
they are all established as the lords of progeny and the lords of all beings.
By them, this entire earth— with its seven continents and its cities—
is indeed to be protected by lords of men for a full thousand yugas.
The detailed account of them through their progeny and their ascetic penance will be told;
these fourteen creations, beginning with that of Svāyambhuva, are to be known.
In their respective offices during the Manvantaras, they remain here one by one;
once their offices have ceased, they take refuge in Maharloka.
Those who have passed away consist of eight and another six;
among these, the lord Vaivasvata is the one who rules now, as he did in previous ages.
O twice-born one, I shall describe those who remain, together with the celestial sages and the Dānavas,
along with all future beings according to their natural creation.
The detailed account of them should be known through the natural disposition of Vaivasvata,
because they are all [descendants] of Vivasvat, neither deficient nor redundant.
However, because of the great abundance of repetitions, I shall not provide detailed accounts of them,
nor of the future Manvantaras, nor likewise of those that have already passed.
Therefore, they should be known according to their divisions as being inherent in each and every family;
indeed, for the sake of their accomplishment, [they shall be explained] in detail and in due order.
The daughter of Dakṣa was the most righteous and renowned as Suvratā;
she was the eldest, the best among all maidens, and the daughter of Vīriṇī.
Having taken that maiden, her father went into the presence of Brahmā,
who was seated upon the Vairāja throne, endowed with both Dharma and Bhava.
Brahmā addressed Dakṣa, who was standing near him and possessed of virtuous qualities:
"O Dakṣa, this daughter of yours, being faithful to her vows, shall indeed give birth [to these beings]."
Then, having heard the word of Brahmā, Dakṣa, Dharma, and Bhava each begot four auspicious sons who were the progenitors of the four social orders (cāturvarṇya).
Those three, together with Brahmā, mentally approached that maiden;
for them who meditated upon truth, the maiden was immediately born.
To them were born four sons who were their equals in appearance; they were fully accomplished in the performance of their duties and endowed with splendor.
Then, seeing those self-manifested beings who were unable to enjoy [sensual pleasures] with their newborn bodies, they heard the speech of Brahmā.
"His son! Mine indeed!"—thus they vied with one another, pulling him away;
having arisen from their own minds, they spoke thus to each other.
Whosoever was equal to another in physical form, he constantly became that person's son; and whoever was his peer in beauty, valor, and honor, [he likewise became his son].
"Let him take her—may it be well with you—who is her equal in appearance; for a son always conforms to his father's form. (Bṛhaddevatā 3.1.48)
"Therefore, a son is equal to one's own self for both father and mother by virtue of their seed.
Having thus made this agreement, they all accepted sons.
When the interval of Cākṣuṣa had passed and that of Vaivasvata had arrived,
there was a son named Raucya, the offspring of the Prajāpati Ruci.
The son of Kavi, named Bhautya, was produced from Bhūti;
thus, two Manus were born in the Vaivasvata interval from Vivasvat.
The illustrious Vaivasvata Manu, as well as Sāvarṇa who is indeed renowned—
he is to be known as the learned lord Manu, the son of Saṃjñā, belonging to the lineage of Vivasvat.
Another son of Savarṇā is remembered as Vaivasvata Manu;
and those four Sāvarṇa Manus are born of the great ṛṣis.
Having perfected their selves through austerity, they shall indeed, in their own future Manvantaras,
be the accomplishers of all purposes and goals.
In the first [Manvantara], that of Merusāvarṇi, the son of Dakṣa, there were three [groups]: the Parās, the Marīcigarbhas, and the Sudharmas;
all these high-souled ones appeared during the interval of Vaivasvata.
These shall be the sons of Rohita, the Prajāpati, who was the son of Dakṣa;
they will be future beings, twelve in each group.
Aiśvara, Graha, Rāhu, Vāku, and likewise Vaṃśa—these twelve are to be known as the Pārās; now learn of the northern ones.
Vājī, Vājijit, Prabhūti, Kakud,
Dadhikrāvā, Vipakva, Praṇīta, Vijaya, and Madhu.
Utathya and Uttama are the two; these are the twelve Marīcis.
Now I shall declare the Sudharmas by name—learn of them from me.
Varṇa, Tathātha, Garvin, Bhuraṇyu, Vrajana, Amita,
Amita-dravaketu, Jambha, and then Aja-śakraka.
The Sudharmans are proclaimed as the Sunemis and the Dyutis;
their Indra at that time shall be known by the name Adbhuta.
Skanda is indeed Pārvatīya, while Kārttikeya is Pāvaki;
Medhātithi is Paulastya, and Vasu is likewise Kāśyapa.
Jyotiṣmat was the son of Bhṛgu, Dyutimat was likewise the son of Aṅgiras;
Vasin was the son of Vasiṣṭha, and Havyavāhana was the son of Atri.
Sutapā and Paulaha—these seven were the sons of Rohitāśva;
Dhṛtiketu, Dīptiketu, Śāpahasta, and Nirāmaya.
Pṛthuśravas, Anīka, Bhūridyumna, and Bṛhadyaśas—
these nine sons are proclaimed as belonging to the first Sāvarṇi.
Now, in the tenth cycle, during the interval of the Manu who is the son of Dharma— the second Sāvarṇi Manu who is yet to be— BndP_3.1.66.
The Sudhāmans and the Viruddhas are remembered as two distinct groups;
they are all radiant, numbering one hundred each, and equal in power.
The hundred vital breaths (prāṇas) which were proclaimed by the sages as "puruṣa" will indeed become the gods of Manu Dharmaputra.
Indra among them will be the learned Bhaviṣya, who is called Śānti;
Haviṣmān will be the son of Pulaha, and the illustrious Sukīrti will be the son of Bhṛgu.
Āpomūrti was likewise the descendant of Atri; Vasiṣṭha is remembered as Āpava;
Paulastya was Apratima, and Nābhāga was indeed Kāśyapa.
And Abhimanyu; these seven are the supreme ṛṣis of the Aṅgiras lineage:
Sukṣetra, Uttamaujas, and the heroic Bhūrisena.
Śatānīka, Nirāmitra, Vṛṣasena, Jayadratha,
Bhūridyumna, and Suvarcas— these ten are remembered as the Manus.
In the eleventh cycle, during the third Sāvarṇa Manvantara, the gods will delight in Nirvāṇa; they will travel at will and move with the speed of thought.
These three groups of high-souled deities are renowned;
each one of them consists of thirty inhabitants of the triple heaven.
The thirty days that the wise know as belonging to a month are the nights for the gods who delight in Nirvāṇa, while the birds are their days.
The third group that shall belong to the deities has been declared;
these gods are proclaimed as the Manojavas and the Mūrtimants.
For these are remembered as the future human sons of Brahmā;
after them, Indra will be the future king of the gods, named Vṛṣa.
Listen now as I proclaim their names, including those of the Seven Sages:
Haviṣmān Kāśyapa and Vapuṣmān Bhārgava.
Āruṇi, likewise Ātreya, Vasiṣṭha, and Naga;
Puṣṭi is to be known as belonging to Aṅgiras, and Niścara as belonging to Paulastya.
Paulaha, Hyatitejas, and the eleven gods;
Sarvavega, Sudharmā, Devānīka, and Purovaha.
Kṣemadharmā, Graheṣu, Ādarśa, Paiṇḍraka, and Maru—
these nine were indeed the sons of Sāvarṇa, the son of Prajāpati.
Now, in the twelfth period, during the reign of Manu Rudraputra,
listen to the account of the fourth Manu, Rudrasāvarṇi, and the gods who belong to his interval.
Five classes of gods who have not yet arrived have been declared:
the Haritas, the Rohitas, and likewise the Sumanasas.
Sukarman, Sutara, Vidvān, Sahasrada,
Parvata, Anucara, Apāśu, and Manojava.
Ūrjā, Svāhā, Svadhā, Tārā—these ten are remembered as being green;
and Tapas, Jñānin, Mṛti, Varcas, and he who is remembered as Bandhu.
Rāja, Rājaka, Svarṇapāda,
Puṣṭi, and Vidhi— these five gods, together with the five previously mentioned, are known as the ten Rohitas.
Now, those gods who are proclaimed as the thirty-three, beginning with Tuṣṭi and the others—they are indeed to be known as the Sumanas; learn of them, O performers of good deeds.
Suparvan, Vṛṣabha, Pṛṣṭha, Kapidyumna,
Vipracit, Vikrama, Krama, Vibhūta, and Kānta.
Understand these gods to be performers of good deeds and exceedingly virtuous:
Varṣa, Divya, Añjiṣṭha, Varcasvī, Dyutimān, and Kavi.
Śubha, Haviḥ, Kṛtaprāpti, Vyāpṛta, and Daśama—
these are proclaimed by name as the gods known as the Sutārās.
Among them, the one to be known as Indra is the highly illustrious Ṛtadhāman;
Dyuti is the son of Vasiṣṭha, and likewise Sutapas is the son of Atri.
The son of Aṅgiras was Tapomūrti, the ascetic; likewise Kāśyapa was Tapasvī;
the son of Pulastya was Tapodhana; and the son of Pulaha was Taporati.
The seventh among them should be known as Bhārgava, who possesses steadfastness in austerity;
these are the seven perfected Ṛṣis in the final Sāvarṇika interval.
Devavān, Anupadeva, Devaśreṣṭha, Vidūratha,
Mitravān, Mitrāsena, Citrasena, and Amitrahā.
Mitrabāhu and Suvarcas were the sons of the twelfth Manu;
furthermore, in the thirteenth cycle, in the future Raucya interval, [these shall be the sons].
The Self-Existent One himself declared that there are only three classes of gods;
for all of them are the mind-born sons of the high-souled Brahmā.
The Sutrāmaṇas, the Sudharmas, and the Sukarmas—
these three are declared to be the future hosts of the thirty gods who drink the soma juice.
The thirty-three deities who are worshipped separately by the ritualists—
with clarified butter, speckled butter, and indeed with the most excellent vessel (graha)— [are all present].
Understand now the thirty-three gods according to their individual divisions:
the Sutrāmans, the Prayājyas, and those who are currently the Ājyāśas.
Those known as the Anuyājyas, who consume the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya), and those called the Upayājyas, the Sudharmas—these are proclaimed as the gods. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍapurāṇa 3.1.100)
Divaspati, that being of great strength, will become their Indra;
they are to be known as the sons of Pulaha’s son and the offspring of Ruci.
Aṅgiras was indeed Dhṛtimat, while he who was Paulastya was Avyaya;
the son of Pulaha was Tattvadarśin, and the descendant of Bhṛgu was Nirūpsuka.
Niṣprakampa was the son of Atri, Nirmoha was likewise the son of Kaśyapa, and Sutapas was the son of Vasiṣṭha; these seven, together with the six previously mentioned, constitute the thirteen.
Citrasena, Vicitra, Naya, Dharma, Dhṛta, Bhava,
Aneka, Kṣatraviddha, Surasa, and Nirbhaya— these are the ten.
These are the sons of Raucya Manu in the thirteenth interval;
and now, in the fourteenth cycle, they belong to the interval of Manu Bhautya.
The five classes of deities that shall exist have been declared:
the Cākṣuṣas, the Pavitras, the Kaniṣṭhas, and likewise the Bhrājitas.
And Vācāvṛddha—these are remembered as the five groups of gods.
Know that the seven notes beginning with Niṣāda are the seven Cākṣuṣas.
They know the seven youngest [sons] as the Sāman chants beginning with the Bṛhat;
they are the seven pure worlds, radiant and possessing seven oceans.
Know that those sages who were elders of speech belonged to Svāyambhuva Manu;
all of them are to be understood as Indras in their respective Manvantaras, possessing identical characteristics.
In brilliance, ascetic power, intellect, strength, sacred learning, and valor—
whatever beings exist in the three worlds, whether mobile or immobile— [are surpassed by him].
O Indras, they indeed surpass all others in every respect through all their virtues;
those who speak falsely about beings are delighted, while those who speak of things as they truly are remain neutral.
The three Vedas were capable of refuting the proponents of the doctrine of non-existence;
they were Agnīdhra Kāśyapa, Paulastya, and Māgadha.
Bhārgava, Agnivāhu, Śuci of the Aṅgiras lineage, Śukra of the Vasiṣṭha lineage, Paulaha, and Mukta; BndP_3.1.113.
Ātreya is said to be Śvājita; now hear of the sons of Manu:
Uru, Guru, Gambhīra, Buddha, Śuddha, Śuci, and Kṛtī.
Ūrjasvī and Subala were the sons of Bhautya Manu;
indeed, these four Sāvarṇa Manus are the sons of Brahmā.
One is Vaivasvata, and Sāvarṇi is called a Manu;
Raucya and Bhautya are considered to be the descendants of Pulaha and Bhṛgu respectively.
Indeed, under the sovereignty of Bhautya alone, the Kalpa is swiftly completed.
Sūta said:
When all those Manvantaras here had come to an end without exception, [the Lord]...
When that many yugas have passed and are exhausted, it is called the dissolution;
at the end of that Manvantara, these seven Bhārgavas were then the gods.
Having enjoyed [the sovereignty] while dwelling in the midst of the three worlds for seventy-one ages called yugas,
the Manvantara then comes to an end along with the Pitṛs and the Manus.
This entire triple world will indeed become supportless;
consequently, those abodes of the inhabitants will then be devoid of their residents.
The stars, as well as the constellations and planets, fall away and become liberated;
then, when those lords of the three worlds have passed away here, [the world is left].
When they have arrived in Maharloka— where those who dwell for a kalpa reside,
where the hosts beginning with Ajita dwell, and where the fourteen long-lived ones abide.
In all the Manvantaras, those fourteen gods are indeed heard to remain in Janaloka with their bodies, together with their followers.
Thus, when the gods have passed away from Maharloka toward Janaloka,
while the elements and so forth remain, they indeed enter into those various stationary beings.
When the great world-regions, such as the earth and others, have become empty,
and the gods who dwell for a kalpa have ascended to union (sāyujya), [the dissolution occurs].
Having withdrawn those [beings] from there at the end of the eon, Brahmā, beholding the great creation, indeed establishes the gods, sages, ancestors, and dānavas once again.

Those people who know that the day of Brahmā ends after a thousand cycles of the four yugas, and likewise his night ends after a thousand cycles of the four yugas— they are the ones who truly understand day and night.
The dissolution of all beings is threefold in its essential nature: occasional, elemental, and absolute; such is this process of re-absorption.
The dissolution at the end of a kalpa is the occasional (naimittika) dissolution of that [Brahmā], characterized by the cessation of restraint;
however, the dissolution of the elements (bhūtas) during the period of re-absorption (pratisarga) is the primordial (prākṛta) dissolution, which is the destruction of the instruments (karaṇas).
And through knowledge, the absolute non-occurrence of causes is proclaimed;
therefore, Brahmā, having withdrawn those gods who dwell in the three worlds, [entered into that state].
The Lord Brahmā strikes down and brings about the dissolution of creation once again; then, desiring to sleep, he withdraws all living beings.
Then, when the end of a thousand yugas had arrived and the dissolution of the age was at hand,
that Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) resolved to establish the subjects within himself.
Then there occurs a continuous drought lasting for a hundred years;
by that [drought], those beings on the surface of the earth who possess little strength perish.
Those very [elements] dissolve here and attain the state of earth;
then the sun, becoming a chariot with seven rays, rose up as the source of light.
The Lord of unbearable rays drinks the water with three eyes;
his seventy rays, which are greenish-yellow, are blazing.
Once again they revolve, slowly pervading the sky;
the terrestrial fire, having wood for its fuel, blazes intensely when fanned by the waters.
Therefore, it is said that the sun shines when it bears water;
the sun does not shine because of drought, nor is it sprinkled with water because of drought.
The sun is not eclipsed by drought; rather, it blazes because of water.
Therefore, he who drinks water indeed blazes as the sun in the sky.
Those seven rays of his drink water from the great ocean;
inflamed by that food, they indeed become the seven suns.
Then those seven rays, having become suns, burn this entire fourfold world in all four directions with their flames.
And by means of those rays, extending both upwards and downwards,
the seven suns blaze forth, possessing the scorching heat of the fire at the end of a yuga.
And those [fires], though blazing with many thousands of rays, stand having surrounded themselves with water,
utterly consuming the earth.
Then, scorched by their prowess, the earth—
with its mountains, rivers, and oceans— became devoid of moisture.
It was completely hemmed in on all sides— below, above, and across— by the rays of the sun, which were blazing, continuous, and variegated.
When the suns and fires have increased in intensity, merged with one another,
and attained a state of oneness, they indeed become a single flame.
That fire, becoming a universal conflagration that destroys all worlds,
swiftly consumes this entire fourfold world with its brilliance.
Then, when all that is moving as well as stationary has dissolved,
the earth becomes devoid of trees and grass, resembling the back of a tortoise.
The entire world appeared like a frying pan;
it was all filled with those flames and blazed intensely.
Whatever beings exist on the surface of the earth and those who have gone into the great ocean,
they dissolve from there and return to the state of the earth.
The islands, the mountains, the regions, and the great ocean—
all that he, the fire whose self is everything, reduced to ashes.
Blazing and resting upon the earth, the kindled fire drinks up the waters from all sides— from the oceans, the rivers, and the netherworlds.
Then, having grown in strength and having transcended the mountains as well as the planets,
that blazing and terrible fire of universal destruction, Saṃvartaka, consumes the worlds.
Then, having split the earth, he dried up the subterranean realm (rasātala);
and after burning Pātāla, he then consumed the world of Vāyu.
Having burned the earth below, he swiftly burns the heavens above for thousands,
millions, and billions of yojanas.
Many crests of smoke rose from that Samvartaka fire,
carrying away Gandharvas, Piśācas, along with Mahoragas and Rākṣasas.
Then, blazing intensely, it burns the iron ball on all sides,
as well as the Bhūrloka, the Bhuvarloka, the Svarloka, and likewise the Maharloka.
The terrible fire of time thus burns the four worlds;
when those worlds have been pervaded by fire from below and above, [the dissolution proceeds].
Having reached that fire, this entire world gradually becomes like a glowing iron ball; indeed, it then shines forth in this manner.
Then, terrible clouds resembling herds of elephants, adorned with flashes of lightning, arise in the sky as the clouds of universal destruction (saṃvartaka).
Some are dark like the blue lotus, some resemble the white water-lily;
some are like beryl, and others resemble sapphire.
Others resemble conch shells or jasmine flowers, while others are like pure black collyrium;
some clouds are smoke-colored, and some are yellow.
Some clouds have the color of a donkey, others resemble liquid lac; some have the hue of realgar, and others are like the color of a pigeon.
Some clouds in the sky rise resembling indragopas, others like haritāla, and some like the wings of blue jays.
Some have the form of excellent cities, some resemble herds of elephants;
some are like mountains, and some clouds are like level ground.
Some resemble pleasure-pavilions, while others are like schools of fish;
they possess many forms and terrible shapes, resounding with fearsome cries.
Then all the clouds fill the expanse of the sky;
thereafter, those clouds, resounding with a terrible roar, become of the nature of the sun.
Having restrained themselves in seven ways, they extinguish that fire;
thereafter, those clouds release rain like a great flood.
They extinguish all that is most terrible and inauspicious, like a fire;
and likewise, the world is completely filled with water that has rained down excessively.
Then fire, overcome by water, enters the waters;
and when the fire has vanished, the clouds arise from the heat of that fire.
Flooding the entire world with vast outpourings of water,
they filled this universe with their torrents, impelled by the Self-Existent One.
Others, however, though they may even overcome the shoreline with floods of water,
the water swallowed by those [beings] remains within them, along with the mountains and other continents.
Again it falls from that ocean back into the sky;
the terrible-souled wind in the heavens envelops it on all sides.
When that terrible Ekārṇava has passed away, with all things stationary and moving destroyed,
and when a thousand yugas have indeed elapsed, it is called the kalpa without remainder.
Then, when the world was enveloped by water, the wise say it was a single ocean;
at that time, earth, water, space, and wind were all one within that ocean.
When the fire had perished and everything had become blind darkness, nothing at all could be discerned—
the terrestrial waters, the oceanic waters, and the divine waters in their entirety.
Flowing without ceasing and attaining oneness, they take on the name "water";
even when coming and going, that is what is traditionally known as water.
It covers this earth, and that water is called the ocean; because it shines with its own splendors, it is so named, for the word *bhās* denotes both pervasion and radiance.
Having pervaded everything as ashes, it is therefore called "Ambhas" (water);
and because of its manifoldness and its swiftness, the root "ara" is indeed said to denote it.
For at that time, because of that [destruction], those men were indeed not swift;
when that day of Brahmā, consisting of a thousand yugas, had passed.
For that same duration of time, the world remains thus as a single ocean;
at that time, all the activities of Prajāpati cease.
When that single ocean has arisen and all things mobile and immobile have perished,
he then becomes Brahmā, possessing a thousand eyes and a thousand feet.
The thousand-headed, benevolent one, with a thousand feet, a thousand eyes, a thousand faces, and a thousand voices;
the thousand-armed, primordial Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), who is declared to be the Puruṣa consisting of the three Vedas.
Ādityavarman, the protector of the world, is the unprecedented, sole, and first Turāṣāṭ;
he is indeed proclaimed as the Great Puruṣa, the Golden Embryo (Hiraṇyagarbha), beyond the realm of Rajas.
At the end of a thousand cycles of four yugas, when everything is submerged in water,
that Lord, desiring to sleep and seeking the absence of light, makes it night.
When all creatures have gone to their rest and lie down in a fourfold manner,
the seven great ṛṣis behold that high-souled Time.
Those who have attained the vision through austerity return to Janaloka.
The high-souled ones, Bhṛgu and the others, whose characteristics have been previously explained, [were born].
Indeed, they behold with their own eyes the seven worlds beginning with Satya;
moreover, during the nights of Brahmā, they constantly behold Brahmā himself.
The seven ṛṣis perceive this dream-time during their own nights;
because it is the supreme state of the kalpas, it is therefore recited as the primordial one.
He, the creator of all beings, having thus reposed within himself again and again at the beginnings of the kalpas, remains as Prajāpati.
Then, having withdrawn everything into himself, the one of great splendor who accomplishes all things dwells there for a night in the waters of the single ocean of darkness.
Then, when the end of the night had arrived, the Lord of Creatures, the Buddha,
being intent on the desire to create, again applied his mind toward emanation.
Thus, when Prajāpati had passed away and become tranquil in that world,
during that Brahma-period of dissolution which was indeed ordained for total restraint.
In that [state], the complete separation of beings from their bodies is indeed recorded;
thereafter, when all those elements have been consumed by the rays of the sun.
At that time, during that dissolution by water, among the foremost of the celestial sages and Manus,
all beings beginning with the Gandharvas and ending with the Piśācas [perished] in every respect.
At the beginning of the kalpa, those beings who had previously fallen into animal births or even into the hells, once they have been purified, indeed take recourse to human birth alone.
Then those [sins] also, having been burnt and shaken off entirely,
are cast into the water as long as the world remains submerged in the flood.
And when the night has dawned, all those beings are born again in their entirety from Brahmā, whose source is the unmanifest.
The seers, the Manus, the gods, and all four classes of progeny—
even for those perfected beings, birth and death are said to occur.
Just as the rising and setting of the sun are observed in this world,
so too are the birth and cessation of beings seen here.
Therefore, existence until the dissolution of all beings is called *saṃsāra*;
just as here all beings are born during the rains.
In every kalpa, the stationary beings and other creatures are likewise produced by necessity;
just as the various signs of the seasons appear in their cyclical succession.
Those very same [worlds] are seen in that manner during the days and nights of Brahmā;
they possess motion during the withdrawal [of the universe] and are fixed during its emission.
At the proper time, all beings enter and emerge from Prajāpati— Brahmā, the Great Lord, the supreme yogin.
He is the creator of all beings again and again at the beginnings of the kalpas;
he is both manifest and unmanifest, the Great God, and this entire world belongs to him.
By the very same path by which the waters were first released upon this earth, they now proceed;
just as they went before, so do the waters go back again by that very same way to heaven.
Just as they revolve here and there by means of both the auspicious and the inauspicious,
mortals, because their existence is conditioned by another body, move upward and downward by the power of the sun.
And those gods, Manus, lords of creatures, as well as other perfected ones (siddhas) who have gone to heaven— they,
being permeated by that [power] and subject to its renown, become beings endowed with dharma through a renewed creation.
Henceforth, O twice-born ones, I shall declare the duration of time until the dissolution of all beings, as well as those Manvantaras that have been explained by me.
Together with the creation of living beings and together with the fourteen gods, all those periods known as yugas indeed constitute one thousand [such cycles]. BndP 3.1.209.
Two thousand of these [days] are called a specific kalpa;
this is to be known as a day of Brahmā—learn its duration.
Indeed, fifteen human eye-winks are recorded as one *kāṣṭhā*, which is equal in measure to a single moment (*labda-kṣaṇa*) created by the Lord.
Nine *kṣaṇas* make one *pañca*; three of those [make] one *viṃśat-kāṣṭhā*.
Seven *prasthas* and seven *dakas* are known as one *lava*, which is slightly more than that.
Thirty *kalās* are to be known as one *muhūrta*, and thirty *muhūrtas* are again [one] day and night; such is the established rule.
In a day and night, there are six hundred and more *kalās*;
these should be understood according to their enumeration, as is the movement of the moon and the sun.
Fifteen nimeṣas constitute one kāṣṭhā; thirty such kāṣṭhās make one kalā;
thirty kalās make one muhūrta; and a kalā is said to be a tenth part of a muhūrta.
Forty kalās are designated as one muhūrta;
furthermore, muhūrtas and lavas have been defined by those who know the measures of time.
Likewise, thirteen palas of water,
according to the Magadhan measure alone, constitute one *prastha* of water.
These four sets of nālikās, with their bases submerged in water,
have apertures made by four gold māṣas and measure four finger-breadths [in diameter].
At both the junctions of day and night, there are indeed two *nālikās* for each *muhūrta*,
occurring constantly throughout all these periods due to the specific movement of the sun.

That which is prescribed as six hundred and ten *kalās* more [than a lunar day] should be known as the human solar day (*aharmānuṣa*), whereas the sidereal day (*nākṣatra*) is ten more [than a lunar day].
This human year, according to the solar (sāvana) measurement, is declared to be one day and night of the gods; such is the definitive conclusion of the scriptures.
But by means of calculation according to days, months, seasons, half-years, and years,
this knowledge is then bound and characterized by designations.
The measure of the *kalās* is designated as a *kalā*;
that which is declared to be a day of Brahmā is remembered as being ten million divine years.
And ten times two hundred thousand,
as well as ninety thousand, and furthermore those others which exist.
Having heard this, the sages were struck with supreme and most wonderful amazement; they then asked even more insistently about that knowledge which transcends all calculation.
The sages said:
"O Saṃprakālana, this measurement is indeed approved by humans;
we wish to hear it according to that measurement, with its essential meaning, its divisions, and its syllables."
Having heard them, that lord Vāyu, who is devoted to the welfare of the world,
spoke these words to them in brief by means of his divine vision.
These days and nights have been previously described here as belonging to the world of mortals;
now I shall declare their number and the total duration of the years at the end of a day of Brahmā.
Four hundred and thirty-two million years according to human reckoning have been calculated by the twice-born as the total number of years.
Likewise, there are ninety-one hundred thousand and eighty thousand years; this is the duration of the Plava [Manvantara].
Indeed, the period reckoned by human calculation lasts until the dissolution of all beings;
then, when those worlds have been consumed by the seven suns,
all four classes of living beings dissolve into the great elements.
When the world was flooded with water and all things, both stationary and moving, had perished.
When the dissolution has ceased and the Lord of Creatures has become tranquil, when all is without light and consumed, enveloped by the darkness of night; BndP_3.1.233.
When this single wheel was presided over by Īśvara,
it is said that the duration of that single wheel should be understood as lasting for as long as the day of the Lord.
The night is his state of abiding in water, and when that ceases, it is remembered as day;
thus his day and night revolve in succession.
For this period until the dissolution of all beings is recorded as a single day and night of the Lord;
it includes all beings within the three worlds, whether they possess motion or are stationary.
They dissolve back into the primary elements; therefore, it is called the dissolution of the elements (ābhūtasaṃplava).
This applies to all beings—those of the past, those of the present, and likewise those yet to come.
The divine number is calculated by multiplying the lower half (aparārdha) by itself;
the upper half (parārdha), when doubled, is proclaimed as the maximum lifespan.
Such indeed is the duration of the stay of the unborn Prajāpati here;
it includes the end of his stay and the re-creation of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin.
Just as the flame of a lamp is extinguished by the force of the wind,
even so Brahmā is completely pacified by the process of reabsorption.
Likewise, when Maheśvara is conjoined with his own [nature] in the form of Mahat and the rest, Mahat dissolves into the Manifest; from that, the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇasāmya) arises.
Thus has this dissolution of all beings been fully described to you by me;
for this is the occasional dissolution of Brahmā, a restraint that thoroughly cleanses.
It has been explained to you in brief; what more shall I tell you?
Whoever should constantly uphold this, or listen to it repeatedly,
or recite it, or even praise it, shall attain great accomplishment.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Dissolution of All Beings," in the fourth section (Upasaṃhārapāda) of the Uttara-bhāga of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
Vāyu said:
By people of uncommon conduct, such as those who subsist on the remnants of oblations (*huta-śeṣa*) and so forth, [the world is sustained].
And indeed, these specific dharmas have been practiced by those who perceive with subtle vision.
These inhabitants of Maharloka dwell together with the gods;
these fourteen Manus have been proclaimed, who increase one's renown.
Those who are past and those who are present, as well as those who are yet to come—
the gods, the sages, the Manus, and likewise the ancestors— [are all sustained by this].
"For all of them have been told by me to take refuge in Maharloka,
together with righteous Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras."
By those who act thus, who are disciplined, endowed with faith, free from pride,
and firmly established in the duties of their social classes and stages of life as prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti,
their authority ceases for as long as the duration of the Manvantara endures.
The sages said:
"O Mātariśvan, regarding that which was spoken by you, O Lord, concerning the Maharloka,"
"But what is established there that must be performed in the world?
To this, the knower of reality spoke these sweet words according to the truth: BndP_3.2.7 //
Vāyu said:
"Fourteen indeed are the places established by the great seers,
which are known as the worlds wherein human beings abide."
Among those, they say that seven were made and seven indeed were not made;
here, the seven worlds beginning with Bhūḥ and ending with Satya are said to be made.
Indeed, the seven uncreated primal abodes,
together with their inhabitants, constitute the foundation that has been fashioned.
The earth, the intermediate space, the celestial realm, and that which is known as the great (mahaḥ)—
these four abodes are recorded as being devoid of caste distinctions.
They say that those things which are produced by specific causes, being subject to decay and excellence,
remain as they are until the dissolution of all beings.
Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka—these are the three stages;
they remain exclusively here due to a lack of self-restraint.
I shall now declare these seven manifest abodes:
Bhūrloka is the first among them, and the second is known as Bhuvaḥ.
The third is to be known as Svarga, while the fourth is indeed remembered as Mahas;
Janas is the fifth world, and Tapas is considered the sixth.
The seventh world is Satya; beyond that is the lightless realm.
From the primordial utterance "Bhūḥ," the world of Bhūr (the Earth) subsequently came into being.
When "bhuvaḥ" was uttered for the second time, the intermediate space (antarikṣa) came into being;
when "svar" was uttered for the third time, heaven (div) indeed manifested.
By means of these three utterances, Brahmā fashioned the world:
from them, the earthly realm became *bhūḥ*, and the intermediate space was known as *bhūvaḥ*.
Indeed, he has gone to the heavenly world, to the sky; this is the certainty established in the Purāṇas.
And since Agni is the lord of beings (bhūta), he is therefore remembered as Bhūtapati.
Vāyu is the lord of the intermediate space (bhuvas), therefore Vāyu is the master of bhuvas;
Sūrya is the lord of heaven (div), therefore Sūrya is the master of heaven.
By the very expansion of Mahā, the Maharloka then came into being;
it is there that the gods whose offices have ceased reside.
Janas, however, is the fifth world; from it, indeed, people (janas) are born.
It is called Janas because of the birth of those progenies, beginning with the Svāyambhuva Manu.
Those who were previously proclaimed as beginning with Svāyambhuva—
when these kalpas are established in the world, then [this] austerity [occurs].
Or "Tapaḥ" refers to that place where the Ṛbhus, Sanatkumāra, and others—who are perpetual celibates (ūrdhvaretas) and whose selves have been purified by austerity—reside. Thus it is called Tapaḥ.
The word "Satya" is a term for Brahman, and it is remembered as pure existence;
therefore, the world of Brahman (Brahmaloka) is Satya, the seventh, and it is radiant.
The Gandharvas, Apsarases, Yakṣas, Guhyakas along with the Rākṣasas,
all the Bhūtas and Piśācas, the Nāgas, and humans as well.
All the gods dwelling in the heavenly world, those dwelling on earth,
the Maruts, the Mātariśvans, the Rudras, and likewise the two Aśvins.
Those who dwell in the sky have no fixed abode; they are the inhabitants of the *bhuvarloka*:
the Ādityas, the Ṛbhus, the Viśvedevas, the Sādhyas, and likewise the Pitṛs.
The sages, including those of the lineage of Aṅgiras, reside in the Bhuvarloka;
these are the gods who travel in celestial chariots (vaimānika) and dwell among the stars and planets.

But those who have passed away and taken refuge on earth—beginning with Śukra and ending with Cakṣus—are pure among themselves, undertaking [their activities] through their respective subtle elements (tanmātra). (Bṛhadbrahmapurāṇa 3.2.30)
Mahar-loka is the fourth; therein dwell those who live for the duration of a kalpa.
Thus have these been described in order, arising from the utterance of Brahmā.
The worlds beginning with Bhūrloka and ending with Maharloka are known as those;
all of them are indeed consumed by the rays of the seven suns.
Mārīci, Kaśyapa, Dakṣa, as well as Svāyambhuva, Aṅgiras,
Bhṛgu, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and others such as these.
All the lords of creatures dwell there together with them;
they are indeed devoid of worldly essence and free from the sense of "mine," for their vital energy is directed upwards.
R̥bhu, Sanatkumāra, and others who are Vairājas rich in asceticism,
are recorded as the [progenitors] of all the Sāvarṇa Manvantaras.
Furthermore, for all fourteen [classes of beings], the causes of rebirth are found by concentrating upon yoga, austerity, and goodness within one's own self.
At the sixth period, one returns; they say that by the opposite process, however, the seventh world belongs to those who do not go back on the path.
The Brahma-world is indeed declared to have the characteristic of being unimpeded;
the earthly world (bhūrloka) is traditionally held to be equal in extent to the surrounding boundary.
The intermediate region between the earth and the sun, which is the atmosphere, is known as *bhuvaḥ*;
and that which lies between the sun and the pole star is known as the heavenly world, *divaḥ*.
That which lies between Dhruva and Janaloka is called Maharloka.
Thus the seven worlds have been explained; now I shall describe their supernatural attainments (siddhis).
All those who dwell in the world of Bhūr are loud-voiced and consist of the essence of taste;
all those who are in the earth and in heaven are drinkers of Soma and drinkers of clarified butter.
Those who dwell in the fourth [realm], residing in Maharloka,
should be known as possessing mental accomplishment characterized by five features.
Immediately, everything desired by them arises through their minds;
these gods indeed worship one another with all kinds of sacrifices.
Those who are past, those who are present, and likewise those who are yet to come—
those previously mentioned as immediate, and again the intermediate ones along with the current ones.
For when the host of gods has passed away, their ascetic practice ceases;
however, for those whose offices have terminated, their mental perfection remains accomplished.
Among them, however, the pure accomplishment (siddhi) is to be known as arising from the mind through mutual interaction.
O Brahmins, I have briefly described to you these four worlds and likewise the conduct of their inhabitants; now I shall explain it to you further.
Vāyu said:
Marīci, Kaśyapa, Dakṣa, Vasiṣṭha, Aṅgiras, and Bhṛgu.
Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
and others like them were first born here as the mind-born sons of Brahmā.
Then, having established the creatures, they always take refuge in the source of beings during the conflagrations at the end of the kalpas and at those times.
When the great elements, beginning with earth, are intensely pervaded by fire,
those flames of the Saṃvartaka fire reach them along with their latent impressions (vāsanās).
All the hosts, beginning with the Yāmas, who dwell in Maharloka,
take refuge in Janaloka itself when the Maharlokas have been set ablaze.
They all possess subtle bodies and remain situated there;
they are equal in their capacities and likewise bear similar forms.
In Janaloka, the cycles of manifestation and dissolution revolve; at the dawn of Brahmā’s night, which originates from the unmanifest source, the world floats away.
At the beginning of the day, all the progenitors from Svāyambhuva down to Marīci were born here in succession, as before, acting as the means of accomplishment.
Indeed, those gods— Yama and the others— are born again here at the dissolutions [of the worlds] in due order, starting from the youngest of Prajāpati.
In the lineage of the gods, those who are remembered as the seven born deities were indeed produced first by the former and likewise last by the latter.
Of those, three kalpa-births have passed for them, and likewise others remain;
those gods are revolving in their entirety according to this sequence.
Having attained a state of extreme velocity again and again ten times over,
all those hosts, having perceived the impermanence of all conditioned things, [attained liberation].
And by the power of the destined event, as well as through the strength of their merit and renown,
all those residing there, being well-disposed, ceased their activities.
Having abandoned those worlds, they attain the Vairāja state;
thereafter, by this very time, the ascetics remain ever-disciplined.
And from the very narration of the Dharma, they were born into their lineage;
having been born here, they indeed fill their respective stations.
In the state of divinity, in the state of a seer, and in the state of humanity— in every way,
all the hosts of gods must thus return ten times.
Those who have been reborn among the Vairāja gods remain there for ten *upaplavas*; then, after staying for a full and complete *kalpa* among the Vairājikas, they [depart].
They evolve in the world of Brahmā according to a sequence of preceding stages;
indeed, when this kalpa of the Vairāja Brahmā-world has passed, [they proceed further].
Furthermore, Vairāja ordained the duration of the kalpa within the unmanifest;
thus, indeed, in the aforementioned sequence, it was established by him who had reached the world of Brahmā.
They are reborn among the Vairāja gods and return ten times;
in this manner, thousands of divine ages have passed here.
But as for those who have attained their final end in the world of Brahmā together with the ṛṣis,
it is not possible to describe their detailed sequence in full.
Because time is beginningless and because it is entirely incalculable, this is exactly as I have described it; of this there is no doubt.
Having heard the meaning of those words, the sages, filled with doubt,
spoke to Sūta, the knower of the Purāṇas, the high-minded disciple of Vyāsa.
The sages said: "Tell us truly what their food was, what their nature was, and what their support was; for how long they remained, and who those Vairājas were."
Having heard those words spoken by the sages, Sūta, the narrator of the Purāṇas, who knew the true nature of the world's purpose, spoke these words with humility: BndP_3.2.71.
Then, having attained the Lord of All, he took refuge in Him whose intellect is pure;
there they remain, free from fever, for ten periods until the dissolution of all beings.
All those wise ones possess subtle bodies and are of solid form;
because they abide within the established order of the world, no [gross] element exists for them.
The Siddhas, Sanatkumāra and the others, who follow the path of yoga, spoke thus:
"O highly fortunate ones, it is exactly so; having fully entered the Praṇava."
"Let us proceed to the world of Brahmā; that will be for our ultimate welfare.
Having spoken thus, they all then resolved upon the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
Having performed sacrifices, those who follow the path of yoga abide as the Self;
they dissolve right there, becoming tranquil like the flames of a lamp.
Having reached that world consisting of meditative cultivation, they all proceeded to the realm of Brahmā, from which a return to this world is difficult to obtain.
Having attained the bliss of Brahman, they have gone to immortality; likewise, from the Vairāja worlds, they proceed upward through the intermediate region of sixfold qualities.
The Brahma-world is fully described as that place where Brahmā resides as the presiding priest;
all those beings there abide with their intellects purified, being essentially of the nature of the Praṇava.
Having attained the bliss of Brahman, they indeed partake in immortality; freed from the three states of existence, they are no longer overcome by the pairs of opposites.
Without exercising sovereign authority, those Brahmās of great majesty were equal to you in their manifestation of power,
victory, sovereignty, stability, dispassion, and insight.
All those inhabitants of the Brahma-world, having attained a state from which there is no returning, shall,
together with Brahmā and the gods, reach the time of universal dissolution.
At the conclusion of their asceticism, those wise ones whose nature is action and who perceive the moment all dissolve into the unmanifest within the state of the intellect.
This is the immortal, pure, eternal, and inexhaustible Brahmasatra; the celestial sages worship this as the eternal sacrifice.
The faith of those such as Apunarbhava and others who have drawn their vital energy upward, and which is produced by the practice of karma, is observed in the Vedānta texts.
There, those practitioners, disciplined and devoted, reach the highest goal;
having abandoned the body and all evil, they go to immortality.
Free from passion, having conquered anger, devoid of delusion, speakers of truth, peaceful, self-controlled, compassionate, and masters of their senses; BndP_3.2.87.
Those heroes who are free from attachment and pure, whose sins have been burnt away by austerities performed without desire, are remembered as those who attain union with Brahman.
For them, the worlds are remembered as unfailing and of immeasurable bliss;
this is the divine station of Brahmā, radiant in the supreme ether,
where having gone, the immortals do not grieve along with Brahmā.
The sages said:
"Why is this called *parārdha*, and what indeed is meant by 'the beyond' (*para*)? We wish to know this; O best of beings, explain it to us."
Sūta said:
Listen to me regarding the calculation of a parārdha and that which is beyond it.
One, ten, and a hundred, as well as a thousand, should be understood according to their numerical sequence; indeed, up to a thousand, ten thousands are called an ayuta.
One hundred thousand is called a *niyuta* by the wise;
likewise, ten hundred thousands are called a *prayuta*.
Likewise, ten thousand is called an ayuta, and ten million is called a koṭi;
ten koṭis are known as an arbuda, and one hundred koṭis as an abja.
The wise say that a thousand times ten million is a *kharva*;
they know that ten thousand times ten million is a *nikharva*.
A hundred thousand times ten million is called a *śaṅku*;
a thousand times ten million is called a *padma*.
Those who know calculation say that ten times a thousand million multiplied by a thousand is indeed what they call the "ocean" (samudra).
A thousand times ten million (koṭīsahasra) is called the last (antya);
a thousand times ten million times ten million (koṭīsahasraprayuta) is designated as the middle (madhya).
A thousand times ten million koṭis is proclaimed to be a parārddha;
the wise say that twice a parārddha is the supreme (parama).
They say that a hundred is called *parivṛḍha*, a thousand is *paripadmaka*; from that, ten thousand (*ayuta*) is to be known, then *niyuta* and *prayuta*.
Arbuda, nyarbuda, and then kharbuda are recorded;
likewise kharva, nikharva, śaṅku, and padma.
The ocean, the end, the middle, the parārdha, and beyond that;
thus, these eighteen places are [enumerated] in the method of calculation.
One should know that hundreds and so forth are designated by the great seers;
the period beginning from the calculation of the Kalpas is recorded as the Parārdha, which belongs to Brahmā.
The remainder of his time lasts until the end of that;
it is reckoned by me as the supreme *parārdha* in terms of number.
For his supreme vigor, supreme lifespan, supreme austerity,
supreme power, supreme dharma, supreme knowledge, and supreme fortitude are all unsurpassed.
It is the supreme Brahman, the supreme knowledge, and indeed supreme sovereignty;
there exists no being higher than that which is beyond Brahman.

For this "other" (para) stands beyond all things; therefore it is reckoned as the "supreme" (param). Brahmā is counted as the "supreme" (para), while half of that constitutes the "supreme-half" (parārddha).
The calculable, the incalculable, and that which is constant according to the Tantras— the calculable is seen through calculation and is explained as being up to the Aparārddha.

When a heap is perceived, there is no [fixed] number; therefore, let that which is uncountable be subtle. Infinity is seen in things such as grains of sand, while another [aspect] is characterized by the absence of defining marks.
That enumeration was performed by the lords, who possess divine vision due to their purity;
thus, being established in knowledge, one perceives everything as Brahman.
Having heard this, all those ascetics of Naimiṣa,
their eyes clouded with tears and their voices faltering with joy, spoke.
All those exponents of Brahman questioned Mātariśvan: "O Blessed One, O Lord, at what distance does the world of Brahman lie? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Purāṇa 3.2.112)
We wish to hear in truth the calculation of the yojana, the means for measuring a yojana, and the exact dimension of a krośa.
Having heard those words of theirs, Mātariśvan spoke sweetly and with humility, exactly as he had seen it and in proper sequence.
Vāyu said:
I shall declare this to you; listen to what I wish to say.
From the unmanifest (avyakta), the manifest portion indeed—the Great One (mahat)—is described as gross.
The tenfold portion of the Mahat is called the gross Bhūtādi;
its magnitude is also ten times greater than that of the Bhūtādi.
The atom is exceedingly subtle, perceivable by the intellect but not by the eye;
it is that which is most indivisible in the world and should be understood as being like the atom.
That subtle particle of dust which is seen when light passes through a lattice is declared to be the first of all measures of magnitude, the atom (*paramāṇu*).
When there is a combination of eight atoms (paramāṇu), it is designated as a mote of dust (trasareṇu); that is called a lotus-pollen particle (padmarajas).
Furthermore, eight *trasareṇus* are traditionally held to constitute one *rathareṇu*;
and when eight of those are brought together, that is known by the wise as a *bālāgra*.
Eight hair-tips (bālāgra) make one louse-egg (likṣā); eight louse-eggs make one louse (yūkā);
eight lice are said to be a barley-corn (yava), and eight barley-corns make one finger-breadth (aṅgula).
Twelve finger-joints are said to be the measure of a *vitasti*;
a *ratni* should be understood as twenty-one finger-joints.
Four cubits (hasta) shall consist of twenty finger-breadths (aṅgula);
a fathom (kiṣku) is to be known as two ratnis, consisting of forty-two finger-breadths.
The wise say that a bow is ninety-six finger-breadths (aṅgulas) long;
this is recorded as the measure of a bow for the calculation of a gavyūti.
A bow-staff pair (dhanur-daṇḍa-yuga) and a nālī are equal when measured by those same finger-breadths;
people who know the reckonings say that three hundred bows constitute a nalva.
Two thousand bows are taught to be one *gavyūti*,
while eight thousand bows are prescribed as one *yojana*.
By this bow alone, one *yojana* is completed;
likewise, a thousand of these should be known as the distance between the treasuries of Śakra.
Listen now to the measurement of Brahmā’s interval according to this unit of the yojana, as calculated by those expert in the knowledge of numbers.
The sun is situated one thousand yojanas above the surface of the earth;
and the moon is one hundred and one thousand yojanas above the sun.
The entire circle of the lunar mansions shines above the moon at a full hundred thousand yojanas.
A hundred thousand is reckoned as this [unit], and doubled again;
