They call the unmanifest the field (*kṣetra*), and Brahman is called the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*).
Their union, produced by similarity and dissimilarity, is without beginning.

Thus, O Brahmins, it should be understood here among the individual souls (kṣetrajñas) in their various creations; and the knower of Brahman (brahmavit) should likewise be understood as distinct from the individual souls.
The state of being an object and not an object is traditionally taught for the field and the knower of the field;
however, Brahman is to be known as the non-object, while the field is said to be the object.
They declare that the field is presided over by the Knower of the Field for the sake of the Knower of the Field;
and because of the multiplicity of bodies, the embodied one is traditionally remembered as being manifold.
And because it is without configuration or confusion, the light that is established [therein] is such that,
indeed, for every individual body, there is the experience of pleasure and pain.
Therefore, the plurality of puruṣas must be understood by one who possesses discernment,
as well as the restraint of these various distinctions when they come into operation.
Then, after a long period of time, all those self-existent ones (svayaṃbhū),
who remained possessed of passion, returned to their natural state.
Together with all those inhabitants of the world of Brahmā who possess the state of union (sāyujya),
there occurred then the cessation [of rebirth] for those who abide within the Self.
Then, among those inhabitants living at that time who perceived faults therein,
there arose a detachment that destroys the doctrine of the self.

Because they perceive those [objects] as being of the nature of the eaten and the eater, through their diversity, those knowers of the field (kṣetrajña) possess distinct knowledge; therefore, they belong to the world of Brahman.

Having transcended the cause within primordial nature (*prakṛti*), all those who perceive diversity abide solely within their own self, characterized by perfect tranquility and the cessation of perception.
All beings, both sentient and insentient, are pure and stainless;
they are known as non-returners who attain final nirvana right there. (BndP 3.2.311)

"Because they are devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) and because of the transcendence of nature at the end of Prakṛti, the Selfs are thus described by the Self-born One as the Prākṛta-pratisarga (the elemental re-creation). [Bṛhadbrahmapurāṇa 3.2.312]
He who, endowed with the conduct of his caste and stage of life, listens to this account of the secondary creation,
shall go to the realm of Śiva, possessed of devotion and free from all affliction.

And that Śūdra who abstains from intoxicants, is devoted to Bhava, has conquered his senses, remains until the dissolution of all beings, and is characterized by non-obstruction; [he attains this state].
He attains the station of the Gaṇas, or a permanent place;
the drinker of liquor rejoices together with other drinkers and hosts of spirits.
"Worshipped upon the surface of the earth, may you become the granter of boons to mortals"—
thus spoke the Blessed Vāyu, offering this boon.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Description of the Supreme City of Śiva," in the fourth section (Upasaṃhārapāda) of the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa, as narrated by Vāyu.
Sūta said:
I shall now describe the withdrawal [of the senses] at the end of the supreme Self-born One.
But when the period of Brahmā’s maintenance has expired, O Lord, at that time...
Just as the Lord clearly manifests this subtle universe,
so too does He swallow the manifest entirely within the unmanifest during the process of withdrawal.

Formerly, when the complete dissolution of the eon had arrived— terrible, great, and indeed imperceptible to anyone— the world-systems, from the dyads (dvyaṇuka) up to the ends of the universe, [were destroyed].
When the end of that Manu, the western one,
has arrived at the conclusion of the Kali Yuga, and that age has perished, it is called the dissolution (saṃhāra).
When that thorough cleansing has occurred and withdrawal (pratyāhāra) has indeed been established,
then, during that withdrawal, there is the dissolution of the elements and the subtle elements (tanmātras).
When that dissolution has set in, brought about by its own nature, there occurs the withdrawal of all transformations beginning with the Mahat and ending with the specific elements.
First, the waters swallow the essence of the earth, which consists of its fragrance;
once its fragrance has been taken away, the earth is then prepared for dissolution.
When the subtle element of smell has perished, the earth becomes the state of water;
then the waters enter it, impetuous and making a great roar.
Having filled all this, they remain and move about;
even that collection of waters, which is their essence, dissolves into the lights.
Then the waters perish there due to the dissolution of the subtle element of taste (rasa-tanmātra);
moreover, their essence being extracted by intense heat, they attain the state of light.
When the water has been swallowed, one perceives fire facing in all directions;
then the fire, having pervaded everything, absorbs that water.
Then this entire world is gradually filled with flames;
when that [fire] has become continuous with its rays extending sideways, upwards, and downwards, BndP 3.3.12.
The wind consumes even the quality of light, its illuminating form;
then it dissolves into that [wind], like the flame of a lamp in a gale.
When the subtle element of form has perished, the fire, deprived of its form, is extinguished;
for the great wind then blows away the heat.
Then, when the world was without light and fire had become wind,
that wind, having reached its own source, [established] its connection with itself.
Moving upward, downward, and across, it agitates the ten directions;
and that ether swallows even the quality of wind, which is touch.
Then the wind becomes stilled, while space remains uncovered—
formless, without taste, touch, or smell, and devoid of material substance.
Filling everything with its sounds, that [ether] shines forth most greatly;
when that has dissolved, what remains is space characterized by sound.
That ether, consisting of sound alone, remains pervading everything;
there, the first of the elements (earth) again devours its subtle sound.
When the elements and the senses have indeed become established simultaneously in the "origin of the elements" (bhūtādi),
this [state] consisting of self-conceit is known as the tamasic origin of the elements.
The Great One, characterized by the intellect, indeed devours even the origin of the elements;
that Great Self is to be known as the faculty of conceptualization and the faculty of determination.
Those who contemplate reality call him by synonymous terms: intellect (buddhi), mind (manas), the subtle body (liṅga), the great one (mahat), and the imperishable (akṣara). BndP 3.3.22.
When the elements have completely dissolved and the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇasāmya) has arisen, then the Great One (mahat) dissolves;
but the equilibrium of the qualities remains established in its own self alone.
All the causal principles of all beings dissolve during the final union;
such is this restraint of the principles together with their causes.
For this is known as the restraint of the principles (tattva-prasaṃyama), O twice-born ones, which causes one to return;
it includes both merit and demerit, austerity and knowledge, as well as the auspicious, truth, and falsehood.
For existence above and existence below, pleasure and pain, the agreeable and the disagreeable—
all this is established within phenomenal expansion (prapañca) and is known to consist of the mere qualities (guṇa).
And for those wise ones who are then devoid of senses, whatever merit and demerit they possess—
all that merit and sin remains established within their own nature (prakṛti).
That very state which belongs to embodied beings is described as being established in the primordial nature (prakṛti) through the merit and demerit of living creatures.
Living beings, through those very merits and demerits situated within their respective states,
again join themselves to bodies, perceiving them as "other" in exactly the same manner.
Both dharma and adharma consist essentially of the gunas;
through their respective causes, they are accumulated here by living beings as the body.
The conscious qualities, presided over by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña),
dissolve during both creation and re-absorption, as do living beings in the cycle of transmigration.
They are joined together, separated, and they move about by means of causes—
the fluctuations (vṛttis) which are indeed rajasic, tamasic, and sattvic.
The constituent qualities (guṇas) proceed in three ways under the superintendence of the Puruṣa:
Sattva consists of the upward region, and Tamas consists of the downward part.
Among these two, rajas is that which impels one forward and causes one to revolve right here;
thus do the three qualities consisting of the mind revolve.
Among all beings in the worlds, that should not be done by one who understands;
for it is through the condition of ignorance that undertakings are initiated by human beings.
These three states are traditionally held to be both auspicious and of the nature of evil;
due to the overwhelming power of darkness (tamas), a living being does not perceive reality as it truly is.
Then, because of not seeing reality, he is subsequently bound in various ways by both the material (prākṛta) bond and the non-transformative (avaikārika) bond.
Bound by sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) through the third [bond], one revolves excessively;
thus these three bonds have been declared to have ignorance as their cause.
The perception of permanence in the impermanent, the viewing of pleasure in suffering, the notion of "mine" in what is not mine, and the conviction of purity in the impure.
For those in whom these defects of mind and defects of knowledge have ceased through the reversal [of ignorance],
and in whom passion and hatred have subsided— that is declared to be true knowledge.
Ignorance is the dense darkness; passion is the fruit of the two types of action;
and from action arises the body, which again gives rise to great suffering. (BndP 3.3.41)
Born of the ear, born of the eye, and likewise born of the skin, the tongue, and the nose—
this thirst, which causes rebirth, arises from suffering through one's own karma.
The fool, possessed of craving, is overcome by the fruits of his own actions;
like a ball of sesame paste, the living being rolls back and forth right there.
Therefore, ignorance is taught to be the root of all misfortunes;
having identified that as the sole enemy, one should apply effort toward knowledge.
For through knowledge one abandons everything; through renunciation the intellect becomes dispassionate;
through dispassion one is purified, and being pure, one is liberated by means of *sattva*.
Henceforth, I shall describe passion, which carries away living beings;
for one whose self is not under control, there arises an attachment to sense objects through the practice of yoga.
The undesirable, the desirable, displeasure, pleasure, distress, and despondency;
likewise, there is no torment upon encountering suffering, nor is there the recollection of past happiness.
Thus, this attachment to sense objects is traditionally held to be the cause of rebirth within this material world of beings,
from Brahmā down to the stationary entities.
Therefore, one should avoid ignorance which is preceded by ignorance;
likewise, for one for whom the teachings of the sages and the conduct of the learned are not authoritative, [there is no dharma].
That which is contrary to the castes and stages of life, and which opposes the teachings of the learned,
is indeed the cause for falling into hell and the womb of animals.
And the cause for being born as an animal is said to be that very same [cause];
it is threefold in the place of torment and sixfold in the animal realm.
Obstruction occurs in every respect toward both causes and objects;
all that which consists of obstruction is traditionally known as lack of sovereignty (anaiśvarya).
Thus, this fourfold tamasic state of the elements and so forth is shown according to their respective natures, as the mind consists of nothing but the quality of sattva.
And by seeing the principles (tattvas) according to their true nature through the vision of reality,
this diversity between the individual soul (sattva) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña)— this is the perception of manifold objects.
The perception of multiplicity is ignorance; from knowledge, indeed, yoga is said to arise.
By that [ignorance] the bound is bound, and by that [knowledge] the liberated is released.
When transmigration has ceased, the one who is liberated is released from the subtle body (liṅga);
indeed, being free from all connection and devoid of sentience, he abides solely in his own self.
And even while abiding in one's own self, one is depicted by the name Virūpa;
thus has this characteristic of knowledge and liberation been declared in brief.
And that liberation has been declared to be threefold by those who perceive the truth:
first, through separation by means of knowledge; second, through the destruction of passion.
The third [cause] is the destruction of craving; thus the cause of liberation has been explained.
Due to the absence of the subtle body (liṅga), there is absolute isolation (kaivalya); and due to absolute isolation, there is the stainless state.
Because it is stainless, it is pure; indeed, nothing else exists that is more so. Hereafter, I shall explain dispassion through the perception of defects.
Regarding both divine and human objects of experience, which possess five characteristics,
one should cultivate neither aversion nor attachment by perceiving their defects.
One should completely avoid the effects of heat, passion, and despondency;
thus, having established himself in dispassion, the embodied being should become free from the sense of "mine."
And having reflected with the understanding that [the world] is impermanent, inauspicious, and suffering, one should,
through extreme concentration, purify the instrument of action belonging to the being.
For one whose impurities have been fully ripened perceives all defects;
thus, at the time of departure, he is likewise [afflicted] by those defects and their attendant signs.
The heat, provoked within the body and impelled by a violent wind,
takes hold of the body and indeed obstructs all the humors.
For, piercing the seats of the vital breaths and cutting through the vital points (marmans),
the wind, provoked by cold, then ascends and departs from above.
And this very [Self] resides in the vital locations of all beings, while knowledge remains contracted and actions are fully engaged. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.3.67)
That living soul, presiding over the navel by means of its own previously performed actions,
indeed causes the eightfold functional activity to cease once again.
Abandoning the body at the end, one then becomes breathless;
thus, being deprived of the vital breaths, one is designated as "dead."
Just as in this world, when one is being led here and there in a dream, that which provides delight belongs to the one who is subject to it; no other such thing exists for you.
The third is the destruction of thirst; thus has been explained the characteristic of liberation.
Indeed, it is the perception of defects in the fivefold objects, beginning with sound.
Absence of aversion, absence of attachment, and the avoidance of joy and distress—
these are indeed the causes of detachment and of the dissolution of the constituent elements.
The eight primary natures (prakṛtis) should be known in their previously mentioned order;
those beginning with the Unmanifest (avyakta) and ending with the elements (bhūta) are to be understood as the manifestations of Prakṛti.
One who is endowed with the conduct of their caste and stage of life, who is disciplined, and who does not contradict the scriptures—
this is the dharma of the castes and stages of life, which is the cause for attaining the abodes of the gods.

The deities occupy eight stations beginning with Brahmā and ending with the Piśācas; for sovereignty, consisting of the powers such as aṇimā and the rest, is indeed the cause characterized by these eight qualities.
When the sign is perceived as non-obstructive and characterized by sound and so forth,
these eight forms are the primordial ones, in their respective order.
But those whose nature consists solely of the qualities (guṇas) become attached to the knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas),
just as those with eyes see individual clouds during the rainy season.
Siddhas of such a kind perceive with their divine eye a living being eating food and drink, as well as entering into various wombs.
Even as it runs horizontally, upwards, and downwards in due order,
the fourfold group consisting of the individual soul (jīva), the vital breath (prāṇa), the subtle body (liṅga), and the instruments (karaṇa) [proceeds].
He is designated by synonymous words that have a single meaning;
this one, whose measure is both manifest and unmanifest, indeed experiences everything in its entirety.
Having understood that which ends with the grace of the Unmanifest and is presided over by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña),
one becomes pure and is indeed liberated through knowledge.
When the reality of the principles has been lost through the vision of the true nature of those principles,
one attains complete nirvāṇa at will once the body has perished and one is fully at peace.
Furthermore, for the knower of the Unmanifest, the instrument of action is also dissolved;
thus, he is liberated from the body of the qualities (guṇas) and from everything beginning with the vital breath.
Just as a sprout does not arise when the seed is burnt, so the knower does not take on another body—
whether physical or mental— belonging to the cycle of worldly existence.
Through knowledge, the unenlightened one who abides in primordial nature (prakṛti) turns away from it;
they say that primordial nature is truth, while modification (vikāra) is called falsehood.
Non-existence is to be known as the unreal, while existence is called the real;
that which is without name and form is designated as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) with name and form.
Because it discerns the field, it is called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña);
because it perceives the field, the Knower of the Field is called auspicious.
Therefore, the Knower of the Field is remembered as such by those who know it;
the Field is described by them as that which consists of your [objective] perceptions, while the Knower of the Field is always the perceiver.

Those who know the field understand it as "kṣetra" because of its destruction (kṣapaṇa), its causality (kāraṇa), its protection from injury (kṣatatrāṇa), and its being the object of enjoyment (bhojyatva).

That which begins with the Great Principle (mahat) and ends with the specific elements (viśeṣa), possessing all forms and characterized by differentiation— that indeed is the Imperishable (akṣara), yet it is said to become the Perishable (kṣara).
Because it indeed flows forth again following that very transformation,
for that reason it is called *jara*.
Because it protects a person from cyclic existence and from the hells,
and because it provides refuge from suffering, it is further designated as a "field" (kṣetra).
Because it possesses the nature of pleasure, pain, and egoism, it is called the "enjoyer";
because it is insentient, the object is its opposite, and is known as the all-pervading Lord.
It does not perish nor does it decay, yet it is extended through transformation; for that reason it is called "akṣara" (the imperishable), and likewise because of its state of being undecayed.
Because he dwells within the city [of the body], he is called *puruṣa*;
because he is perceived as being within the city, he is designated as *puruṣa*.
Now speak of the Puruṣa; he who has been thus described is spoken of by the ignorant as follows:
"He is pure, appearing like the stainless [ether], the knower, yet devoid of knowledge. (BndP 3.3.96)
Whether it be "it exists" or "it does not exist," whether it be another, or bound, liberated, moving, or stationary—
none of these are found therein, because that which is without cause is inexpressible.
Because it is pure, it is indeed not an object of sight; because it is the seer, it possesses equal vision. It acts through self-realization, being neither deficient nor causeless.
Contemplating that which is to be grasped through its existence by means of inference, the knower is not deluded when he perceives the Knower as the peaceful reality whose nature is vision.
Then that which is to be designated among both the visible and the invisible is the unsurpassable, difficult-to-sustain Supreme;
the Knower is not perceived here as something separate in any way whatsoever.
In that same way, the causal self restrains the self by means of its own nature;
it abides right there within its own self, in the causal primordial matter.
Whether it be "it exists" or "it does not exist," or again "here" or "there," or whether it be unity or diversity, or even the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) or the person (*puruṣa*).

Whether it be a self or indeed selfless, whether conscious or even unconscious, whether it be an agent or even a non-agent, or whether it be an enjoyer or even that which is to be enjoyed. (BndP 3.3.103)
Having gone to which the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), stainless and ineffable—because it cannot be described—it does not return; it is ungraspable by means of logical arguments.
It is beyond reasoning because it is inconceivable and entirely beyond verbal expression; it is the reality that cannot be spoken with words nor reached by the mind.
When the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) has become free from qualities, pure, tranquil, diminished, stainless, devoid of pleasure and pain, restrained, and has attained peace; BndP_3,3.106 //
Furthermore, since that [reality] is devoid of self, there exists neither the expressible nor the inexpressible;
from that [reality], moreover, arise these two: withdrawal and expansion, as well as the manifest and the unmanifest.
It is emitted and indeed swallowed; it abides in manifestation.
Governed by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), everything proceeds once again toward creation.
One should attain the presiding ground at its conclusion through conscious effort;
the conjunction between those two, produced by similarity and dissimilarity,
is known to be beginningless and is remembered as arising from the Great Puruṣa.
For as long as the period of creation and re-absorption lasts, the world remains withdrawn within Him;
for previously, it was set in motion by His very conscious will solely for the sake of the Puruṣa’s purpose.

This [nature], preceded by primary creation and secondary dissolution, whether originating from primordial matter or brought about by the Lord, is indeed beginningless and endless; preceded by self-conceit, it approaches the world, causing it to tremble with fear.
Thus has been described this third, primordial creation, characterized by its cause;
indeed, by knowing that within this [creation], one is ultimately liberated from time.
Thus has this secondary dissolution (pratisarga) of the three worlds been recounted by me in detail and in its proper sequence; what more shall I relate?
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Secondary Creation," in the fourth section on the Conclusion of the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa* as proclaimed by Vāyu.
The sages said:
"We have heard this very great narrative recounted by you."
Together with the Manus for the sake of the subjects, and together with the gods and the ṛṣis.
Of the ancestors, Gandharvas, and spirits; of the Piśācas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas;
of the Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, and even of the birds.
Most wonderful deeds, various certainties regarding the Dharma,
diverse applications of narratives, and a foremost, unsurpassed birth.
O Sauti, as you relate this to us in gentle words,
it gladdens our minds and ears like nectar, providing such pleasure.
Having thus gratified the Sūta and honored him, all those great ṛṣis engaged in sacrificial sessions asked once more about the process of creation.
O son of great wisdom, how will creation proceed again when all bonds have dissolved and the qualities are in equilibrium within the state of darkness?
For when the transformations have not been emitted and the unmanifest Self remains established,
one is then suddenly united with Brahman through the yoga of non-engagement.
"How will creation come into being? Tell that to us who ask you.
Thus addressed, the Sūta Lomaharṣaṇa then spoke.
He began once more to explain the process of creation:
"In this regard, I shall describe to you how the creation will proceed."
That [inference] should be understood as being like the previous [perception]; learn it from me in brief.
I shall now explain reasoning (tarka) based on logic, consisting of both the perceived and the inferable.
Because words turn back from it along with the mind, having failed to reach it— being as unmanifest, beyond perception, profound, and difficult to attain.
Intermingled with its modifications, the *guṇa* exists in a state of equilibrium;
and the *pradhāna* abides in a state of similarity with the *puruṣas*.
For the dharma and adharma of living beings always dissolve into the unmanifest;
dharma, which consists of the essence of pure being (sattva), is established in the quality of goodness (sattva).
The dharma whose essence consists solely of darkness resides in the quality of darkness;
for as long as these two remain in the equilibrium of the qualities, they both abide in an undifferentiated state.
Every action of Pradhāna will proceed with intelligence as its precursor;
the Kṣetrajña will preside over those Guṇas with intelligence as its precursor.
Thus, through such conceit, he will again fall into that state when the two—
the field and the knower of the field— must once more be set in motion.
And both of them will attain the relationship of the enjoyed and the enjoyer;
therefore, the unmanifest Imperishable, consisting of the qualities, remains in a state of equilibrium.
Presided over by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), that [Prakṛti] indeed undergoes differentiation;
from that, the manifestation of both the Field and the Knower of the Field will clearly emerge.

Presided over by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the primary matter (sattva) will produce the transformation consisting of twenty-four qualities, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣa).
For the sake of favoring primordial matter (pradhāna), the Primordial God gazes upon the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the Puruṣa who is about to set forth.
The two origins are without beginning and are both considered subtle;
they are joined with an eternal union, as is the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) itself.
Then, when [the gods] were powerless, two boons were granted that were not preceded by conscious intent:
one was infallible and the other was unfailing, both remaining as constant as water and fish.
Those two, having previously engaged in activity, will again attain everything;
the ignorant are set in motion by the qualities known as rajas, sattva, and tamas.

At the time of manifestation, one who is overcome by *rajas* attains the state of the Great Principle (*mahat*), the primary elements, and the specific objects; through the medicinal herbs that are the ultimate limit of the *guṇas*, a human being reaches the state of the specific objects and the sense organs.
For that meditator who speaks the truth, the qualities of passion (rajas),
goodness (sattva), and darkness (tamas)— which are mutually opposed— become manifest through their respective causes.
Indeed, from beginning to end, they shall wander everywhere through the field of ignorance;
having accomplished their tasks, those possessed of self-conceit are born again.
Indeed, all beings emerge from the Unmanifest even before creation;
those who were previously carriers of life, whether they be effective practitioners or ineffective ones.
But all those who are not fully pacified, along with their stations and activities,
will undertake their tasks and arise again and again.
Dharma and adharma, consisting solely of the qualities (guṇas),
indeed initiate each other either through mutual impulsion or through favor.
At the beginning of creation, Śarva undergoes transformation for the sake of equalizing the emission;
the qualities (guṇas) are directed toward him, and therefore that [emission] is pleasing to him.
Whatever actions those qualities acquired in a previous creation,
those very same they undertake again and again as they are being created.

Violent or non-violent, gentle or cruel, righteous or unrighteous, truthful or false—impregnated by those very qualities, beings enter [into new births]; therefore, that which accords with their own nature is what pleases them.
The diversity among the great elements, among the objects of the senses, and among material forms,
as well as the separation of the elements from their qualities, proceeds [from this].
Thus has this secondary creation been recounted to you by me in brief;
now I shall describe the origin of Brahmā in summary as well.
From that unmanifest cause, which is eternal and consists of both the existent and the non-existent,
Maheśvara is born from Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
Furthermore, he is born as the creator known as Brahmā;
he then creates the worlds, which consist of the qualities characterized by egoism.
From that Great Principle (mahat) arises the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and from that, the elements and the senses proceed simultaneously from the Self; indeed, the elements and the senses emerge at once.
The creation proceeds from the elements and from the divisions of the elements;
their detailed components shall be proclaimed to you according to my knowledge and as I have heard it, just as before— let it be understood in that very same way.
Having heard this— concerning the origin of the world, its stable maintenance, and its dissolution— the sages of Naimiṣa,
having attained the purificatory bath at that sacrifice, became pure and reached the meritorious world.
Just as you, having performed the sacrifices to the gods and others according to the prescribed rites and having reached the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), are purified;
so too, at the end of your lives, having cast off your bodies and accomplished your purpose, you shall reach the world of merit and rejoice.
Having seen and touched him at that time, all those residents of Naimiṣa who were performing the sacrificial session departed for heaven, having performed their ritual ablutions.
Likewise, you brahmins as well, having sacrificed with many kinds of sacrifices,
shall go to heaven at the end of your lives, O best of the twice-born.

The first quarter is the *prakriyā* (the formal exposition), while the *kathā* (the narrative) consists of the *parigraha* (the introduction), the *anuṣaṅga* (the incidental discussion), the *upoddhāta* (the preliminary statement), and the *upasaṃhāra* (the conclusion).
In this very way, the venerable one, who is devoted to the welfare of the world of Vāyu, spoke directly of the ancient Purāṇa consisting of four quarters, which is esteemed by the world.
O best of sages, having performed a sacrificial session at Naimiṣa for the sake of the sages,
you have attained that grace which is fully perfected and endowed with the origin and dissolution of all beings.
Having correctly understood this creation as proceeding from primordial matter (pradhāna) and likewise as being brought about by the Lord (Īśvara),
the wise man does not fall into delusion.
The Brahmin who, being learned, hears this ancient history, or causes it to be heard, or likewise teaches it; ||| BndP_3.4.47 |||
In the abodes of Mahendra, he rejoices for eternal years;
having attained union with Brahman, he rejoices together with Brahman.
By proclaiming the fame of those high-souled lords of subjects,
those renowned rulers of the earth, one proceeds toward the state of Brahman.
This Purāṇa, spoken by Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, the proclaimer of Brahman, is auspicious, conducive to fame and long life, meritorious, and equal in authority to the Vedas.

One who has shaken off evil and conquered heaven is fit for becoming Brahman,

Inexhaustible and fulfilling all desires, it attends upon the ancestors;

likewise, those men among the three social classes who study it [attain the same].
Having heard this history, he set his mind upon dharma;
as many as there were hair-pores on all his bodies, [so many years did he practice].
For as many thousands of millions of years as there are syllables, he rejoices in heaven;
having attained union with Brahman, he rejoices together with the deities.
This ancient scripture, which removes all sins, is meritorious, purifying, and glorious; Brahmā gave this Purāṇa to Mātariśvan in the past.
From him it was obtained by Uśanas, and from him also by Bṛhaspati;

Savitṛ spoke it to Mṛtyu, and Mṛtyu, in turn, to Indra;
Indra spoke it to Vasiṣṭha, and he also to Sārasvata.
Sārasvata gave it to Tridhāman, and Tridhāman to Śaradvat; Śaradvat, however, gave it to Triviṣṭa, who then gave it to Antarikṣa.
From Carṣi it went to Antarikṣa, and he also gave it to Trayyāruṇa; from Trayyāruṇa, Dhananjaya received it, and he indeed bestowed it upon Kṛtañjaya.

Tṛṇabindu spoke it to Dakṣa, and Dakṣa proclaimed it to Śakti;
Parāśara, while still in the womb, heard this from Śakti as well.
From Parāśara it was obtained by Jātūkarṇya, and from him the lord Dvaipāyana;
and furthermore, O best of the twice-born, it was received by me from Dvaipāyana.
And this was further declared by me to my son Amitabuddhi;
such indeed is the statement compiled from Brahmā and the other supreme teachers.
And the gurus should be diligently honored by the wise;
[this practice] is auspicious, conducive to fame and long life, meritorious, and the accomplisher of all goals.

This sin-destroying [text] should always be heard by Brahmins with self-restraint; it must not be heard by one who is impure, nor by one who is wicked, nor by one who has not resided [as a student] for a full year.
This supreme purifier must never be given to one who lacks faith, nor to an ignorant person, nor to one who has no son, nor to one who is not a worthy recipient.
They say that the Unmanifest is his source, the Manifest is his body, and Time is his movement;
they say fire is his mouth, the moon and sun are his two eyes, the quarters of space are his ears, and the wind is his breath.
The Vedas are his speech, the intermediate space is his body, the earth is his feet, the stars are the pores of his skin;
the entire sky is his heads, and indeed, the sciences as well as the Upanishads are his tail.
With a disciplined mind, I bow down to that God of gods, the progenitor of all beings, whose essence is sacrifice, who is established in the realm of truth (satyaloka),
the most excellent of the excellent, the granter of boons, Maheśvara, the primordial Brahmā.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Revolving of the Cosmic Egg," in the fourth section on the Conclusion of the Uttara-bhāga of the Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa, spoken by Vāyu, in the twelve-thousand-verse compendium.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.

Seeing all those various living beings enveloped by the darkness of ignorance and devoted solely to their genitals and bellies, he reflected upon them.
As he was thus reflecting and traveling over this earth,
he reached the supremely meritorious and excellent city of Kāñcī.
There, the self-possessed king worshipped Śiva, who dwells at Dramekāmra on Mount Vāraṇaśaila, as well as Kāmākṣī, the destroyer of the elephant's taint.

"By what means may they be liberated? You ought to tell me this.

It was performed by Durvāsas first, and after that by you.
"May my excellent instruction, proclaimed among the worlds by you high-souled ones who have become the teachers of all beings, be established; this is my boon."
For I am the origin of all beings, the primordial creator, the self-effulgent Lord, and the agent of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of all things.
He is the triple-formed one, transcending the three qualities (guṇas), devoid of qualities, yet the refuge of qualities.

Or Śiva, having propitiated her through the power of meditative yoga,

O best of sages, by means of penance alone that is performed with contentment,
may the gods, the sages, the perfected ones (siddhas), humans,

Hayagrīva said:

Seeing her, whose eyes were like those of a young deer, the bull among sages said:

That which was unobtainable even for Brahmā and the other gods has been obtained by me through good fortune;

"O gentle one, go as you please toward that which will have a beautiful outcome.

Sometimes taking divine garlands and unguents, sometimes divine ornaments, and sometimes singing or laughing; BndP_3.6.23.

Intoxicated by the sovereignty over the three worlds,
you indeed insulted her who was upheld by Mahādevī and is worshipped here by Brahmā and the other gods.
"Since the world, including its gods, asuras, and humans, is ruled by you,

Then Vijayaśrī followed the Daitya Bali,

Then, having observed inauspicious omens in the city of the immortals,
he summoned Bṛhaspati and spoke these words.
O Blessed One, knower of all phenomena, skilled in the knowledge of the three times,
inauspicious omens such as have never been seen before are now appearing.
"What would their fruits be, and what might the means be?

Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, cows, horses, donkeys, camels,

for the sake of ten Brahmins and their dependents, a king may slay a single twice-born man.
For the sake of one hundred Brahmins and their dependents,
or for the sake of five knowers of the Brahman, a Brahmin should indeed punish another Brahmin with a single fine of three thousand [paṇas].
One should punish a Vaiśya for the sake of ten Vaiśyas, or likewise for the sake of [all] Vaiśyas;
and in the same way, one should punish a single twice-born man for the sake of a hundred Vaiśyas.
For thousands of Śūdras, however, he should fine a Brāhmaṇa;
for a Vaiśya, half of that hundred; and for a Śūdra, half of that ten.
For the sake of kinsmen and friends, one may take three-quarters of the wealth;
for the sake of a wife and children, one-quarter; but for one's own sake, nothing at all.
Having begun to kill oneself, or having killed a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a cow, a horse, or any other [living being], one is not stained by the faults [of such acts].

It is said that when the duty of protecting them is performed and gifts are given, one gains merit possessing the superior qualities previously described;
likewise for those who engage in the act of seeing them, bowing to them, and serving them, as well as for those who act in a manner consistent with them.

Even in times of distress and for the sake of one's own life, one may eat pure foods after having killed [the animal].
One should not cook food for one's own sake, nor should one slaughter animals for one's own sake;
one who cooks for the sake of the gods or for the sake of Brahmins is not defiled.
In ancient times, the Blessed Māyā, intent on reviving the world,
created all the gods as well as the asuras and humans.
For the sake of protecting them, he created even the fourteen types of sacrificial animals and the various sacrificial rites, and having performed these, he spoke to them.
"O men, worship the gods with animals according to this ritual;
those who offer what is desired shall be nourished and purified by sacrifice."
He who does not follow this wheel thus set in motion shall become poor and even a denizen of hell in birth after birth.
For the sake of the deities, for the sake of the ancestors, likewise for a guest or a guru,
and upon the arrival of a great personage, a twice-born man may slaughter pure animals.
In times of distress, a Brahmin who eats meat that is pure incurs no fault; however, he should perform those actions that are prescribed and avoid those that are forbidden.

by you this entire karma, both auspicious and inauspicious, has been fashioned.

the sacrifices were likewise devised by you alone through my mouth at the great sacrifice.

Having spoken thus, the Grandfather vanished even before their eyes;
and he performed great sacrifices according to the very procedure prescribed by him.
And he performed sacrifices with supreme power, even after slaying animals fit for the altar;
however, because the specific divisions of those acts have been declared in the Vedas, they are not mentioned here.
Women and Śūdras may consume meat, except for a Brāhmaṇa;

This body, born of Śiva, has indeed attained the state of Śiva;
awaken, O bound soul (paśu), for you are not non-Śiva, you are indeed Śiva.
The Lord is the creator of the entire world, as well as its origin and dissolution;
since Rudra is superior to the universe, you are indeed Rudra, O bound soul (paśu).
By this [mantra], having slain a horse, a cow, an elephant, a camel, a buffalo, or the like—
whether for one's own sake or for the sake of another— one is not tainted by faults.
Even houses that cause harm— such as those inhabited by serpents, rats, or scorpions—
are [purified] for those established in the householder stage who desire the fruits of their ritual actions,
those great souls of auspicious luster whose mental resolves are spontaneously fulfilled.
For others, the sacrifice of animals may serve to fulfill their desires and meritorious works;
however, for them, their desired goals are accomplished through recitation, burnt offerings, worship, and so forth.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of Violence and Other [Vices]," in the Lalitopākhyāna of the Hayagrīvāgastyasaṃvāda within the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Indra said:
"O Blessed One, everything has been explained; however, the definition of violence and the rest [remains to be told]."
What is the definition of theft? Tell me that in detail.
Bṛhaspati said:

greater than that is the sin committed against one who has placed trust and sought refuge."
Having killed the most wicked man in the world, whether he be a Śūdra or one born of the lowest caste,
there is no atonement for him, for his sin is greater than that of killing a Brāhmaṇa.
For one who knows Brahman, for a poor man who has acquired wealth with great difficulty,
or for one who has many sons and a wife and desires to live by means of that wealth—
there is no expiation for the sin of stealing such property.
The theft of the property of one who trusts him is said to be even more grave;
whether the person is trusting or untrusting, one should not take the wealth of a poor man.
Therefore, whoever kills without hesitation one who steals gold or jewels from gods or the twice-born shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
The sin resulting from theft is ten times greater for each subsequent object in the following descending order: one's teacher, a deity, a twice-born, a friend, a son, and one's own self.
One who seizes another's wealth becomes tainted by sins that increase tenfold at each successive stage— from an outcaste, a person born of a Śūdra woman, a Vaiśya, a Kṣatriya, and even a Brāhmaṇa.
In this very context, they cite this ancient history,
which is a most profound secret and the destroyer of all sins.
Long ago, in the city of Kāñcīpura, there was a thief named Vajra.
In that beautiful and excellent city, all were endowed with every prosperity; they were free from disease, self-controlled, happy, and filled with compassion.
In this city, which was abundant with all forms of sovereignty, that thief nevertheless stole a great deal of wealth by taking it little by little.
Out of greed, he dug a pit in the forest and deposited it there;
he concealed it at midnight once [the king] had departed from that place to a distance.
A certain Kirāta, having approached and seen him, took ten parts of his load while remaining unnoticed by him, and departed carrying the burden of wood.
Having covered that with stone and diligently filled it with earth, he returned to his city; Vajra, too, departed out of a thirst for wealth.
Having thus seen so much wealth, he cast it down upon the ground;
and the Kirāta, having reached his home, spoke joyfully to his beloved wife.
"O timid one, while I was going to gather wood on a deserted path, I found this wealth; take it, O seeker of riches."
Having heard that and having taken it, she placed it inside and then, reflecting upon these words, spoke thus to her husband: ||| BndP_3,7.17 |||
"The brahmin who constantly frequents my houses will, upon seeing me, soon become possessed of great fortune. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa 3.7.18)

If one were to remain among women of the four castes, one might become a favorite of the king; however, fortune does not abide for long with a Bhilla, a Kirāta, an actor, or one born of the lowest caste, due to the curse of the one born from an anthill.

that speech which has been heard before can never be in vain.

Having heard those words, which were prompted by his future good fortune,
he looked here and there for a place suitable for the Bahūdaka vow.

which was to be accomplished through a great abundance of materials.
When all the wealth had been given to the laborers,
he saw that the work remained incomplete and became overwhelmed with anxiety.
I followed that thief named Vajra in secret;
by him alone was vast wealth scattered in many ways upon the surface of the earth.

Having taken that very substance in the same manner, he filled the causeway with it;
by means of that, the temple of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow was also surrounded by water in its center.

in the middle of its embankment, he constructed a great temple dedicated to Śaṅkara.

by that means, he also made the most excellent and highly precious fields his own.

he addressed many Brahmins, headed by Devavrāta and others.

"Where am I, a Kirāta named Vīradatta, a seller of wood?"

"O best of the Brahmins, everything has been accomplished by you through your very compassion; likewise, O twice-born ones, accept this from the mouth of Devavrāta."
With contented minds, those high-souled and mighty beings gave him the name Dvijavarman and her the name Śīlavatī.
For the sake of protecting them, the self-controlled one,
together with his kinsmen and his wife, joyfully made his dwelling right there.
To please all the twice-born, he gave this city the name Devarātapura, designating it by the name of his domestic priest.
Then, having fallen under the power of time, Dvijavarmā died; at that moment, the messengers of Yama, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra arrived.

in the midst of this, the sage Nārada arrived and spoke.
Let them not engage in mutual combat; let them listen to my words.
This Kirāta formerly constructed the Setubandha with great valor.
Becoming like the wind, he moves alone until the death of the possessor of wealth;
he may seize the property from many, as long as their deaths likewise occur.
When all the messengers had departed, having heard what Nārada had spoken,
he moved through the atmosphere for twelve years, becoming like the wind.
The sage said to his wife, "There is no fault whatsoever on your part;
by the merit performed by you, go from here to the world of Brahmā."
Seeing her husband become like the wind, she no longer desired the abode of Brahmā; having reached a state of supreme world-weariness, she spoke thus to the sage:
Without that husband of mine, I shall not go to the Grandfather;
I shall remain right here until my husband likewise regains his own body.
Therefore, I shall follow whatever destiny he has; or rather, what need is there for either avoidance or action on my part or his?
Having heard these words of hers, the ascetic, being pleased, said:
"Indeed, your body, consisting of enjoyment, is capable of performing action through karma."
"By my power, there shall be a remedy; I tell you this:
having bathed daily at the great sacred ford, one should indeed worship the Lord together with Ambikā while remaining without food."
Having worshipped Śiva with devotion while subsisting on roots, tubers, and fruits,
and having meditated upon Maheśāna in his heart, he should recite the mantra of the Hundred Rudras.
A slayer of a Brahmin is liberated from sins by [reciting this] one thousand and eight times;
he is liberated from all other sins as well—of this there is no doubt.
Having thus instructed her, the ascetic gave her the Rudrādhyāya;
and having shown favor to that woman, he vanished on the spot.
Having resolved to act for the sake of his master's pleasure, he performed the supreme recitation;
freed from the fault of theft, he regained his own body.
Then the thief named Vajra met his end;
others who possessed that wealth also met their end.
Yama, however, having summoned them, spoke these words.
"By you, however, evil has been committed, yet by fate, merit has also been acquired.
What do you wish to enjoy as the fruit of that which was ill-done or that which was auspicious?"
Having heard these words of his, Vajra and the others then said:
"The fruit of good deeds is experienced first, and afterwards that of evil."
Yama spoke again: "O sons, friends, and wives, by the power of this very [man], all of you go quickly to the third heaven."
Having ascended that foremost of celestial chariots and taken refuge in the protection of the twice-born,
they swiftly went to heaven, endowed with the fruits appropriate to their merit.
Having transcended all the worlds by means of the armor of the twice-born, Dvijavarmā, accompanied by his wife,
attained the status of a leader of the Gaṇas and even today rejoices on Kailāsa.
Indra said:
O high-minded one, please explain the gradations of these merits,
as well as those meritorious acts such as the construction of embankments that increase one's merit.
Bṛhaspati said:
Having obtained half the fruit of the merit, the highly illustrious Dvijavarman [attained it];
Vajra obtained half of that, and the others were endowed with half of that.
Action is divided into four types according to the activities of mind, speech, and body;
it is destroyed by those very same actions when they are performed as their antidotes.
Indra said: What is the nature of liquor (āsava), what is its defect, and what is its quality?
Furthermore, what food causes defects? Tell me that in detail.
Bṛhaspati said:
Liquor made from flour, that from palm-juice, that from *kaira* flowers, that from *mādhūka* flowers, and that produced from molasses—
each subsequent one is less sinful than the preceding, by half and then half again.
For the three castes beginning with the Kṣatriyas, liquor (āsava) is said to be drinkable;
for women as well, it may be drunk starting from the third [caste], with the exception of Brāhmaṇīs.
A maiden who has lost her husband, as well as one who has reached puberty,
and a woman who drinks liquor out of greed even when her husband is present— these should be abandoned.
She is known as "the insane woman"; one should abandon her like an outcaste.
For the twice-born, this [penance] shall consist of ten, eight, six, or four [measures];
for women, it shall be half of that; and in the case of union with her husband, it shall be a quarter.
Having drunk liquor through delusion, a twice-born man shall perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances;
he shall also recite the Gāyatrī ten thousand times, or likewise the Jātavedas mantra.
Or a man may recite the *Ambikā-hṛdaya* and become purified;
even a Kṣatriya [is purified], for among the three castes, the purification is successively half and half less than that of a twice-born.
For women, the penance may be half of that or even a quarter; or she may have it performed by twice-born men.
Alternatively, she may attain purification by reciting [the mantra] a thousand times while submerged in water.
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Gaurī, Caṇḍikā, Tripurāmbikā,
Bhairava, Bhairavī, Kālī, and Mahāśāstrī are the Mothers.
There are other powers as well; for their worship, honey is recommended.
However, a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedāṅgas may perform the sacrifice even without it.
Eating what was offered by them, being non-different from them and having them as their very self,
those streams of devotees go, untainted, to the supreme goal.
For every sin committed, whether intentionally or unintentionally, this expiation is prescribed:
the remembrance of the feet of Parāśakti.
That lowest of men who drinks liquor without having first worshipped the Supreme Power shall dwell for as many years as there are drops in the liquor in the Raurava hell.
But he who drinks liquor out of a desire for pleasure is the lowest of men;
there is no atonement for him except by falling upon a rock or into fire.
A twice-born man should not drink [liquor] out of delusion, nor out of greed, nor even out of desire,
nor out of favor toward great men, nor out of remorse for his past actions.
Through the worship of the Supreme Power, as well as by restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas),
and by the Cāndrāyaṇa and Kṛcchra penances performed for a specific number of days,
a Brāhmaṇa shall be purified from the fault; however, if the act was intentional, purification requires double the effort.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of Theft and Drinking," in the Lalitopākhyāna of the Hayagrīva-Agastya Saṃvāda within the Uttara-bhāga of the Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Indra said:
"What is the act of approaching a woman who should not be approached? What is the fault, and what is the expiation?"
O tiger among sages, you should explain this to me in detail.

Bṛhaspati said: Regarding what is called "approaching those who should not be approached"— namely, a mother’s sister, the wife of a guru, and the beloved wife of a maternal uncle— there is no atonement for having gone to these.
Whatever sin exists in sexual union with one's mother, that same sin exists in union with one's sister;
likewise for union with the wife of a guru—for many gurus are traditionally recognized.
He by whom the teaching of Brahman, beginning from the instruction of Brahmā up to the Vedānta philosophy,
is explained as one whole, is called a Mahāguru.
On one side is the instruction of Brahman, and on the other side are the Vedas and the Shastras;
he alone is to be known as the Teacher (ācārya), while the others are merely instructors (deśika).
For the teacher, the penance lasts until death; for the spiritual preceptor, it lasts until his satisfaction is attained.
One should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve years, reducing it by one year for every six years [of service].
Having approached the wife of his maternal uncle, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance for six years;
but if a Brāhmaṇa approaches a woman of his own caste, he must likewise do so.
Having fasted for three nights, one should perform a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas);
thus, one is purified in three nights from approaching an unchaste woman of the same caste.
After five days, one becomes the consort of a Kṣatriya; after seven days, even of a Vaiśya woman, such as the wives of Cakrins, Kirātas, fishermen, blacksmiths, and so forth.
Purification occurs after twelve days through the worship of the Earth-goddess;
having approached a woman of the lowest caste out of negligence, a Brāhmaṇa becomes pure after one year.

The temple slave-girl (*devadāsī*), the Brahman slave-girl (*brahmadāsī*), the independent one, and the Śūdra slave-girl—these are declared to be the four kinds of slave-girls; the first two are equal to Kṣatriyas.
If a twice-born man, out of delusion, treats his own female slave as equal to another woman who is a courtesan, or treats her as one of low birth, he incurs the fault mentioned regarding that act.
Having approached his own sister-in-law during her menses, one should perform the Prājāpatya vow;
for approaching another woman of the same class, the penance is double, and for a Kṣatriya woman, it is fourfold.
One should treat a Vaiśya woman with eight [blows], a Śūdra woman with sixteen,
and one born of a mixed caste (saṃkara) with thirty-two, just as one would treat a Vaiśya or a Śūdra woman.
But he who, out of delusion, desires to approach his wife while she is in her menses,
becomes pure by bathing, putting on different clothes, and performing the aforementioned expiation.
Having fasted for the remainder of that day and bathed, one should perform the ritual;
likewise, having approached another woman, one should carry out the purpose as instructed by her.
If a man approaches a maiden without the permission of her parents and without the prescribed rite, purification occurs through fasting for three nights; he must then marry her.
But he who, having given his daughter to one man, gives her to another, or he who subsequently approves of it,
is purified by fasting for half a day (twelve hours) with the permission of his parents.
He who, being known by his parents, remains in a state of virginity for a month,
should be recognized as a *vṛṣala*, excluded from all religious rites.
If she is discovered by her parents after she has gone to another married man for the purpose of destroying him, she becomes a widow; she shall not obtain the one who went there first.
Through the favor of the twice-born and according to the rites of marriage,
one should likewise perform acts of renunciation, as well as those prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti.
Even if she was married at first, upon her death, another woman may be given by the father as a means for one who desires enjoyment; however, she is not fit for all ritual acts.
The entire world, from Brahmā down to a tiny ant, including all that is stationary and moving,
is said to consist of the five elements and to be endowed with the four latent impressions (vāsanās).
Birth, eating, excretion, sleep, and fear are always present;
without food, a living being cannot exist, and food is said to arise from desire.
Therefore, even for all living beings, Madana is difficult to overcome;
having fashioned him in the form of both male and female, the Creator of the Universe [acted] by means of that very Madana.
In the beginning, he initiated the process consisting of creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
by his engagement in that process, all things proceed, and by its cessation, one attains the imperishable state.
Now listen as I speak at once of that secret and its means, by which even those lacking in wisdom may attain liberation through worldly activity alone. BndP_3.8.27 //
Vāsudeva is the ancient Puruṣa, the soul of all;
and this Lakṣmī is indeed the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), the mother of the entire world.
For the sake of satisfying the five and the fivefold self, churning should be performed most intensely;
if churning is performed in this way through the power of the mantra, it will succeed.
Both of them are performers of mantra-rites; no fault is found in them.
This downward course belongs solely to those who possess the power of asceticism;
yet even for those two, this occurs regarding their own wives by the force of destiny.
Even for those two whose hearts are softened by devotion to the Goddess— who is the essence of mutual identity and unity—
if there is even the slightest sin on forbidden days, [it shall be removed].
"This is the Mother, the Sustainer of the World; this is the Person, Sadāśiva.
Now, for the gratification of the twenty-five principles, she is being churned."
And if churning is performed through the power of these mantras, both of them are performers of meritorious deeds; no fault exists for them.
And hear this, O Lord of the Gods: it is a supreme and great secret, which effects the simultaneous destruction of all sins whatsoever.
Endowed with devotion and faith, having bathed and remaining submerged within the water,
one should recite the fifteen-syllable mantra one thousand and eight times.
And by propitiating the Supreme Power (Parā Śakti), one is liberated from all sins;
by that, even the evils committed over ten million kalpas are destroyed.
One shall be freed from all calamities and shall obtain every desired object.
Indra said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, devoted to the welfare of all beings,
you ought to explain the specific nature of sin arising from association."
Bṛhaspati said:
"The sin born of association is declared to be fourfold:
the principal agent, the collaborator, the instrumental cause, and the one who consents, in that order."
In due order, sin is reduced by one-tenth at each stage; purification occurs according to the path previously described.
Intoxicating liquor, *kalañja*, resinous exudations, mushrooms, *gṛñjana*, garlic, *kaliṅga*, and likewise the *mahākośātakī*— BndP_3,8.41.
The *biṃbī*, the *kavaka* mushroom, the *hastinī*, the *śiśulambikā*,
the *audumbara*, the eggplant (*vārtāka*), the *kataka*, and the *bilva-mallikā*.
One should specify that their sin is ten times less in each successive case.
[The sinner] who sells cities, villages, limbs of a Vaiśya, the limbs of a courtesan, or presents [to a king].

A servant, one residing in the city, one dwelling in a wretched village, one who is accused, a physician, a forest-dweller (Vaikhānasa), a devotee of Śiva, one who lives off women, and a seller of food— [these are excluded].
A professional soldier, a wandering mendicant, and one who reviles Vedic conduct—
by eating their food, one becomes progressively ten times more degraded.

One should declare that sin to be self-inflicted and prepared with oil as previously described; however, if it is seen by those [deities] and consumed by them, one should designate that sin as released.
If one eats the food of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras— such as boiled rice— even if it is cooked in oil and unseen [by others], one incurs a quarter of the sin.
When that half-measure was seen by her, she fashioned it into a slave-girl for the twice-born;
however, when that rice was seen, it became three-quarters of a share for a courtesan.
The food of a cowherd is like that of a Śūdra, except for the four products of the cow;
however, cooked food combined with oil, clarified butter, and molasses from a Vaiśya does not cause defilement.
A Brahmin woman who has fallen [from her status] is like a Vaiśya woman; nothing at all is seen by one who looks at her.
Having eaten the food of a *brūva*, a twice-born man should perform one hundred *prāṇāyāmas*;
or else, having muttered the *adrupada* mantra three times while submerged in water.
One should recite either this "idaṃ viṣṇu" mantra or the "tryambakaṃ yajāmahe" mantra while submerged within the water;
having fasted for one night, one is then purified from sin.
Alternatively, one should sprinkle the food with water while reciting the *Abliṅga* and *Pāvamānī* verses; then, having muttered the *Annasūkta* and the hymn beginning with "Bhṛgu vai vāruṇiḥ."
Having recited the verse beginning with "brahmārpaṇam," and having undertaken the observance by fasting for one night, he will thereafter become pure.
But after a woman has eaten, she should say, "May the food be [for the gods]"; she should then feed one or more twice-born men.
For in times of distress, a Brāhmaṇa who eats their food incurs no fault.
Having consecrated [the food] seven times with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," and meditating upon it with the sense of "I am that," one who eats is not tainted by faults.
Alternatively, by meditating on Śaṅkara and reciting the Tryambaka mantra with the realization "I am He," one is not defiled by faults due to that knowledge.
O Lord of the Gods, listen to these words of mine, this secret:
having meditated upon the Goddess, the Supreme Power (Parā Śakti), and having recited the fifteen-syllable mantra.
The twice-born who daily eats that which has been offered to the Buddhas and others incurs no fault from the food,
nor does he have any fear of poverty.
For one who recites this, there is no fear born of disease, nor likewise any fear of enemies; for him there is only liberation, and constant auspiciousness everywhere.
This detailed account of even the most heinous sins has been told to you, O Śakra, as well as the expiation for them; what else do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Lalitopākhyāna of the Hayagrīvāgastyasaṃvāda in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Indra said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, most excellent among those who possess knowledge of the three periods of time!"
That misdeed and its remedy have been correctly described by you.
By what ripening of karma has this calamity come upon me?
O best among speakers, tell me what atonement there is for it.
Bṛhaspati said: Then, from Kaśyapa and Diti, one known as Danu was born;
her father gave that beautiful maiden named Kanyā to Dhātṛ.
From her was then born a son named Viśvarūpa, of great luster,
who was eternally devoted to Nārāyaṇa and had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
Then the lord of the Daityas chose the son of Bhṛgu as his domestic priest, saying:
"You are authorized over this kingdom, just as Vāsava is over the gods."
Furthermore, in former times, while you were seated in the Sudharmā assembly hall,
you once posed a question to the sages in their presence.
"Between cyclic existence and pilgrimage to sacred fords, which is superior?
Having determined this, may you all speak out of favor toward me."
To provide an answer to that question, they all began to speak;
however, I had already stated it previously by the power of the sacred ordinance.
Hearing that "pilgrimage to sacred sites is superior to worldly existence," all those sages became enraged and quickly cursed me.
"Go quickly to the land of action (Karmabhūmi) with your poverty and your few sons. Having been cursed thus by those enraged ones, I entered Kāñcī dejected.
Seeing the city bereft of its domestic priest, you, with a mind agitated by anxiety,
together with the gods, respectfully [approached him] for the sake of the office of family priest.
Thus entreated, Viśvarūpa, the best among those who radiate heat,
became the nephew of the Dānavas and the domestic priest of the gods.
The one of great asceticism did not harbor excessive enmity even toward the Daityas;
at that time, the lord of the Daityas and Vāsava became equal in strength.
Then, O King, being enraged and desiring to slay the lord of the Dānavas, you quickly went to the forest where your own penance was practiced.
Seated upon his throne, he was like a mountain with three peaks surrounded by sages; the three Vedas made the quarters of the sky resonant as he remained solely devoted to the flow of the Brahman.
But considering him to be beneficial to all beings and favorably disposed toward you,
you yourself have indeed severed his heads simultaneously.
Joined with that sin and tormented again and again,
he was then led to a cave in Mount Meru and remained there for many years.
Then, having heard his words and understood them from the sage's speech, he,
tormented by grief for his son and filled with rage, cursed you.
"May Vāsava quickly become shorn of his splendor by my curse!
Then let the gods be leaderless, dejected, and oppressed by the Daityas."
Deprived of both you and me, all the gods fled;
having gone to the abode of Brahmā, they bowed and related what had occurred.
Then he reflected upon a remedy for that evil;
however, the Self-born Lord was unable to find a remedy for it at that time.
Then, surrounded by the gods, he approached Nārāyaṇa.
Having bowed and offered praise, the four-faced one reported that account;
and the Leader of the World, having reflected in many ways, out of compassion [acted].
Having divided that sin into three parts, he then assigned them to three locations:
among women, upon the earth, and among trees; and he granted them a boon as well.
Then, there shall be union with a husband and the attainment of sons even during the fertile seasons;
moreover, for all trees, there shall be the state of being reborn after being cut down.
Madhusūdana bestowed upon them lands for the filling of excavations;
yet in those places, the impurity quickly became saline and barren soil, devoid of moisture.
Having emerged from that abyss, you have become Indra, the leader of the gods,
and have attained the glory of sovereignty through the grace of the Supreme Lord.
Consoled by those very words, the Creator spoke to Janārdana:
"O Sage, let my curse not be in vain; let it take effect at another time."
Having heard those words of the sage Amitatejas, the Blessed One,
knowing the future course of events, departed in silence, filled with joy.
"During all this time while you were protecting the three worlds,
you oppressed even Mount Kailāsa because you were intoxicated by the pride of your sovereignty."
Then the venerable sage Durvāsas, sent by the omniscient Śiva and desiring to cause your fall from your state, uttered a curse.
The same single result has arisen from both curses;
now behold, the three worlds have become devoid of prosperity.
O Vāsava, neither sacrifices proceed, nor do gifts;
neither restraints, nor observances, nor austerities exist anywhere at all.
All the brahmins, too, became bereft of prosperity, their minds afflicted by greed;
for the most part, they were devoid of strength, lacking fortitude, and became atheists.
The earth will become utterly devoid of medicinal herbs and lacking in vitality;
the sun will take on a greyish appearance, and the moon will be bereft of its luster.
The consumer of the oblation was devoid of luster, his form obscured by dust;
the quarters of the sky were not serene, nor was the firmament clear.
All the deities appear weak, as if they were something else;
the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving, seem as if their very foundation has perished.
Hayagrīva said:
Even as Bṛhaspati and Indra were thus conversing,
the great Daityas, led by Malla, began to harass the heavenly realm.
Arrogant in their strength, they destroyed the entire Nandana grove and struck all the garden-keepers with their weapons.
Having broken through the rampart and entered the interior of the city,
they tormented all the gods residing in the palace to the utmost degree.
They brought forth all the jewels of the Apsarases in their entirety; then all the gods, being utterly unimpeded, performed [their rites] with great intensity.
Hearing such a cry, Vāsava abandoned his seat and,
followed by all the gods, became intent on flight.
Having reached the abode of Brahmā, the bull-bannered god,
with a dejected face, related in its entirety all the activities of the Daityas exactly as they had occurred.
Having heard that, even the Creator, seeing Indra accompanied by all the gods yet deprived of his splendor, spoke these words.
Seek refuge in Mukunda, the lordship over whom all the gods desire;
he is the enemy of the Daityas and the creator of the world, and he will ordain your welfare.
Having spoken thus, Brahmā himself, the Grandfather,
accompanied by him and all the gods, approached the Ocean of Milk.
Then Brahmā and the other gods praised the Blessed Janārdana, the Great Lord of all worlds, with the most excellent words.
Then the blessed Vāsudeva, the eternal one, who is ever intent on protecting the world, being pleased, spoke to those gods who were his own portions.
The Blessed One said:
"I shall provide for you by augmenting you with my own splendor;
whatever is now spoken by me, let that be carried out by you."
"Cast all the most excellent medicinal herbs into the ocean of milk;
and do so here even while making peace with the asuras."
"O gods, having made Mount Mandara the churning-stick and Vāsuki the rope,
let the nectar be churned while I stand as your assistant."
All the Dānavas should also be addressed with conciliatory words, saying:
"The fruit [of our actions] is indeed common to both you and us."
When the ocean of milk is being churned, the nectar that arises from it—
by drinking that, you shall become strong and immortal.
I shall act in such a way that the Daityas shall not obtain even a trace of the nectar, and shall instead be left with nothing but suffering.
Thus were all the gods addressed by the illustrious Vāsudeva;
then the gods entered into an alliance with the incomparable Daityas,
and having gathered various kinds of medicinal herbs, the gods and asuras [prepared the elixir].
Having cast the moon— more stainless than the waters of the ocean of Śrī— into the water,
and having made Mount Mandara the churning rod and Vāsuki the rope,
they began to churn the Lord of the Sea with great effort.
On the tail-end of Vāsuki, all the gods were stationed together,
while on the head-end the Daityas were assigned there by Śauri.
Though those Daityas were powerful, their bodies were all scorched by the fires of his breath from that mouth, and they then became devoid of luster.
Being repeatedly drawn by the wind favorable to them, which was impelled by Viṣṇu, the gods were refreshed as they pulled at the tail-end.
The glorious one, in the form of the primordial tortoise, took his station in the midst of the ocean of milk as Mount Mandara whirled about.
And in the midst of all the gods, Mādhava, assuming another form,
swiftly dragged Vāsuki from one side, while from the other side he did so in the midst of the Daityas.
The divine sage, having supported that mountain in the form of Brahmā while it was crossing the ocean,
repeatedly [stabilized it] with another great splendor.
By one splendor he strengthened the gods so that they became powerful,
and by another splendor, which was capable of enduring force, he himself became powerful.
Then, while that ocean of milk was being churned by the gods and the dānavas, Janārdana, the possessor of all powers, strengthened the serpent.
Surabhi, who is worshipped by the gods, appeared before them;
O ascetic, at that time both the gods and the Daityas attained great joy.
Furthermore, while that Ocean of Milk was being churned by the gods and the dānavas, the siddhas in heaven were then wondering, "What is this? (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍapurāṇa 3.9.66).
The goddess Vāruṇī arose, her eyes rolling with intoxication;
she stood before the Asuras, smiling.
The Daityas and Asuras did not accept it at all; because they possessed no *sura* (divinity), they were therefore designated by the term "Asura."
Then she stood before all the gods;
the gods joyfully accepted her as indicated by the Supreme Lord.
Because they received her (sura), they are celebrated by the word "sura" (gods).
Then, as it was being churned further, the great tree Pārijāta appeared,
perfuming the entire world with its fragrance.
O divine sage, hosts of apsarases— possessing exceedingly beautiful forms, steadfast,
and enchanting to all the worlds— manifested themselves.
Thereupon the Moon arose; Maheśvara took him, while the various species of serpents seized that which had arisen as poison.
Then Janārdana took that jewel known as the Kaustubha.
Thereafter, from the fragrance of his own body, a great medicinal herb named Vijayā was born, which intoxicates even the great herbs; Bhairava took her up.
Then the god Dhanvantari himself appeared, wearing celestial garments,
holding in his hand a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) filled with nectar.
Then, O treasury of austerities, the gods and the Daityas from all sides became joyful in mind, and the sages were likewise satisfied at that time.
Then Śrī, the bestower of boons, dwelling within the blooming lotus and holding a lotus in her hand, rose up from that great ocean of milk.
Then all the sages, with contented hearts, praised the supreme Śrī with the Śrīsūkta, and the Gandharvas sang the highest hymn.
All the hosts of Apsaras, led by Viśvājī, danced;
and the holy rivers, headed by the Gaṅgā, stood ready for the purpose of bathing.
And taking water placed in pure vessels from the eight elephants of the quarters, they bathed that Śrī, the dweller in the lotus.
And the personified Ocean of Milk gave to her a garland of lotuses and the most excellent Tulasī, which had arisen from the singular union with Hari.
And Viśvakarman presented her with divine ornaments;
wearing celestial garlands and garments, adorned with divine jewels,
Ramā went to the chest of Viṣṇu while everyone looked on.
The Tulasi was indeed worn by that powerful Viṣṇu;
and that goddess, the supreme sovereign of all the worlds, who dwells upon the chest of Viṣṇu, beheld the gods with a gaze moist with compassion.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Churning for Nectar," in the Lalitopākhyāna of the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Hayagrīva and Agastya in its Uttara-bhāga.
Hayagrīva said: Then the gods, headed by Mahendra, [were addressed] by the powerful Viṣṇu.
Having accepted [the task], the great sages attained supreme joy.
But all those Daityas, beginning with Malaka, having turned their backs on Viṣṇu,
were abandoned by the goddess Śrī and fell into great distress.
Then the Daityas seized the golden jar, filled with the essence of the supreme nectar, which rested in the hand of Dhanvantari; thereupon,
