From the center of that, there arose an unsurpassed wheel-shaped form;
in its center was the Great Goddess, possessing a radiance like the rising sun.
She who revives the world, whose essence is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva,
the ultimate limit of the quintessence of beauty, that ocean of the rasa of bliss.
Resembling a hibiscus flower, with a garment of pomegranate blossoms,
adorned with all ornaments, she is the sole abode of the erotic sentiment.
She possesses the moonlight of her glance from the corners of her eyes, rippling with waves of compassion;
her hands shine with the noose, the goad, the sugarcane bow, and the five arrows.
Beholding that Great Goddess, all the gods, including Indra,
bowed down again and again with joyful hearts to her who is the soul of all.
As soon as they were looked upon by her, they all became free from fever;
their limbs were restored, they became more firm, possessed of adamantine bodies and great strength, and they praised the Great Goddess Ambikā, the bestower of all goals. (BndP 3.12.75)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Lalitā," in the *Lalitopākhyāna* within the *Hayagrīvāgastya-saṃvāda* of the latter section of the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa-mahāpurāṇa*.
The gods said:
"Victory to you, O Goddess, Mother of the World! Victory to you, O Goddess, higher than the highest!"
Victory to you, O abode of auspiciousness! Victory to you, O essence of the art of love!
Victory to you, O left-eyed one; victory, O beautiful Kāmākṣī!
Victory to you, who are worshipped by all the gods; victory, O Kāmeśī, the bestower of honor!
Victory to you, O Goddess composed of Brahman, whose essence is the sap of the nature of Brahman!
Victory to you, O Supreme Nārāyaṇī, who gladdens the entire world!
Victory to you, O beloved of Śrīkaṇṭha! Victory to you, O Śrī Lalitāmbikā!
Victory to you, O Goddess Śrī Vijayā! Be victorious, O bestower of prosperity and fortune!

Salutations to her who is higher than the highest, the protectress of the three worlds, for the sake of that which has been born, that which is being born, and for the sake of one's sacrifices and charitable works.
Salutation to the Self consisting of the *kalā*, *muhūrta*, *kāṣṭhā*, day, month, season, and year; salutation to the one with a thousand heads, a thousand mouths, and a thousand eyes.
Salutations to you, O Goddess, who are adorned with the lotuses of a thousand hands and feet;
you who are subtler than the subtlest and greater than the greatest.
O Mother, you are higher than the highest, the splendor even of those who possess greater splendor;
may Atala be your feet and Vitala your knees.
The region of the waist is Rasātala, and your belly shall be the Earth;
the heart is Bhuvarloka, while your mouth is declared to be Svarloka.
O Mother, the moon, the sun, and fire are your eyes; the quarters are your arms;
the winds are your breaths; and all the Vedas are your speech.
The creation of the worlds is your play; Śiva, who consists of consciousness, is your friend;
eternal bliss is your food; and the hearts of the virtuous are your dwelling place.
The visible and invisible forms and worlds are Your own;
Your thick locks of hair are the stars, and they are Your flowers.
May Dharma and the other virtues be your arms; may Adharma and the others be your weapons;
and likewise, may the Yamas and Niyamas be the hairs upon your hands and feet.
Your breasts are the utterances *svāhā* and *svadhā*, the causes of the world’s sustenance;
your nose is the regulation of breath (*prāṇāyāma*), and your tongue is Sarasvatī.
O most excellent one, your senses are withdrawal (pratyāhāra), your intellect is meditation (dhyāna);
your mind is the power of concentration (dhāraṇā), and your heart is absorption (samādhi).
The trees are the hairs upon your body; the dawn is your garment;
the past, the present, and the future, as well as eternity itself, are your form.
She who is the form of sacrifice, the sustainer of the world, the universal form, and the purifier—
she who was originally composed of compassion created all living beings.
Though residing in the hearts of people, she is invisible and of a delusive nature.
Salutations to that Great Goddess, who by her own play effects the differentiation of name and form;
abiding while presiding over them, she is unattached and grants all purposes and desires. Salutations again and again to her, the Great Goddess, the embodiment of all powers!
Salutations again and again to that Goddess, by whose command fire, sun, moon, and wind, as well as the elements such as earth and the rest, proceed.
Salutations again and again to that Goddess, who at the beginning of creation created the primordial Creator, and who, being herself the first, sustained him alone.
Salutations again and again to that Goddess, by whom the immeasurable earth is supported as it is held in space, and upon whom the sun rises.
Salutations again and again to that Goddess, from whom the entire universe arises, in whom it remains firmly established, and into whom it dissolves at the time of its end.
Salutations, salutations to you who are Rajas, to Bhavā; salutations, salutations to her who is established in Sattva;
salutations, salutations to you who are Tamas, to Harā; salutations, salutations to Śivā who is beyond the Guṇas.
Salutations, salutations to you, the sole mother of the world; salutations, salutations to you, the sole father of the world.
Salutations, salutations to you, whose tantra is the form of all; salutations, salutations to you, whose form is the mechanism of all.
Homage, homage to you, the foremost teacher of the world; homage, homage to you, the sovereign power of all speech.
Homage be to Lakṣmī, the sole delight of the universe; homage, homage to you, O Śāmbhavī, the universal power.

O Mother, how can I describe that supreme power which is without beginning, middle, or end; which is not composed of the five elements; which is inaccessible to speech and mind; whose majesty is beyond reasoning; which is formless, free from duality, and outside the range of perception?
Be gracious, O Sovereign of the Universe, adored by all; be gracious, O Mistress of Knowledge, whose form is the Vedas.
Be gracious, O Thou who consistest of Māyā, whose body is composed of mantras; be gracious, O Sovereign of All, who art the form of all things.
Having thus reflected, all the gods, together with Indra, repeatedly paid homage to the Great Goddess and truly sought refuge in her.
Then that goddess, being pleased, seeing Vāsava prostrate before her,
invited him to choose a boon, she who grants boons to all embodied beings.
Indra said:
"O Lord of Daityas, if you are pleased with us who are oppressed by our duties, grant us this boon:
give us back our lives, for we have come to you seeking refuge."
The illustrious Goddess said:
"Having myself utterly conquered Bhaṇḍa, who is born of the race of Daityas,
I shall before long restore to you the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile."
May all the hosts of gods likewise be fearless and joyful,
as well as those men who shall praise me with devotion by means of this hymn.
They shall always be vessels for the glory and fame of the Dharma;
endowed with knowledge and discipline, they shall be free from disease and long-lived.
"By my grace, may they become rich in sons, friends, and wives"—
thus the gods obtained their boon, as did the mighty Indra, lord of the gods.
Beholding her again and again, they attained supreme delight.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The King of Hymns to Lalitā," in the *Lalitopākhyāna* within the dialogue between Hayagrīva and Agastya in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa-mahāpurāṇa*.
Hayagrīva said:
At that very time, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, [arrived].
Then, desiring to see the Goddess of the Gods, he arrived together with the great seers.
Then Viṣṇu arrived, mounted upon the son of Vinatā;
Śiva also arrived, mounted upon his bull, along with the Sovereign Lady of All.
The celestial sages, Nārada and others, assembled before the Great Goddess;
all the hosts of Apsarases also came to that Mahādevī.
The Gandharvas, headed by Viśvāvasu, as well as the Yakṣas,
and then Viśvakarman, the lord of artisans, were commanded by Brahmā.
Then the Blessed Goddess Durgā, the presiding deity of all mantras, constructed a divine city just like the city of the immortals.
The goddesses presiding over the sciences (vidyādhidevatās), who were dark-complexioned, approached Ambikā,
as did the Mothers beginning with Brāhmī, each surrounded by their own respective hosts of beings.
For there are the supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā*, and yoginīs by the millions;
as well as the Bhairavas, the guardians of the fields (*kṣetrapālas*), and the Great Teacher who leads the hosts.
Then Mahāgaṇeśvara, Skanda, Baṭuka, and Vīrabhadra,
having arrived, bowed down and praised the Great Goddess.
Then, [he beheld] that beautiful city, with its watchtowers, walls,
and archways, abounding in stables for elephants, horses, and chariots, and resplendent with royal thoroughfares.
And he saw the beautiful houses of the neighboring vassals, ministers, soldiers, and the twice-born, as well as those of the vetālas, male servants, and female slaves.
The divine city of Rājagṛha was situated in the center; it was adorned with gates and towers, provided with many halls, and graced by beautiful assembly halls.
And he beheld the auspicious assembly hall of the lion-throne, composed of the nine precious gems;
in its center was a divine lion-throne fashioned from wish-fulfilling jewels.
Beholding that which is self-luminous, beyond duality, and resembling the rising sun, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, reflected: BndP_3,14.13 //
But whoever, even if they are a fool, abides having taken hold of this [mantra],
by the power of this city he shall become superior to all the worlds.
Neither is a woman alone worthy of the kingdom, nor is a man without her;
for the sacred tradition declares that one should be consecrated when possessed of the marks of a great man and joined by a favorable wife, together with the preceptor of auspicious rites.
This woman of excellent form shines forth as the very goddess of love incarnate;
her husband must be the best in the three worlds, and none other than Śaṅkara.
Jaḍila, Muṇḍadhārī, Virūpākṣa, and Kapālabhṛt; Kalmāṣī, with limbs smeared with ashes, adorned with the bones of the cremation ground.
"Even though he is an abode of inauspiciousness, she who is supremely auspicious should choose him"—
while Brahmā was reflecting thus, Maheśvara appeared before him.
Possessing the loveliness of ten million Kāmadevas, endowed with a divine body,
wearing celestial garments, garlanded, and anointed with divine perfumes and unguents.
Adorned with a crown, necklaces, armlets, earrings, and other ornaments,
he appeared before them, assuming a form that enchants the world.
Then Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, embraced that boy and made him known by the name Kāmeśvara, for he possessed a most desirable form.
"Having resolved that this bridegroom is indeed worthy of that supreme Śakti," they then approached her together with him.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara praised that supreme power;
but upon seeing that fawn-eyed woman, the youth Nīlalohita became possessed by the god of love and forgot all his ritual duties.

She too, seeing him— slender-limbed as he was, like the god of love incarnate— felt her entire body possessed by passion and considered him to be her own soul. Both of them, afflicted by love, remained intent on gazing at one another.
They were knowers of the distinctions between all things, steadfast and wise;
their conduct was unknown to others, and for a moment their minds became unsettled.
Then Brahmā spoke to the Great Goddess, the sole leader of the world:
"These gods, sages, and hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases desire to see you, the sovereign, together with your beloved in this supreme battle."
"O Goddess, who is that most fortunate man worthy of you as a husband?
For the sake of protecting the world, resort to the Supreme Person."
"Be the queen of this city; remain seated upon the excellent throne, consecrated by the highly fortunate, stainless gods and sages."
We wish to behold her seated upon her throne with her beloved, adorned with all ornaments and endowed with the insignia of imperial sovereignty.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Madanakāmeśvara," in the Lalitopākhyāna within the Hayagrīvāgastyasaṃvāda of the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Having heard those words, the Goddess, her lotus-face graced with a gentle smile,
then spoke these words to the gods headed by Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
"O gods, I am always independent, wandering and acting according to my own will;
however, he who conducts himself in accordance with me shall become my beloved."
Having agreed to that with "So be it," the Grandfather (Brahmā), together with all the gods,
spoke words consistent with dharma and artha to the Great Goddess.
The purchase by time, the purchase by price, that given by the father, and the self-choice;
thus is the marriage of woman and man fourfold.
A courtesan is one purchased with money; a female slave is one bought for a price;
a wife is one wedded according to the Gandharva rite; and one given by her father is a wife bestowed by her father.
A wife who shares the same duties as her husband and is obedient to her father is like that supreme Brahman which is non-dual and devoid of the states of being and non-being.
From that [Brahman], which consists of consciousness and bliss, Prakṛti was born;
you alone were that Brahman, for she, Prakṛti, is indeed you.
You alone are beginningless, the embodiment of all causes and effects;
indeed, yogis such as Sanaka and others seek you alone.
Indeed, they praise you alone, who consist of both existent and non-existent karma, who are manifest and unmanifest, whose nature is compassion, and who are the very essence of the five Brahmas.
For you alone create in the beginning, and you alone indeed sustain [the world] in an instant;
therefore, out of a desire to show favor to the worlds, take a certain Puruṣa as your consort.
Thus addressed by Brahmā and all the gods,
the Goddess raised a garland in her hand and cast it into the midst of the sky.
For that garland, released by her, illuminating the expanse of the sky,
then fell indeed upon the neck of Kāmeśvara.
Then the gods, led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, rejoiced;
and the clouds, stirred by gentle breezes, rained down showers of flowers.
Then the Creator spoke to the Blessed Janārdana:
"O Hari, the marriage of these two auspicious ones must be performed according to the prescribed rite."
This auspicious moment has arrived for the gods, bringing welfare to the world;
for the Great Goddess is of your form, and you too are her innate consort.
"You ought to grant this auspicious woman to him for his happiness and fulfillment.
Having heard those words of his, Trivikrama, the God of gods, [replied].
He gave her to Śaṅkara with affection according to the prescribed rite,
in the presence of all the foremost gods, sages, ancestors, and divine yogis.
Ādikeśava performed auspicious rites for Śiva and Śivā;
all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, presented them with offerings.
Brahmā gave them a sugarcane bow with a core of adamant, indestructible;
and Hari gave them an unfading, imperishable flower-weapon.
Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures, gave them the serpent-noose;
and Viśvakarman, the lord of the people, gave them the goad.
Agni gave him a crown; the Moon and Sun gave him two earrings;
and the Ocean himself bestowed upon him ornaments made of the nine precious gems.
Then the lord of the gods gave him an inexhaustible vessel of honey-wine,
and Kubera presented him with a garland made of wish-fulfilling gems.
The Lord of Lakṣmī himself gave him the umbrella indicative of universal sovereignty,
and Gaṅgā and Yamunā gave him two moon-bright whisks.
And the eight Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, as well as the two Aśvins,
the guardians of the quarters, the Maruts, the Sādhyas, the Gandharvas, and the lords of the Pramathas,
being fully satisfied, bestowed their own respective weapons upon her.
They gave chariots, horses, and elephants of great speed and great strength;
camels free from disease, and those horses devoid of hunger and thirst—
possessing forms like thunderbolts, equipped with weapons and all their trappings.
Then they performed the auspicious consecration for the sovereignty of Śiva and Śivā;
thereafter, he constructed a celestial chariot named Kusumākara.
The Creator fashioned it with unfading garlands, eternally impenetrable by weapons,
moving at will through heaven, earth, and the intermediate space, and endowed with perfect prosperity.
Merely by smelling its fragrance, delusion, disease, and the destruction of the eyes perish at that very moment; it is auspicious and brings delight to the mind.
Then, having placed both of those divine husband and wife upon that celestial chariot, which was enchanting with its canopy, parasol, and flagstaff, and which was made of pure gold; BndP_3.15.29.
Attended by hosts of gods with various musical performances of lutes, flutes, drums, and other instruments, she departed from the king’s palace.
The mistress of the monastery proceeded along the street, beautifying it with her own splendor, while thousands of apsarases stood upon the tops of the mansions.
Showered with parched grain and unbroken rice by the city women,
and being gladdened by auspicious verses and the sounds of lutes, flutes, and other instruments,
she proceeded very slowly through the streets and alleys.
Having accepted the rite of lustration (nīrājanā) performed by the water-dwellers,
he descended from the top of the celestial chariot and entered the great assembly hall.
Seated upon the lion-throne together with the divine Śambhu, she,
the omniscient one, fulfilled every desire that the great multitude there wished for, merely by their mental longing and by her glance as a witness.
Having witnessed that conduct of the Goddess, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
then bestowed upon her the names Kāmākṣī and Kāmeśvarī.
By his command, even the wondrous cloud rained down upon that city precious objects and divine ornaments.
The wish-fulfilling gem, the celestial desire-tree, Lakṣmī,
and the cows of plenty stood at every house for the sake of the Goddess’s victory.
Free from other activities and qualities, they rejoiced at all times, ever united with all their desires and purposes, as they devoted themselves to her alone, who is of a single flavor and form.
The Grandfather (Brahmā), Hari, Mahādeva, and Vāsava, as well as the other lords of the quarters and all the hosts of deities; BndP_3.15.39.
The celestial sages such as Nārada and others, the yogis such as Sanaka and others, the great sages such as Manu and others, and those whose wealth is austerity such as Vasiṣṭha and others.
The Gandharvas, Apsarases, Yakṣas, and whatever other divine races there are,
who dwell in the heavens, on earth, and in the intermediate space, crowded together.
And they all lived in that city without any crowding.
Thus, the queen, being so affectionate toward him, pleased no one other than all the people by her constant and great devotion.
In the great world of mortals, the queen milked from the wise king all his desires— the objects wished for by all the inhabitants of the earth.
While Sāmbika was the sole sovereign of the three worlds with Kāmaśaṅkara,
ten thousand years passed like another mere moment.
Then, on one occasion, the venerable sage Nārada arrived, and having bowed to the Supreme Śakti, he spoke with humility: *Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* 3.15.46.
O Supreme Sovereign, You are the supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, and the ultimate purity;
yet You consist of the mental constructs of the imagination regarding the existence or non-existence of me.
O auspicious one, your manifestation has occurred for the sake of the world’s prosperity;
your activity is indeed for the destruction of the wicked, for the elevation of the virtuous,
and for the protection of the righteous.
"O Goddess, this demon Bhaṇḍa oppresses the three worlds;
he must be conquered by you alone, for he cannot be defeated by other gods."
The gods, who have resided here for a long time solely intent upon serving you,
shall now depart for their respective cities at your command.
"May these inauspicious and empty [places] become full of prosperity from this moment on!
Thus addressed by Nārada, the Goddess, the sovereign of all,
dispatched the immortals to their respective abodes.
Having honored Brahmā, Hari, Śambhu, and the lords of the quarters beginning with Vāsava according to their merit, Ambikā then sent them away.
Then, even after being sent away so that they might abandon their offense, the gods performed service to Śiva and Śivā with their respective portions, as if to their own primordial parents.
This narrative bestows long life and is the cause of all auspiciousness;
it recounts the manifestation of the Great Goddess and her royal consecration.
The wise person who, having risen at dawn, recites this endowed with devotion and faith,
shall become enriched with wealth and his speech shall become like nectar.
For that wise person, no evil exists either in this world or in the next;
he attains vast fame as well as equality with the most excellent.
Unshakable prosperity shall be his, and well-being at every step;
he shall never experience fear, for he will become radiant and heroic.

He who constantly recites [the mantra] at the three junctions of the day, having meditated upon the Mistress of the Lion Throne, becomes free from the threefold suffering and is fulfilled by the goals of human existence.
Within six months, the best of reciters shall attain great fortune.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Wedding Festival," in the Lalitopākhyāna of the Hayagrīvāgastya-saṃvāda within the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Brahmāṇḍa-mahāpurāṇa.
Now, that Mother of the worlds, the supreme goddess Lalitā,
set forth to conquer the Daitya Bhaṇḍa, the thorn of the three worlds.
They created seven oceans in the shape of mṛdaṅga drums;
with the abundant sounds of those mṛdaṅgas, they filled the sky.
There were mṛdaṅgas and murajas, paṭahas and atukulīṅgaṇas,
selukas, jhallarīs, rāṅghās, huhukas, huṇḍukas, and ghaṭas.
There were also ānaka drums, paṇavas, gomukhas, and ardhacandrikās;
likewise mṛdaṅgas, ḍiṇḍimas, and those with a barley-corn-shaped middle or a fist-sized middle.
The Jharjharas, the Barītas, those born of the divisions of Iṅgīs and Aliṅgyas,
the Uddhakas, the Caituṇḍas, the Niḥsāṇas, and others, the Barbaras.
The sounds *huṃ* and *kākatuṇḍa*, as well as other varieties of musical instruments,
resounded when struck by the armies of the Śaktis during their exertion for battle.
The goddess named Saṃpatkarī, who had emerged from the goad-weapon of Lalitāparameśānī, set forth together with her powers (śaktis).
Attended by rows of many millions of elephants, horses, and chariots,
the sovereign lady of prosperity is as crimson-red as the rising sun.
He mounted the elephant named Raṇakolāhala, who was fond of the battle with his trunk raised in intoxication and resembled a mountain.
A great army, making a terrible roar, followed after her,
scraping the sky with its flickering rows of banners.
And upon the chest of that woman, whose husband was accomplished, the thorn-like armor— dense and thick— shone as it rested there, crowded by her full breasts.
The trembling sword-blade held in his hand shone like the terrifying,
curved frown of the Lord of Time (Kālanātha).
Like mountains shaken by the onset of a cataclysmic wind,
ten million excellent elephants followed after her.
Then, born from the glorious weapon of the noose of the goddess Śrīlalitā,
she who possesses exceedingly swift prowess mounted her horse and moved ahead.
Accompanied by her, the army— consisting mostly of horses and rippling with the sound of neighing— roamed about,
tearing up the surface of the earth with their hooves as if with spades.
The Vanāyus, Kāmbojas, Pāradas, those born in the Sindhu region,
the Ṭaṅkaṇas, the mountaineers, the Pārasīkas, and others as well.
The Ajāneyas, Ghaṭṭadharas, Daradas, Kālavandijas, those born of Vālmīka and Āyavana, and the Gāndharvas— these are the horses.
The Kirātas born in the eastern regions, as well as those originating from the borderlands,
are well-trained, capable of carrying loads well, swift, and steady-minded.
They are knowledgeable of the specific intentions of their master, capable of enduring great battles,
endowed with many auspicious marks, and have conquered both anger and fatigue.
At the five streams, they were disciplined, endowed with the Śakvarī verses, and possessed of the Plava meters.
Endowed with the splendor of fruit-pearls and possessed of white shells,
they also bear the divine lotus, the divine jewel, and the divine svastika.
Then horses, swift as the wind, followed her, bearing auspicious marks such as the *svastika*, the *śukti*, the *gaḍura*, and the *puṣpagaṇḍikā*, which bestow long life and sovereignty.
He was named Aparājita, possessed of exceeding brilliance and restless energy;
his body was exceedingly tall and lofty, and his face shone with a radiant helmet.
On both sides, the circle of its quivering mane was cast down,
while the clouds were driven away by the tossing of its thick tail.
Resplendent with jeweled bells fastened to its shank-like legs,
it seemed to play music with the fierce, harsh clattering of its hooves.
The great drum of the earth’s surface resounded repeatedly for the prosperity of Vijaya,
manifesting its rhythmic progression as it went along.
Under the guise of swaying chowries, it bore two wings as it were;
it was equipped with charming trappings and adorned with a network of tinkling bells.
Making the Asuras roar with the deceptive sound of these [beasts],
the Great Goddess, mounted upon her horse, rode forth.
Holding a noose, a goad, a staff, and a horse-whip in her four arms,
she is resplendent with great valor.
Resembling the rising sun and shimmering with waves of blazing golden girdles,
she moved along mounted upon a horse, as if making the steed dance.
Then the sound of the proclamation drums for the departure of the illustrious Daṇḍanāthā made the world deaf, like the roar of a surging ocean.
Some raised spears with uplifted arms, piercing the ten directions with their hard adamantine shafts;
others were like stones hurled from upraised arms.
Some, joined with the vanguard of the army of Śrī Daṇḍanāthā,
took up swords and shields and leaped forth with fierce resolve.
Crowding the ranks of the extreme army, the female staff-bearers, warding off others with hundreds of cane-strikes, surged forward with great power.
Then, in that city, spears with high-flying banners, marked with the signs of buffaloes, deer,
and lions, moved forth.
Then, thousands of Śaktis with shimmering hands rushed forth from the illustrious Daṇḍanāthā and seized her white parasol.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Military Expedition for Victory," in the Lalitopākhyāna of the Hayagrīvāgastya-saṃvāda within the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
In the departure of Daṇḍanātha, the sky shone with countless white-gleaming umbrellas, appearing as if adorned by innumerable lunar discs.
The darkness, which had become dense within due to the sun’s parasols being joined together by their rays, was further dispelled by the luster of that jewel on his staff.
Filling the quarters of the sky with a dense, blazing shadow of vajra-light,
hundreds of kinds of palm-leaf fans, led by those with boar faces, did not move in the presence of Bali.
Fierce, with staffs and other weapons, they are intense and terrifying, bearing tridents in their hands;
their hair is flaming and tawny-hued, and they illuminate the quarters of the sky like flashes of lightning.
As if burning the multitudes of Daityas with the fiery arrows of his sharp shafts,
the armies of the Lord of the Staff marched forth, running at the head of the vanguard.
Then [there appeared] goddesses whose forms, ornaments, weapons in their hands, and personal vehicles were identical to those of the goddess Potrīmukhī.
Dark as the *tamāla* tree, tawny-haired, and with cruel eyes.
Mounted upon a thousand buffaloes, those with the faces of boars set forth;
then the illustrious Daṇḍanāthā [departed] from her excellent chariot drawn by a circle of elephants.
Having descended from the great lion, he mounted his own vehicle,
known as Vajraghoṣa, whose circle of manes was like smoke.
His face was manifest with a hideous form and wide, gaping eyes;
the clicking sound of his bared fangs deafened the very horizons.
With claws resembling the hard shells of the primordial tortoise,
they seemed to rend the circle of the earth as they plunged down to the subterranean realm of Pātāla.
Mounting her lion-vehicle, which was three *yojanas* in height and whose tail was raised aloft, the Commander-in-Chief set forth.
When that destruction of the asuras had begun, and he was ablaze with wrath,
the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, fell into great agitation.
Will she, like a female boar, consume the entire universe this very day in her wrath?
Or will she split the earth in two with the blow of her tusks? (BndP 3.17.14)
"Or else, with the blows of his plow, he will agitate the oceans"—
thus did all the hosts of gods in the sky tremble at heart.
Having gone forth, they beheld from afar those who had arrived in celestial chariots with great trepidation;
and those gods, with palms joined in reverence,
paid homage to them while repeatedly chanting the twelve names in the sky.
Agastya said:
O Lord, O horse-faced one of great wisdom, tell me what the twelve names of that goddess are, for I have a great curiosity regarding them.
Hayagrīva said:
Listen, O Pot-born One (Agastya), to the twelve names of that goddess;
by the mere hearing of them, she will become gracious.
The fifth is Daṇḍanāthā, Saṃketā, and Samayeśvarī.
Likewise, Samayasamketā, Vārāhī, Potriṇī, Vārtālī,
Mahāsenā, and Ājñā Cakreśvarī.
O Sage, these are proclaimed as the twelve names, including "Arighnī.
A human being who stands within the vajra-cage known by these twelve names shall never encounter suffering in times of distress.
With these names, those dwelling in the clouds highly praised Saṃketā;
and for the sake of bestowing grace upon them, she set forth once again.
Then, as the lords of mantras touched the feet of the Saṃketayoginī,
a trumpet resounded in the sky, signaling their departure.
An army of Śaktis marched forth, adorned primarily with ornaments of love, possessing the dark luster of tigers, and holding lutes in their hands.
Some sing and dance with voices like the call of intoxicated cuckoos, while others play lutes,
flutes, drums, and other instruments with graceful rhythmic steps.
The dark-hued Śaktis set forth, gladdening the people of the world;
some had peacocks as their vehicles, and some had swans as their vehicles.
Some were mounted upon mongooses, some were seated on cuckoos;
all were dark-complexioned in form, and some were positioned in palanquins.
And some, intoxicated by the honey of the *kādaṃba* flowers and mounted upon Sindh horses,
set forth further and further ahead, placing the Lord of Mantras at their head.
Then, having mounted the great chariot adorned with a lofty circle of banners, she— clad in armor the color of the rising sun, her eyes rolling with intoxication— [proceeded].
Her lotus-face was enchanting with tiny beads of perspiration;
she gazed with a multitude of side-long glances, accompanied by slight dances of her creeper-like eyebrows.
That entire army, though exceedingly arrogant in its power, was [overwhelmed] by his great insignia:
the peacock-feathered trident-banner.
In the midst of these and all other powers,
the Mistress of Mantras emerged, dark as a rain cloud and possessing a radiant manifestation.
The inhabitants of heaven praised her with sixteen names;
hear those sixteen names, O Pot-born One (Agastya).
She is the practitioner of song, the dark one, the deep-blue one, the mistress of mantra;
she is the female reciter, the presiding counselor, the sovereign lady, and the beloved of Śuka.
Vīṇāvatī, Vaiṇikī, Mudriṇī, the beloved of Priyaka,
Nipapriyā, Kadaṃbeśī, and she who dwells in the Kadamba forest.
And these sixteen names, O Pot-born One, are always Madā and so forth;
whoever, being embodied, praises the Queen of the Ministers even once with these,
the entire three worlds undoubtedly remain in his hand.
Wherever the Lord of Mantrins casts his glance,
there the enemy army falls utterly, devoid of fear.
Whatever discourse there may be regarding the sovereignty of Lalitāparameśānī,
as well as the discourse concerning the Śaktis, that bestows victory everywhere.
Then, from the white dove held in the hand of Saṅgītayoginī,
the science of archery emerged, bearing a ready bow.
Endowed with four arms, the hero with three heads and three eyes, full of devotion, bowed to the Sovereign of Pradhāna and said this: *Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍapurāṇa* 3.17.39.
O Goddess, leader of counselors, you are proceeding to battle against the lord of the Asuras, Bhaṇḍa; therefore, I must provide assistance to you.
O Mother, take up this most mighty bow called Catrañjīva,
which is the destroyer of the Dānavas throughout the worlds.
And take these two quivers, rich with inexhaustible arrows and adorned with gold,
for the destruction of the Daityas and as a token of my favor.
Having thus bowed her head with devotion according to the science of archery,
Priyaka’s beloved took the bows and quivers that had been offered.
And Śūkapriyā, taking up her great bow Citrajīva,
repeatedly drew the string and produced a loud twanging sound.
The world was filled with the sound of the bow of the goddess Saṃgītayoginī,
and the minds of those in the celestial realms were not satisfied by the abundance of their own bliss.
And Yantriṇī— these two attendants of hers suddenly bore the parrot and the lute and waited upon her.

Wearing [ornaments] that produced an exceedingly captivating sound through the swelling resonance of her virtues, accompanied by the jingling of her swinging bracelets, she, dark as a rain cloud, became most enchanting.
Adorned with a variegated life-arrow, that yoginī of song shone like a cluster of kadamba flowers, with her umbrella-like kadamba and her bow.
Sharp as the sidelong glance of Kālī, terrifying with its dancing serpent,
the arrow shone brilliantly as it was held in his uplifted right hand.
Afterwards, goddesses endowed with dark splendor, bearing bows and arrows, attended upon her as she was mounted on the chariot of the Geya-cakra.
Numbering thousands of akṣauhiṇīs, possessing fierce speed and languid with intoxication,
they filled the quarters with sweet-sounding shouts of "kilikila."

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The March of the Army of Daṇḍanātha and Aśyāmalā," in the Lalitopākhyāna of the Hayagrīva-Agastya Saṃvāda within the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Then the Sovereign Lady appeared, leaning upon a blazing goad and holding a noose resembling a serpent;
she bore a bow made of the wood of the *aikṣva* tree with jingling bracelets, and held five arrows of radiant flowers.
Scattering her own body— a torrent of radiance— more intensely crimson than even the thousandfold splendor of the rising sun,
she seems to create a celestial sphere composed of moonlight with the loveliness of her face.
She was radiant with a circle of white parasols, ten *yojanas* in length, which overspread the three worlds and,
being composed of pure pearls, attained the likeness of the lunar disc.

And she was fanned by a quartet of whisks, beautiful as the luster of jewels, attended by a host of chief female attendants led by Vijayā, and as skillful as the tender sprouts of the *haritakānti* plant under the light of the new moon.
Indicating her status as the sole sovereign through her power, with her territories and armies adorned by hundreds of emblems of imperial sovereignty,
her majesty was being extolled by the songs and musical performances of the immortals, and she shone with brilliant radiance.
Beyond the range of speech and beyond the range of the intellect, it cannot be conceived as having such-and-such a form; it is peerless and without equal.
She touches upon the pride of sovereign splendor belonging to the wheel of power that completely fills the womb of the three worlds,
for those who have performed service with a competitive zeal to be first, their heads crowned with large handfuls of joined palms bound in devotion.
She cast sidelong glances at the faces of Brahmā, Śiva, Viṣṇu, and the foremost of the chief gods who were raining down praises;
she suddenly held the three worlds to be composed of light, arising from her five blazing flower-arrows.
Showers of auspicious parched grain for victory were scattered by throngs of Apsarases possessing a brilliance like lightning;
they were led by Kāmeśvarī and others, endowed with lovely splendor and enchanting in their martial attire.
Constantly attended at the vicinity of his feet by those whose splendor eclipses the sun with the brilliance of their flaming weapons,
[the city] possesses a tilaka named Śrīcakra, where a banner ten yojanas high pierces through the mass of clouds on high.
Driving the chariot in the work of battle, which was equipped with a succession of extremely powerful and loud-sounding weapons,
she shone in the conflict with a captivating splendor, her body draped in a spotless garment of rising golden-yellow luster.
Being praised by twenty-five gods who were exceedingly skillful at quelling the sins of conceptual proliferation, Lalitā set forth toward the battle.
Agastya said:
O great-minded Vījinvaktra, grant me the elixir for the ears through twenty-five names of Lalitā Parameśānī.
Hayagrīva said:
Śrī Lalitā is the lion-throned Great Queen, Parāṅkuśā,
Cāpinī, Tripurā, and indeed Mahātripurasundarī.
Sundarī, Cakranāthā, Sāmrājī, and likewise Cakriṇī;
Cakreśvarī, Mahādevī, Kāmeśī, and Parameśvarī.
She is beloved by the King of Desire, she who reaches the pinnacle of desire, the sovereign of the wheel;
she is the Great Vidyā, the auspicious one, the consort of Anaṅga, and the all-pervading Pāṭalā.
She is known by twenty-five names: Kulanāthā, Āmnāyanāthā, Sarvāmnāyanivāsinī, and Śṛṅgāranāyikā.
Those fortunate ones who praise the highly blessed Lalitā, the Supreme Goddess,
attain good fortune, the eight supernatural powers (siddhis), and great fame.
Thus, agitating a great army with her fierce impetuosity,
the enraged Lalitāmbikā advanced toward the demon Bhaṇḍa.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Expedition for Victory of the Army of Lalitā Parameśvarī," in the *Lalitopākhyāna* within the dialogue between Hayagrīva and Agastya in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa-mahāpurāṇa*.
Agastya said:
Regarding those [divinities] who reside on the various joints (*parvan*) of the sovereign chariot, the king of wheels (*cakrarājaratha*),...
The deities are known by manifest names; please announce their names.
O horse-faced one, tell us their entire number, their auspicious distinctions of color, and their divine weapons.
Hayagrīva said:
The ninth section concerning the radiant chariot has arrived;
therein the Siddhidevīs are described—listen to their names from me.
Aṇimā, mahimā, and likewise laghimā, garimā,
īśitā, vaśitā, and prāpti as the seventh perfection (siddhi).
Prākāmya, Muktisiddhi, and Sarvakāmābhidhā—
these goddesses have four arms and resemble the Japā flower in color.
Holding a wish-fulfilling jewel, a skull-cup, a trident, and the collyrium of accomplishment,
they are full of compassion and attended by yogins.
There, in the eastern half, are the eight Śaktis beginning with Brahmā:
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and Cāmuṇḍā as the seventh.
Mahālakṣmī and Aṣṭamī have two arms and red bodies;
they hold a skull and a blue lotus and are clad in red garments.
Alternatively, some describe meditation in another way:
[visualizing deities] with forms similar to Brahmā and others, and bearing weapons similar to those of Brahmā and others.
They are proclaimed as bearing the supreme insignia of Brahmā and the other [deities];
those goddesses who abide in the upper regions possess the most exalted mudrās.
With hands as beautiful as lotuses, engaged in the formation of mudrās,
they resemble the pomegranate flower and are enchanting in their yellow garments.
Four-armed, holding shields and swords with their two pairs of hands,
their eyes rolling and red with intoxication— listen to me as I name them.
The mudrā that agitates all, likewise the one that puts all to flight,
the mudrā that effects the attraction of all, and likewise the one that brings all under control.
The *sarvonmādana* mudrā, the staff (*yaṣṭi*), the great goad (*mahāṅkuśā*) for all,
the *sarvakhecarī* mudrā, and likewise another, the *sarvabījā*.
The ninth is Sarvayoni, and likewise Sarvatriśaṇḍikā;
these are the mudrās of Siddhi, Brāhmī, and the others—these are the manifest Śaktis.
Listen to me as I recite the names of those known as the Guptas, who were previously mentioned and who, mounted upon red chariots, set out to effect the destruction of the demon Bhaṇḍa.
The art of attracting desire, the art of attracting the intellect, the art of attracting the ego, and the art of attracting sound. (Bṛhad-yogiyājñavalkya-purāṇa 3.19.17)
The eternal one who attracts touch is the digit (kalā) who attracts form;
the eternal one who attracts taste is the digit who attracts fragrance.

The art of attracting the mind is eternal; the art of attracting steadfastness is a craft; the art of attracting through mindfulness is eternal; the art of attracting by listening to the name is a craft.
The power that eternally attracts seeds, the power that eternally attracts the self, the eternal power that attracts nectar, and the power that attracts the body. (BndP 3.19.20)
These sixteen powers, who are the forms of the digits of the moon,
having reached the eighth joint, are proclaimed by the name Guptā.
Resembling coral trees, enchanting with gentle smiles,
they possess four arms and three eyes, and are radiant with the moon and sun as their crowns.
O Agastya, bearing bows, arrows, shields, and swords, and possessing divine splendor,
they set out for the purpose of slaying the demon Bhaṇḍa.
On the seventh lunar day, those whose names are kept most secret took up residence in the chariot of the wheel, which resembled a lamp burning at evening.
Together with Anaṅgamadanā, who was afflicted by the passion of the bodiless one (Anaṅga),
there were also Anaṅgalekhā, Anaṅgavegā, and Anaṅgāṅkuśā.
These goddesses, whose splendor arises from their recitation, are intent on embracing the bodiless one (Kāma);
they hold a sugarcane bow, flower-arrows, a flower-ball, and a blue lotus.
Possessing abundant prowess by the command of Lalitā,
they stood as if blazing with fury against the demon Bhaṇḍa.
Then, there are those who rely upon the sixth chapter of the Cakrarathendra,
headed by Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, and endowed with the name of the tradition (sampradāya).
With their masses of hair arranged in braids, radiant with vermilion tilakas,
they were of exceedingly fierce nature and possessed a luster equal to the fire of cosmic destruction.
They possess a fire-arrow, a fire-bow, a sword in the form of fire,
and a shield known as the fire-wheel, their bodies blazing with light.
Enraged toward the lord of the Asuras, these powers of command, born from the ashes of Kāma,
belong indeed to the highly majestic Lalitā.
The power that agitates all, as well as the one that causes all to flee;
the power that attracts all, and likewise the one that gladdens all.
She is the power that utterly deludes all, the power that paralyzes all,
the power that causes all to yawn with exhaustion, and the power that intoxicates all.
The power that accomplishes all aims, the power that fulfills all prosperity,
the power consisting of all mantras, and the power that brings about the destruction of all dualities.
Thus indeed have the names of the traditions been told;
now, those situated in the fifth section are known as the Kulottīrṇas.
And they, resembling the color of a red lotus,
possessed radiant forms and bore an axe, a noose, a mace, a bell, and a jewel.
"O Pot-born One, enumerate the names of these as well— those who are enraged against the enemies of the gods, their faces contorted with frowns."
The Goddess is the bestower of all accomplishments, likewise the bestower of all prosperity;
she is the Goddess who makes all dear and the performer of all auspiciousness.
The Goddess is the bestower of all desires and the liberator from all suffering.
The Goddess who pacifies all death, who wards off all obstacles,
who is beautiful in every limb, and who bestows all prosperity.
These ten goddesses, whose hearts are filled with compassion, have been described;
they reside at the fourth joint of the wheel and possess a luster equal to a string of pearls.
Ten [goddesses] renowned by the name Nigarbhayoginī are proclaimed:
Sarvajñā, Sarvaśakti, and likewise Sarvaiśvaryapradā; 3,19.42.
The Goddess consists of all-knowledge, she is the destroyer of all diseases,
her very nature is the support of all, and likewise she is the remover of all sins.
The goddess who consists of all bliss, whose very nature is universal protection, is to be known as the tenth deity; she bestows the fruits of all desires.
These [goddesses] are to be known as four-armed, wielding a vajra, a spear, a javelin,
and a discus, intent upon the slaying of the demon Bhaṇḍa.
Now, those who reside on the third spoke of the Lord of Chakras are the lords of speech, renowned by the name of the Secret Yoginīs.
With hands holding arrows and bows resembling the blossoms of the red *aśoka* tree,
their entire bodies covered by armor, they are adorned with lutes and books.
Vaśinī, Kāmeśī, Bhoginī, and likewise Vimalā;
Aruṇā, she who is called Javinī, Sarveśī, and likewise Kaulinī.
These eight goddesses are remembered as the causes for the destruction of the Daityas;
now, [I shall describe] those residing on the second joint of the sovereign chariot-wheel.
Holding a bow and arrow, a drinking vessel, a citron, and a small sword,
they are endowed with eight arms and reside upon the three seats.
Carrying a noose, a serpent-noose, and a bell of great sound,
they were intoxicated with wine and kept their secrets most strictly concealed.
Kāmeśī, Vajreśī, and another, Bhagamālinī—
these three goddesses are remembered as being filled with wrath toward Bhaṇḍa.
Possessing majesty equal to Lalitā and splendor equal to Lalitā,
these are proclaimed as the eternal inner circle (antaraṅga) of the Śrī Devī.
Now, in the great seat of Ānanda, during the middle section of the chariot,
fifteen syllables are said to have their dwellings arranged all around.
The lunar-day goddesses (tithinityās), whose forms are Time itself, remain pervading the entire universe;
their brows are knit with agitation against the Daityas, beginning with the demon Bhaṇḍāsura.
Possessing forms identical to those of the goddesses and bearing weapons identical to those of the goddesses,
they exist in age after age for the benefit of the worlds.
O Pot-born one, learn their names from me:
Kāmeśī, Bhagamālā, and likewise Nityaklinnā.
Bheruṇḍā, Vahnivāsinī, Mahāvajreśvarī, as well as Datī, the goddess Tvaritā, and the ninth, Kulasundarī.
Nityā, Nīlapatākā, Vijayā, Sarvamaṅgalā,
and Jvālāmālinikā— these fifteen are proclaimed in the Acintya [Tantra].
Accompanied by these goddesses, whose minds were ever intent on her service,
the Supreme Sovereign went forth to conquer the wicked demon Bhaṇḍāsura.
The lords of the mantra-practitioners performed a song in the great wheel, the supreme chariot;
seven sections were spoken there, and hear now those [teachings] of the Goddess.
Seated upon the central cushion of the Geyacakraratha chariot,
she is called Saṃgītayoginī, the most beloved of the Śrī Devī.
That very first section was the dwelling place of the minister;
then the second section was located in the Geyacakra on that excellent chariot.
Rati, Prīti, and Manojā, holding lutes and bows in their hands,
dark as the tamāla tree in appearance, were capable of uprooting the dānavas.
The deity of the arrows of the Mind-born [Kāmadeva], fully developed in the third joint,
consists of Drāviṇī, Śoṣiṇī, Bandhinī, and Mohinī.
These five, known as Unmādinī and the others, holding flaming bows in their hands and possessing great majesty, were present there at the base during that festival.
Kāmarāja, Kandarpa, Manmatha, Makaradhvaja,
and the fifth, Manobhava— these are the enchanters of the three worlds.
Their foreheads were radiant with musk-tilaka marks, adorned with pearls,
their entire bodies covered in armor, and they possessed the luster of palāśa blossoms.
These five desires were declared for the purpose of slaying the demon Bhaṇḍāsura;
they resorted to the fourth section of the sovereign chariot of the wheel of victory.
The foremost Brahmī and those previously mentioned, with Caṇḍikā as the eighth and supreme;
at that festival, Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī are likewise situated below.
Rati, Prīti, Kīrti, Śānti, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi are the Śaktis;
with eyes red with wrath, they set out to slay the exceedingly powerful Daitya.
O Pot-born One, the maidens who hold the spear and the discus have been described;
they are Vāmā and the other sixteen who have reached the fifth stage.
They sang songs for the lord of chariots; hear their names from me:
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Śānti, Śraddhā, and Sarasvatī.
Śrībhūśakti, Lakṣmī, Sṛṣṭi, Mohinī,
as well as Pramāthinī, Āśvasinī, and likewise Vīci.
Then there are Vidyunmālinī, Surānandā, and Nāgabuddhikā;
these, possessing the luster of kuruvinda gems, are intent on agitating the world.
Providing a great abundance of ambrosia at every step,
others were clad in adamantine armor and radiant with loud laughter;
they bore adamantine clubs, *śataghnīs*, and *bhuśuṇḍikās*.
Then, the Bhairavas, headed by Asitāṅga and others, who were terrifying with their weapons, took their place upon the sixth section of Gītirathendra.
Bearing tridents and drinking vessels, they possess a dark blue luster;
they are Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, and Unmattabhairava.
Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra—these are the eight Bhairavas;
they are established in the seventh section of the Gītirathendra.
Mātaṅgī, Siddhalakṣmī, Mahāmātaṅgikā,
and Mahatī Siddhalakṣmī— these are red in color and bearers of arrows and bows.
Beneath that very archway are Gaṇapa and Kṣetrapa, as well as Durgāmbā and Baṭuka; all of them hold weapons in their hands.
Right there, below Parvaṇi, are Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī;
Śaṅkha and Padma, the two treasures (nidhi), all of whom hold weapons in their hands.
Enraged against the enemy of the world, Śakra and the others, ending with Viṣṇu— the lords of the ten directions— [approached] Bhaṇḍa of fierce prowess.
On that lunar day (parvan), those who have taken refuge below take on the forms of the Śaktis:
the Vajra, the Śakti, the Kāladaṇḍa, the Aṅkuśa, the Pāśa, and likewise the Dhvaja.
Holding a mace, a trident, a blade of darbha grass as a weapon, and a thunderbolt,
these lords of mantrins constantly serve her, endowed with devotion.
Eager to carry out Lalitā’s command through the medium of their lord, the minister, they sought to slay the wicked and arrogant Asuras, who were thorns to the universe.
Near the chariot of the wheel of songs, the guardians of the directions took their positions;
and Mantriṇī was stationed at the gate for all the gods.
The petition of the Great Goddess bestows the accomplishment of one's purpose;
and the petition of Rākṣī is likewise performed by way of the principal gate.
Indeed, just as the attainment of results occurs for servants,
otherwise how could these [servants] possess such power, blazing with splendor?
Regarding the approach to the Illustrious Goddess, whose power is invincible:
she [the goddess] is indeed known as Saṅgītavidyā, and she is exceedingly dear to the Illustrious Goddess.
In the accomplishment of all tasks, she never transgresses what has been commanded by the Goddess anywhere within the sovereign empire of Śrī Devī’s power. She is the ministering lady over all rites.
She is capable of not acting, of acting otherwise, and indeed of acting;
therefore, all the guardians of the directions, desiring victory for the illustrious Goddess,
perform only service to her, who is the supreme sovereign.
Thus, the names of the goddesses stationed on the excellent royal chariot-cakra of the illustrious Goddess Lalitā have been fully recounted. (BndP 3.19.93)
In the destruction of the demon Bhaṇḍāsura, her divine weapons were also described,
and the Geyacakras and the goddesses of the Parvas were proclaimed.
Those men who hear these names of all the goddesses shall be liberated from all sins and become victorious.

Thus, in the Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa, in the Uttara-bhāga, within the Hayagrīvāgastya-saṃvāda, in the Lalitopākhyāna, in the section concerning the revelation of the names of the deities stationed on the chariot of the Śrī Cakra-rāja,
Hayagrīva said:
"The five sections of the supreme Kiricakra-ratha are as follows:"
And listen, O wise one, to the names of the deities, by hearing which there is victory.
First, the Mistress of the Staff arrived at the stage known as Parvabindu;
there she devoured the multitude of thorns that were the unruly ones of the world.
Causing the Goddess Jayaśrī to dance with various kinds of flames.
The proud Dānavas were shattered by the blows of his uplifted tail,
while the night was illuminated by the rays of the young moon-like fangs.
The creeper-like body of the great chariot of the Kiricakra, dark as a mass of monsoon clouds, always appears as if adorned;
it is a female elephant that has brought forth the entire host of Āvartaka clouds as its offspring.
Residing upon the second spoke of that very nave of the chariot are indeed three:
Jṛmbhinī, Mohinī, and Staṃbhinī;
they resemble blossoming pomegranate flowers and are the crushers of all the Dānavas.
And they held pestles, plows, and vessels for wine, set with clusters of gems,
upon their sprout-like hands which were encircled by rings of blazing rubies.
With their exceedingly sharp and terrifying eyes, as if burning the Daitya soldiers with their flames,
they fearlessly serve the Boar-faced one.
Residing in the third section of the great chariot Kiricakra are the five goddesses beginning with Andhinī, who have established their abodes within the divine machine.
Tearing asunder the three worlds with their harsh, boisterous laughter,
they assumed the guise of women while appearing like the flames of the fire at the end of an aeon.
Desiring to lick the blood-soaked ground of all the armies of the asura Bhaṇḍa,
they were blazing as they licked with their flickering tongues.
Constantly serving Daṇḍanāthā, who possesses formidable prowess,
they have taken refuge in the fourth section of the great chariot of Kiricakra.
Excluding the fifth and also excluding the eighth, there are six goddesses beginning with Brahmā,
whose bodies consist of the blazing flames of the six cakras.
As if subduing the Dānavas with a great flood of valor,
they attend upon that region by the command of Daṇḍanāthā.
Beneath that very same joint reside the swift ones, having taken their places:
Yakṣiṇī, Śaṅkhinī, Lākinī, and likewise Hākinī.
Śākinī and Ḍākinī, whose unified form is Hākinī— the seventh— these possess the prowess of fierce, staff-like arms.
As if drinking up all beings, as if drinking up the earth itself, they consume the skin,
blood, flesh, fat, and bones of their enemies.
Then, with their hideous faces, they drank the marrow and the semen,
filling the ten directions with their harsh lion-like roars.
They are called the Lords of the Elements (dhātunātha), bestowers of the eight supernatural powers beginning with atomization (aṇimā);

In devouring the wicked Daityas and cutting them down to the very root,
the wise have severed all calamities for those possessed of devotion.
They are called the Lords of the Elements (dhātunāthas), residing within all the elements;

In just half a moment, those who had accomplished many thousands [of feats] emerged,

[This applies] to those who commit treachery against their own mistress, those who violate their own pledges,
those who commit treachery against the Veda, and those treacherous enemies of the heroes.
They are equal to the devourers of wicked Daityas who commit sacrilege against sacrifices;

On the second side of that very mountain peak, in a divine palace,

And two [maidens] were fanning her with chowries, their trembling bracelets like moving vines,

With eyes always rolling and faces always smiling,

On both sides, he has taken up his two excellent weapons—

With this pair of weapons,

At the very front of that army division,

Day and night, the Daṇḍanātha goddesses, who have offered millions of Dānavas as oblations into the fierce heat of their preeminent and supreme wrath, attend upon Lalitā.

Vārtālī, Vārāhī, and that supreme one, Vārāhamukhī.
Andhinī, Rodhinī, Jṛmbhiṇī, Mohinī,

Terrifying with his fierce lower lip like the staff of Death,

With a gurgling roar, as if laughing at the buffalo of Time,

Beneath that very mountain peak dwell the various deities of the eight directions, Indra and the others, who have made their abodes in painted forms.
Indra and the Apsarases, numbering sixty-four crores, arrived to announce the successful accomplishment of Lalitā’s task.
The Siddhas, Agni, the Sādhyas, and likewise the Viśvedevas;

Brahmā, the two sons of Aśvinī who are experts in the science of medicine,

The bees were fully satiated by the nectar dripping from the stalks of their hoods;

Jṛmbhiṇī, Staṃbhinī, and Mohinī—
these three [goddesses] are at the end of that very radiant Kiricakra parvan.
Bearing a skull and a mace, with hair standing on end and a massive body,

With a great vajra-laugh of Aṭṭahāsa, he rent asunder the circle of the Brahmāṇḍa;
with the sound of his ḍamaru drum, he split open the hollow interior of heaven and earth.
Carrying in his hand the serpent-noose joined with Phūtkārī-Tripurā,

And standing near him was the lion that served as her vehicle;

The characteristics of the lion, the vehicle of the Goddess of the Gods, have already been described above;

Adorned with all ornaments and weapons like those of Daṇḍinī,

Drohiṇī, Śyāmā, and their mistress.
Filling their skulls with upward-flowing streams of blood,

Then, near those goddesses who have the faces of jackals,

With a great roar of "huṃ," he displayed his white brilliance in his belly,

On that very same festival day, his excellent vehicle remains;

The river of wine flows on, assuming a divine form;

Whenever the Daitya Bhaṇḍa engages in battle,

That too will become a marvel in this very year, there is no doubt;

Beneath that very same mountain peak, in the eight directions and indeed also above,

They were great and most formidable, renowned for their vast prowess;

At the time of the end of the kalpa, by the command of Daṇḍinī, those who devour the universe— beings of exceedingly fierce nature— bared their fangs and bit their lips together.

Yamajihva and Ekapāda, as well as Kāla and Karālaka; Bhīmarūpa, Hāṭakeśa, and likewise the one named Acala.

Wherever the chariot of the king of wheels is, there is the supreme chariot of song;

Desirous of achieving the destruction of the demon Bhaṇḍa, she shook;

All beings were agitated at the departure of Laliteśa;

The Gandharvas, the celestial singers, beginning with Viśvāvasu,

Reciting verses of victory and auspiciousness with powerful songs,

Filled with joy and intoxicated with passion, the seven seers, Vasiṣṭha and the others, danced at every step in the forms of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
Increasing the glory of victory with mantras in the form of Atharvan hymns,
they nourished it just as a great fire’s most purifying flame is fed by an oblation.
Those supreme beings gladdened her with great blessings;
being thus praised by them, Lalitā shone resplendently upon her excellent chariot.
In order to utterly defeat the demon Bhaṇḍāsura, he set out together with his soldiers and his uplifted weapons.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Deities of the Kiricakra Chariot," in the Lalitopākhyāna of the Hayagrīvāgastya-saṃvāda within the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Brahmāṇḍa-mahāpurāṇa.
Having heard the sound of the departure for the procession of Goddess Lalitā,
the inhabitants of the city of the demon Bhaṇḍāsura were seized by great agitation.
And there, on the shore of the great ocean near the mountain of Mahendra, was the city of the wicked-minded demon Bhaṇḍa, who was possessed by evil desires.
That place became famous throughout the three worlds by the name Śūnyaka;
indeed, it was the eternal abode of the Daitya Viṣaṅga’s elder brother.
In that very city, which was a hundred yojanas in extent,
all the gods were terrified by the agitation caused by the arrival of the Goddess Śrī.
That entire city of the Asuras, extending for a hundred yojanas,
was repeatedly enveloped as if by smoke produced by portents.
Even at an improper time, the walls in the city of the Daityas were shattered;
great meteors, whirling about, fell from the expanse of the sky.
The first of the portents, an earthquake, occurred;
the entire city of Śūnyaka blazed there.
At that very moment, the inhabitants of the Daityas' city experienced a trembling of their hearts;
likewise, the herons, vultures, and cranes perched upon the tops of the banners did so as well.
Having seen [the sun] in the solar orb again and again, many flesh-eaters there cried out loudly; they were not even looked upon with eyes.
Suddenly, harsh voices from the sky spoke,
and everywhere in all directions, soiled comets were seen.
Smoking and causing agitation among the Daityas and Rākṣasas,
the ornaments and garlands of the Daitya women fell off prematurely.
Crying out "Alas! Alas! from afar and with tearful eyes, they wept together for their mirrors, their armor, their banners, and their collections of swords.
The gems and the silken garments repeatedly became soiled throughout the palaces,
the moon-chambers, and the pleasure-houses on every side.
In watchtowers, cow-pens, marketplaces, and assembly halls;
in quadrangles, shrines, porticos, and ramparts.
In dwellings that are auspicious on all sides, in houses with the *nandyāvarta* design,
in those with decorative panels, in agitated inner courtyards,
in all *svastika*-shaped structures, and in the recessed chambers of the inner apartments.
At the gate-towers, on the door-panels, at the junctions of the roof-ridges, in the windows, in the courtyards, in the sacrificial hearths, and in the threshing-floors; ||| BndP_3,21.16 |||
Everywhere in the cities inhabited by the Daityas,
harsh and loud cries uttered by living beings were heard from the multitudes of people.
The fierce, leafy, and terrifying forest became slack on all sides; the sun was beheld by the crows with their harsh cries,
and tens of millions of skulls let out shrieks as they fell to the earth.
Drops of blood-water fell upon the middle of the sacrificial altars,
and masses of hair, grey with smoke, flew out in every direction.
Having observed the portents occurring on the earth, in the atmosphere, and in the heavens, all the city-dwellers, being greatly terrified,
reported them to Bhaṇḍa, whose prowess was renowned.
And that Bhaṇḍa, his fortitude unshaken by those multitudes of portents arising from Pracaṇḍa, returned to the place of the mantra.
Like Mount Meru, the lord of the Daityas occupied an unsurpassed throne, which was variegated with many jewels and possessed a form of diverse parts.
Illuminating all the quarters with the dense rays of the jewels set in his shimmering crown, that lord of the Dānavas shone forth.
In a great assembly pavilion one yojana in extent,
his younger brothers then attended upon him as he sat upon a lofty lion-throne.
Viśukra and Viṣaṅga, possessed of great strength and prowess,
were terrifying with their staff-like arms that had become thorns to the three worlds.
Never transgressing the command of their elder brother again and again,
they increased their great fame gained in the conquest of the three worlds.
With their heads, they did not even touch his soft footstool;
having performed a prostration at his feet, they both sat down upon the ground.
Then, while that foremost of the enemies of the gods remained in that place,
all the neighboring lords of the Daityas arrived to see him.
Indeed, there was no counting of those individual armies;
pronouncing each their own name, they bowed down to Bhaṇḍakeśvara.
And he remained for some moments, looking upon all those asuras with glances whose pupils were exceedingly steady.
Viśukra spoke to that elder brother, the lord of the Dānavas,
with a voice like the roar of the bolted gates of the great ocean being churned.
O Lord, their strength and prowess have been shattered by Your staff-like arms;
they are sinners, of vulgar conduct, evil-minded, and the lowest of gods.
Finding no refuge anywhere else and overcome by despair,
they fell into a fire filled with blazing flames and met their destruction.
A certain woman, born from that god and proud of her strength,
was indeed created by the gods, Vāsava and the others, themselves.
Furthermore, their prowess was incited by those men of great zeal;
they were accompanied by numerous female attendants and adorned with various weapons.
"Alas, what a cruel stroke of fate! They are coming indeed to conquer us;
will a mere multitude of weaklings defeat us, who are so powerful? (Bṛhadbhārata Purāṇa 3.21.36)
"In that case, this attempt to shatter a stone with a mere fragment of a leaf,
though it may be conceived as a means to destroy [the enemy], serves only for ridicule."
Is this not a mockery? Is this not shameful? Would there not be fear even of our own vanguard warriors?
Śakra and the other denizens of the three heavens,
as well as Brahmā and the rest, fell into a state of dejection, their bodies weary from my strength and weapons.
What talk can there even be of Viṣṇu? That Maheśvara is terrified;
what mention can there be of others here? Those guardians of the quarters have fled.
By our sharp, invisible arrows that strike the limbs,
the gods have been rendered everywhere pierced in their armor and deprived of their arrogance.
Even for us, who possess such great prowess and the heat of our arms,
some woman runs toward us today to thwart our victory.
Even though she is a woman, she must never be disregarded;
for even a minor enemy should not be underestimated by those who know themselves and desire victory.
Therefore, servants should be dispatched to drive her away;
having dragged that woman, arrogant with pride, by her hair, she must be brought here.
"O King, after a long time, that wicked woman will resort to the status of a maidservant for the fawn-eyed women dwelling within your inner apartments."
Indeed, from each single soldier among these armies who stands as an adversary,
the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, truly tremble in fear.
"O Dānava, the mind of the Lord is indeed the authority," having thus informed Bhaṇḍa Daitya, he further increased his anger.

But the great being Viṣaṅga, wise and discerning in his investigation, spoke thus to the haughty chief of the Daityas: BndP_3,21.48: "The great being Viṣaṅga, who knows how to investigate and is possessed of insight, said this to the arrogant first-born of the Daityas."
"O Lord, subduer of enemies, you alone know every matter to be done;
nothing should ever be spoken to you, for you abide on the path of statesmanship."
Everything should be done after careful deliberation; deliberation is the supreme course.
For if an action is undertaken without deliberation, it cuts away one's very roots.
Spies should be diligently dispatched to the enemy's camp;
one who desires the certain attainment of victory must ascertain their strength and weakness.
With spies as his eyes, firm in wisdom, and always suspicious in mind,
he should maintain an appearance of being unsuspecting while keeping his counsel secret from even his own ministers.
Employing the six expedients toward every worthy object, a king attains victory; a fool, however, is swiftly destroyed.
Any undertaking whatsoever that is begun without due reflection leads to destruction;
however, an action performed after careful deliberation specifically bestows victory.
Whether they be animals, women, or even lowly persons, kings must not show contempt for their enemies; for power may manifest anywhere.
By a certain being born from a pillar, who had assumed the body of a human-animal,
Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain among all living beings.
For in ancient times, a woman named Caṇḍikā, who was manifested by me,
slew Niśumbha, Śumbha, and Mahiṣa in battle.
In that connection, many Daityas were destroyed by her;
therefore, I say: let no contempt whatsoever be shown toward women.
For power alone is everywhere the cause of the glory of victory;
we have no fear of those who, having attained the status of being the substratum of power, possess either female or male gender.
Power, however, shines forth from all sides by its very nature within this cycle of existence;
therefore, let the activity of that wicked desire be understood by you.
"O Lord, let this be investigated: who is she, from what has she arisen, what is her conduct, what is her support, what is her strength, and who are her companions?"
Thus addressed by Viṣaṅga, he said: "What deliberation can there be regarding those of great splendor?
Within our army are one hundred commanders of akṣauhiṇīs, beings of immense power."
"You are capable of drinking up the oceans and burning the triple heaven;
O you of sinful conduct, why do you vainly fear women?"
All of that was previously observed by me through my spies; first, a certain woman named Lalitā appeared before us.
This woman of delicate form possesses a name that corresponds exactly to her reality;
yet she has neither strength nor valor, nor does she have a place in battles.

And that [host] was devoid of discernment, being entirely devoted to illusion; through its very existence, it perceived a multitude of women as belonging to itself, though they did not exist in reality.
Did you not produce [it], yet it does not act in such a manner? Or rather, let there be great power according to the principle stated by you.
By whom can Bhaṇḍa, whose greatness transcends the three worlds, be conquered?
Even now, the inhabitants of heaven, rendered unconscious by the crushing impact of the strength of my arms,
are not even capable of drawing breath.
Some were in the depths of the netherworlds, some in the waters of the oceans,
some in the far corners of the directions, and some in the groves of mountains.
Melted with grief and utterly terrified, having abandoned their wives, sons, and prosperity,
those wretched beings wander about in disguised attire, fallen from their positions of authority.
She does not know such prowess of my arms; for she is a weak woman who has only recently been born, and it is because of that that she indulges in such pride.
Foolish women, whose reckless impulses are in vain, do not understand; deluded as to what ought and ought not to be done, they rush headlong toward their own destruction.
Or else, if the denizens of heaven— such as the Mahoragas, Siddhas, or Sādhyas, who are fierce in battle— approach placing her at their head;
Whether it be Brahmā, or Padmanābha, or even Rudra, the lord of the gods,
or any other protectors of the quarters— I am capable of crushing them all.
Or else, the commanders in my armies, intoxicated by battle,
will grind the enemies down like ripe karkarikā fruits.
