These and other such heroes, equal to Hiraṇyakaśipu and equal to Hiraṇyākṣa, are my sons of great strength.
From each one of them were born more than a hundred heroic sons;
these generals of mine, who were arrogant in their conduct, were pursued by my sons.
In battle, they will destroy the arrogant, lowest of immortals;
whatever enraged ones there may be in the fight, even those superior hosts of thousands of *akṣauhiṇīs*,
shall be reduced to ashes— alas, what need is there to speak of the weak?
All her illusory displays and the playful manifestations of Mahāmāyā on the field of battle were reduced to ashes by his power.
"Let not your mind be distressed by that vain suspicion," having said this, Bhaṇḍa, the lord of the Daityas, rose from his royal throne.
He spoke to his own general, the mighty Kuṭilākṣa:
"Rise up! Equip the entire army with armor on all sides!"
Station troops all around Śūnyaka and at the gates; secure the fortresses and prepare hundreds of catapults.
Evil sorceries must be performed by the ministers and the priests;
prepare your weapons, for this battle has arrived.
"Now, dispatch whichever among the generals is most formidable to the front,
accompanied by a multitude of various forces and terrifying in appearance."
Therefore, at the time of battle, having assembled and conquered that foolish woman— who was not proud even toward the divine being— he dragged her by the hair.
Having thus addressed the commander of the army, the lord of three thousand [divisions],
the great being Kuṭilākṣa, he himself went to the inner apartments.
Then, as the goddess Śrī was descending, the sounds of her procession— drums and the noise of conchs—
were heard by the lords of the Daityas, causing them extreme anguish in their ears.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Egoism of the Asura Bhaṇḍa," in the Lalitopākhyāna of the Hayagrīva-Agastya Saṃvāda within the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Now, following the echoing resonance of the conch-shells of the army of the illustrious Lalitā,
the sound of kettledrums arose from the lords of the asuras as they prepared for battle.
By him, who had crushed the quarters of the sky, who agitated the ocean of the womb [of the earth],
and who deafened the world, the triad of worlds trembled.
Crushing the multitude of the quarters and shattering the mountain caves,
the roar of the Daityas' war-drums filled the expanse of the sky.
The drum of the enemy of the gods resounded loudly and discordantly with the fierce sound of the great roar of "huṃ" uttered in fury by Narasiṃha.
Then, making a tumultuous sound of "ki-li-ki-li," tens of millions of Daityas,
filled with rage, armed themselves against that Supreme Goddess.
Another, his body covered with armor variegated with jewels,
shone like the lofty Mount Rohaṇa in motion.
A certain soldier brandished a well-polished dagger, which was like the fierce Night of Doom and had been concealed by a blacksmith.
With the tip of his uplifted lance,
he simultaneously performed various maneuvers on the path while mounted upon his horse.
Some warriors mounted upon elephants of towering stature,
which resembled mountains driven by the force of a cataclysmic wind.
With spears, mallets,
hammers, slings, *druhaṇas*, *bhuśuṇḍīs*, axes, and even clubs.
With maces, *śataghnīs*, tridents, and arrows,
with half-moons, great discs, and those with curved bodies and serpent-like faces;
With various types of serpent-headed arrows, with bows such as the Śārṅga,
with staffs, slings, thunderbolt-arrows, and excellent stones.
With middle-finger-sized [blades], fist-sized [blades], with fronds, and even with fragments;
with daggers, with middle-angled [blades], and with hundreds of serpent-like fangs.
With thousands of weapons such as nooses, with noose-tipped beaks, and with crow-beaks—
such extremely fierce instruments that snatch away life.
Tens of millions of Daityas had their hands and forearms grasped [by others] and were clad in armor;
some were horse-riders, some elephant-riders, and others were riders of donkeys.
Others were riders of camels, riders of wolves, and riders of dogs;
there were those who rode upon crows and other such birds, as well as riders of vultures and riders of herons.
Others ride upon tigers and the like, while others ride upon lions and the like;
some ride upon śarabhas, and others ride upon bheruṇḍas.
Mounted upon boars, mounted upon serpents, and mounted upon spirits and the like— thus they proceeded toward Lalitā, riding upon various kinds of mounts.
With their inner minds overwhelmed by intense anger,
they set out toward the crooked Dānava named Durmada, the commander of the army;
accompanied by ten akṣauhiṇīs, he was sent against Lalitā.
Accompanied by warriors who were fierce in their strength, as if desiring to consume the entire universe,
that commander-in-chief marched toward Lalitā.
Shattering the fourteen worlds with the clamor of his drums and manifesting loud bursts of laughter, he went forth, intoxicated and with that [terrible] face.
Then, commanded by the asura Bhaṇḍa, the mighty Kuṭilākṣa stationed Tālajaṅgha, accompanied by ten akṣauhiṇīs, at the eastern gate of the city of Śūnyaka for the purpose of its protection.
At the southern city gate, he stationed ten thousand akṣauhiṇīs for the sake of protection, appointing the Daitya named Tālabhuja as their commander.
At the western city gate, he stationed for the sake of protection a Daitya named Tālagrīva, accompanied by ten akṣauhiṇīs.
At the northern gate of the city, however, he commanded the mighty Tālaketu,
accompanied by ten akṣauhiṇīs, for the purpose of protection.
He assigned ten akṣauhiṇīs, arranged in a circular formation, to the city’s outer wall and to the houses with their turrets.
Having thus provided protection for the empty city with fifty akṣauhiṇīs, he reported that event to his master.
Kuṭilākṣa said:
"O Lord, by your command this army has been assigned for the protection of the city;
previously, Durmada was sent against that wicked Lalitā."
"By merely becoming our servant, that woman has indeed become utterly hopeless;
nevertheless, the duty of protecting the city must be performed by kings."
Having spoken thus to the Daitya lord Bhaṇḍa, the exceedingly arrogant Kubalākṣa,
accompanied by his generals, prepared his own army.
The Dānava messenger, previously dispatched by Kuṭilākṣa,
arrived with his army and drums, and surrounded Lalitā’s forces.
Uttering cries of "kila-kila," thousands of soldiers there fell upon the spear-wielding troops with their swords brandished.
And those Śaktis, with raised staffs and the sound of bursting laughter,
their luster like blazing weapons, fought with the Dānavas.
A battle took place between the Śaktis and the Dānavas, which illuminated the three worlds and turned the sky into a mass of rising dust.
The dust, rising from the rows of chariots,
intensified by the trunks of elephants and scattered by the breaths of horses, reached a great roar.
Beholding him approaching, surrounded by ten akṣauhiṇīs,
Saṃpatsarasvatī rushed toward him in battle out of anger.
Presided over by powers equal to those that bring prosperity,
the horses and rutting elephants crushed the army of Dānava.
When a tumultuous battle broke out with a clamor of shouting, while dust was being stirred up and kettledrums were being beaten; BndP_3.22.38.
A vast ocean of blood surged here and there from the thousands of Dānavas being struck down by the spears.
The banners lay prostrate, their shafts severed by arrows;
along with the multitude of parasols, their respective emblems were cast down.
On the battlefield, crimson with blood, the circles of fallen umbrellas bore a resemblance to the snowy rays of the moon amidst the red clouds of twilight.
Like the fire at the end of an aeon with its crest of flames in the beautiful ocean,
the hosts of the Daitya armies surrounded the multitudes of Śaktis.
With their necks severed by the edges of weapons blazing with power and intent,
heaps of the heads of the Dānavas fell upon the surface of the battlefield.
The surface of the battlefield became entirely covered with heads that had bitten lips, were cruel with frowns, and had eyes bloodshot with rage.
When this time had thus arrived, which brought terror to the wheel of the world,
the Śaktis, intensely enraged, crushed the army of the Daityas.
Struck here and there by weapons of power and rendered unconscious,
the Dānavas perished there, struck down by the might of the goddess Saṃpad.
Then, having comforted his own broken army, Durmada, the subduer of enemies,
mounted a camel and suddenly rushed toward the host.
With its long neck held high and its back struck with cruel blows,
the mount, an elephant-like camel, trembled as it was driven by that intoxicated man.
With angry hearts, they followed that wicked one who was mounted upon a camel;
all of them, though terrified, desired to fight with spears for the sake of giving protection.
He covered the quarters with broad-headed arrows possessing glittering tips, just as a cloud covers a forest with rain, showering the enemy host that brings about prosperity.
Struck by that invincible being with many arrows,
Saṃpatkari’s army became as if paralyzed for a moment on the battlefield.
Then Saṃpandikā, casting a gaze red with anger and mounted upon a war-elephant amidst the tumult of battle, fought with him.
In that battle, her hand— made exceedingly lovely by the jingling of swaying bracelets— having drawn the bowstring back to her ear, [held] the bow.
Due to his lightness of hand, he did not perceive the drawing back nor the releasing;
he saw only the circle of the bow during the holding of the arrow.
The arrows, released from the bow of Sampatkarī, their tips clearly reflecting the contact with the sun’s rays, utterly consumed the enemies.
Then a fierce battle took place between him and Durmada;
from their mutual collision, sparks flew forth like swarms of bees.
First, by the arrows discharged, a darkness arose between the Goddess of Prosperity and the enemy of the gods, eclipsing even the sun.
And in that interval, sparks born from the intense clashing of arrows displayed a cleverness in their whirling motion.
Mounted upon that elephant, whose flanks were covered with armor and who raised a great clamor,
he displayed many kinds of prowess in the battle.
With his hand he struck some Daityas, with kicks others,
and other Dānavas with blows from his uplifted tusk-like mace.
Some enemies were slain by his tail, others by his roars,
some by the crushing of their limbs, and others likewise by his claw-strikes.
By striking with his broad chest, he crushed certain Daityas;
that elephant of the goddess Saṃpad performed a dexterous maneuver.
Intoxicated with extreme pride and inflamed by anger, he struck off with a single firm feathered shaft the single jewel situated upon Saṃpatkarī’s crown.
Then, pierced in the chest by the arrows released by her whose eyes were red with rage,
Durmada quickly gave up his life.
Then, after letting out a tumultuous roar, other excellent soldiers and the foremost leaders of the Śakti army slew those preeminent Dānavas.
The remaining Daityas, rendered powerless by spears and arrows,
fled from the field of battle and took refuge in the empty city.
Then, having heard that account, the lord of the Dānavas became enraged.
Blazing as if within himself with fierce power,
that one of terrible gaze touched his sword for the sake of hand-to-hand combat and spoke to the commander of the army, Kuṭilākṣa, who was standing nearby.
How did that wicked woman cause the fiercely intoxicated and powerful one to fall in battle? Alas, how painful is the course of destiny!
That power which was never thwarted among the gods, the yakṣas, or the lords of the nāgas— even he,
Durmada, has been slain by a woman.
To conquer that wicked woman and to forcibly seize Kaca,
dispatch the army commander named Kuraṇḍa, who is fierce in battle.
Having been summoned by him, Kuṭilākṣa went forth and,
before the lord, called forth Mahābala, Kuraṇḍa, and Caṇḍador-daṇḍa.
That Kuraṇḍa, having arrived, paid homage to his master and commanded him;
Kuṭilākṣa said to him, "Go and prepare the soldiers."
"You are skilled in illusion and expert in various modes of combat; you are adept at treacherous warfare—subdue that woman."
Thus instructed by that crooked-eyed one in the presence of his master,
Kuraṇḍa, of fierce prowess, quickly departed from the city.
Surrounded on all sides by twenty akṣauhiṇīs,
crushing the sphere of the earth with elephants, horses,
and foot soldiers, Caṇḍa Kuraṇḍa, the elder brother of Durmada, went forth to battle.
Making the horizons tumultuous with his cries, though his mind remained steadfast,
he departed on a swift horse, seized by the planetary spirits of grief and anger.
Taking up his Śārṅga bow with its terrible twang and loud sound,
he rained down streams of arrows upon the great army that was rushing toward him.
O wicked one, having slain my younger brother— who was intoxicated with pride and fierce in battle—
why do you vainly carry this great arrogance, which is but a mere fragment of a tiny portion of valor?
And now, behold me as I shall send you to the city of Death with these volleys of iron arrows!
Let the Pūtanas of battle drink your exceedingly heart-stealing and most sweet body-fluid, which has emerged from your wounds— a novel delight for women.
"O wicked woman, you shall now experience the fruit of that transgression arising from the slaughter of my younger brother; behold the strength of my two arms! (BndP 3.22.82)
Thus threatening Saṃpatkarī,
who was mounted upon a noble elephant, he encouraged his army to crush the forces of Śakti.
Then Caṇḍī, intent on crushing that army of the highly powerful Kuraṇḍa, rallied her own troops.
Then, having mounted her horse and approached with affectionate tenderness, she whose curiosity had been aroused by the unprecedented sight spoke these words to her: BndP_3.22.85.
"O friend, bringer of prosperity, listen with affection to my words:
grant me the opportunity to perform this battle, which is preeminent in its virtues."
"Endure for a moment in battle; he shall fight with me alone.
You have been requested as my friend; do not entertain any doubt in this matter."
Having heard these words of Queen Saṃpadā, Śucismitā turned back the army that had set out toward Kuruṇḍa.
Then, presided over by Śaktis possessing the hue of the rising sun,
the horses— swift as the wind— were like waves upon the ocean of the army.
Repeatedly scratching the earth with their hooves,
they fell in a single stream at the front of Kuraṇḍa’s army.
In the acts of moving forward and backward, in the divisions of the gaits, in the revolutions and evolutions, in the various types of paces, and in the fivefold striking of the hooves; BndP_3,22.91.
And in the battle, he encouraged the horse with four types of signals originating from the tips of his hands and feet— signals that were clever and understood by the horse’s heart.
Encouraged by Kuraṇḍa, the intoxicated Dānavas fought together with the armies of Ambikā’s forces who were mounted on horses.
While this battle between the spears and the enemies of the gods was thus proceeding,
he mounted a swift horse named Aparājita and charged toward the ill-behaved Kuraṇḍaka, who was mounted on a steed.
Beautiful with her swinging braid, radiant as a digit of the autumn moon,
her lovely face was like the orb of the cool-rayed moon reddened by the twilight.
As if smiling in the midst of battle, the horse-faced goddess, grasping her jeweled bow,
showered Kuraṇḍa with a torrent of arrows.
Hurled by those mounted on horses,
the gold-feathered arrows with stone-tipped heads spread across the ten directions, pervading the intermediate spaces of the quarters.
The elder brother of Durmada, the enraged Kuraṇḍa of fierce prowess,
overwhelmed those mounted on horses with arrows discharged from his Śārṅga bow.
Tearing through the army with his fierce hooves at extreme speed,
the horse-riding Aśvatara crushed the Dānavas.
From her neighing, the roar of the ocean at the time of cosmic dissolution was eclipsed from afar,
as it overwhelmed the many enemies who had been brought there by her.
As the host of Daityas fled here and there,
she who has the horse as her seat released her own divine noose-weapon, which was blazing in form.
From that noose, millions of other nooses, terrifying as serpents,
repeatedly bound that entire army and rendered them unconscious.
And that Kuraṇḍaka, enraged by the bond of the soldiers,
severed her jeweled bowstring with a single arrow.
Having cast aside her bow whose string was severed, she, mounted upon her horse and exceedingly enraged,
hurled a goad into the chest of that evil-minded one.
By that blazing hook, his life-blood drained away,
Kuraṇḍa fell to the ground like a tree shattered by a thunderbolt.
Then, certain fierce Putanas, spat out by his goad, devoured that army— which was like a flow of nooses— and were destroyed.
When Kuṇḍa, the commander of twenty akṣauhiṇīs, had been thus slain,
those remaining Daityas fled away in haste.
Hearing that Kuraṇḍa, along with his younger brothers, had been struck down in battle by the forces of Śakti,
even the lord of Śūnyaka sighed like a serpent.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Slaying of Durmada and Kuraṇḍa," in the Lalitopākhyāna within the Hayagrīva-Agastya Saṃvāda of the Uttara Bhāga of the glorious Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa.

Now, when Kuraṇḍa had been struck down by her mounted on the horse, the Dānava Bhaṇḍa spoke these words to Kuṭilākṣa once more, desiring to fight again: BndP_3.23.1: "When Kuraṇḍa was cast down by her mounted on the horse, the Dānava Bhaṇḍa spoke this to Kuṭilākṣa, desiring to fight once more."
That which was not even conceivable in a dream, that which was never heard before,
and that which was not suspected in our minds— this very calamity has now arrived.
The two brothers Kuraṇḍa and Durmada were virtuous and well-disposed;
this great power belongs to the deceitful and wicked slave-woman.
Henceforth, dispatch Karaṅka and the other four commanders of the five armies, along with a hundred akṣauhiṇīs, onto the field of battle.
Those heroes, intoxicated by battle and ready to cast away their bodies in combat,
will by all means conquer that woman of wicked wit and wanton charms.
Having heard these words of Bhaṇḍa,
Kuṭilākṣa, filled with great agitation, summoned Karaṅka and the other generals.
Having paid homage to their master, they were incited by Kuṭilākṣa;
blinded by rage, they departed from the city as if leaping into fire.
Hearing the unbearable sound of the war-drums of their departure, the elephants of the quarters quickly reeled about with their ears shattered.
And a hundred akṣauhiṇīs set out for Ketumāla;
with its surging horses and other mounts, it shone with intoxicated elephants.
Crowded with neighing horses, filled with the cries of shouting soldiers,
with trumpeting elephants and the roaring of chariot wheels, that host set forth.
With his radiance extinguished by the dust of the earth struck by the rims of the wheels,
the sun appeared as if shrouded by a heavy fall of snow.
The entire circle of the world became as if composed of dust,
and in some places it was filled with sound by the harsh clanging of iron mallets.
Overwhelmed by the rising masses of dust, the soldiers of the Daitya army could no longer perceive even the extent or the number of the host.
Banners of many forms, adorned with figures of fish, serpents, and other creatures,
moved along like fish in a great ocean amidst a mass of dust.
Seeing them rushing forward toward Lalitā’s army,
all the immortals were terrified by the fear of a defeat for their own forces.
Those five haughty generals, Karaṅkamukha and the others,
performed a most powerful illusion named Sarpiṇī in the battle.
By them was conjured up a wicked female serpent,
a sorceress of enchanting appearance, smoke-colored with smoke-hued lips and smoke-colored breasts.
Like the great ocean, with a belly containing extremely deep caverns,
she moved before the Śaktis in battle, terrifying their minds.
Like another wicked Kadrū, she was adorned with many serpents;
she was the source of origin for snakes whose bodies were composed of illusion.
Waving upon the surface of the earth at the vanguard of the generals,
she, crying out with a terrible roar, caused them to reel in many ways.
In that very same way, those evil-souled lords of the Asuras— Karaṅka and the others, who were lustful for the five kinds of flesh— formerly deceived them by means of illusion.
Then the battle of the gods' enemies with their spears commenced,
as they were incited by one another's heroic taunts and possessed of intense fury.
Due to the extreme confusion, their respective powers and the Dānavas themselves could not distinguish one another; nevertheless, with weapons in hand, they continued to strike.
In that place, where fire was produced by the clashing of one another's weapons and the intervals between the quarters were obscured by the flowing streams of discharged arrows; BndP_3,23.24.
Where elephants were being swept away by the flood of many rivers of blood,
and where the circles of chariots lay motionless, submerged in the mire of flesh;
In that place where blood flowed like a torrent shimmering with scattered hair as its moss, and which was terrifying with the exceedingly harsh and destructive roars of lions; (BndP 3.23.26)
At the root of the darkness of passion, which brings satisfaction to the rākṣasīs,
blood flows from the necks of the daityas severed by the sword and the arrows.
When the terrible battle with the darts of the enemies of the gods had commenced, she,
being urged by the five [brothers], took her own power and emitted many serpents from her body like a female serpent.
Resembling Takṣaka and Karkaṭaka, with splendors headed by Vāsuki,
they possess various forms and colors and are terrifying with their diverse glances.
The three worlds were scorched by the flames of various kinds of poisons:
dārada, vatsanābha, kālakūṭa, and others besides.
And there is the Saurāṣṭra poison, the terrible Viṣa, and another, the Brahmaputra; then the Śauklikeya, which has been acquired, and other poisons as well.
With their own mouths and flickering double tongues, the serpents,
scattering [venom] upon the army of Śakti, rushed forth from the bodies of the female snakes.
Smoke-colored, two-faced, and exceedingly terrifying serpents,
blazing with anger, rose up from the pair of eyes of the female serpent.
Yellow-colored snakes with three hoods and terrifying faces with fangs emerged from the hollows of the female serpent's ears in tens of millions.
Holding their heads, complete with hoods, at the tips of their tails,
those hooded serpents emerged from the mouth of the blue-bodied female serpent.
And others, possessing strength and color, four-faced and four-footed,
emerged from her nostrils, endowed with fierce radiance.
From her large breasts, which were covered by a hanging great hide,
and from her navel-pit, many blood-colored and terrifying beings emerged.
And the lords of serpents rose up, bearing the *halāhala* poison,
biting at Śakti’s army and burning it with their poisonous fires.
Binding them with coils of their hoods and striking them with circles of their crests,
these serpents threw the army of Laliteśī into utter confusion.
Though they were repeatedly shattered by millions of weapons and spears, they remained unharmed.
Those who extend their kinship increase higher and higher;
many serpents perish, while others are born again.
At the moment one is destroyed, many others arise;
since the serpent that is the root remains corrupted, she does not perish.
Therefore, when the snakes created by him were destroyed, other snakes arose;
and from that, the bodies of Śakti’s soldiers [were consumed] by the fires of poison.
Being consumed by suffering, they became overwhelmed in battle as the Śaktis and Cakras were rendered bewildered as to what should be done by the serpents.
Those five Dānavas displayed many kinds of prowess;
one of them, mounted upon a chariot yoked with hundreds of donkeys, appeared like a lordly elephant.
Another commander of the Bhaṇḍa daitya army, named Vajradanta, crushed Śakti’s host with a sharp-edged discus.
Indeed, by the impact of his adamantine arrow, he caused a tumultuous battle;
then Vajramukha himself [struck] the exceedingly great Cakrīvant.
Another powerful commander of armies, named Vajradanta, having mounted [his elephant], crushed the circle of spears with the edges of his tusks.
Mounted upon a chariot drawn by a pair of vultures,
he struck with his arrows those wicked generals who had incited him in the battle.
And a hundred akṣauhiṇīs fell in a single moment,
along with a wicked serpent-woman who was possessed of many illusions.
Moment by moment, she dispatched crores of hooded serpents;
seeing her army thus shattered, she became agitated with rage.
Nakulī, mounted upon Garuḍa, descended onto the field of battle;
she shone like molten gold and was born from the lovely palate.
Having the form of the entirety of speech and possessing teeth made of diamond,
she unleashed her own power there against the serpent.
With his lofty shoulders presided over by her,
Garuḍa, scattering mountains with the flapping of his wings, advanced into battle like a moving Mount Sumeru.
Seeing the terrifying serpents born from the illusion of the female serpent,
the female mongoose opened her mouth wide, her eyes bloodshot with rage.
Then, from the thirty-two crores of teeth of the goddess Śrī Nakulī,
thirty-two crores of mongooses with the luster of gold were born.
Tearing apart the circles of female and male serpents here and there,
and destroying their venom by the crushing of their own fangs,
the poison-destroying golden-brown mongooses roamed through the terrible battle.
With ears pricked up from the touch of rage, their every hair bristling, the mongooses,
with mouths wide open, bit at the snakes as they sprang forward.
From each illusory serpent, Babhru produced one [counter-serpent] and,
with the striking of his sharp teeth, tore its body to pieces.
In the battle, mongooses leaped about, licking with their leaf-like tongues their corners of the mouth, which had turned crimson from the blood flowing from the bodies of serpents.
The bodies of the serpents,
being bitten by mongooses, writhed repeatedly with their coils coiled up in extreme agitation.
In that battle, the jewels carved upon the hoods of hooded serpents whose lives had perished after being bitten by mongooses shone brilliantly.
With their circles of hoods shattered by the blows of Nakula and emerging from them,
the hoods shone like the flames of the great fire of his malice.
When the illusory web of snakes had been thus torn apart by circles of brownish-yellow light, the female serpent gave way to anger.
Having waged a great battle with her, that Nakuleśvarī fixed an exceedingly cruel Gāruḍa weapon upon her arrow.
That Gāruḍa weapon, illuminating the quarters of the sky with its unrestrained flames,
entered the body of the female serpent and dried up the serpent's illusory power.
With the destruction of the power of illusion (māyā-śakti), the serpent vanished;
and with her destruction, the five leaders of the armies fell into a state of wrath.
That female serpent, by whose power you had held all the gods in contempt as your general,
has been reduced to nothing but a story through the prowess of Nakula.
Therefore, the soldiers, exceedingly enraged by the destruction of their own forces,
overwhelmed that army of Nakula with a single concerted effort using floods of weapons.
Though she was but one, that mistress of armies, mounted upon the chariot of Tārkṣya, became fivefold in battle by virtue of her light-handedness, raining down a shower of weapons.
With spears, maces, and slings by the thousands,
and with tusks as hard as the essence of diamond, he bit into the vital points and joints.
Then the servants of the Daityas, uttering terrible cries of "Alas!
Alas!", were thrown into confusion by mongooses with fierce teeth.
Leaping up from the sky, some, emitting terrible shrieks,
filled the quarters with their cries as they blazed with rage against the army of his enemies.
Some bit his ears, others bit his nose, and some bit the surface of his head; others, having approached from behind, bit him as well, their actions unrestrained.
Maimed, their armor shattered, and their weapons dropped in fear,
those enemies of the gods fell, overwhelmed by mongooses.
Some, entering the gaping mouths of their enemies,
pulled out the coils of serpents and bit the surface of their tongues.
Others, in the form of mongooses, entered the ears of the enemies of the gods;
appearing in subtle forms, those tawny creatures entered various apertures.
Beholding his own troops thus overwhelmed by mongooses and appearing wretched, Karaṅka gave way to anger.
And there were other commanders of armies as well, dexterous of hand and possessed of great strength.
Like clouds pouring forth showers of rain,
the arrows released from the full-drawn bows of the generals of the Daitya army fell with a tawny hue;
they struck a harsh impact against the tips of the tusks of the elephants.
From more than a hundred elephants belonging to the generals of the army, struck by the multitudes of arrows from the general’s allies,
fire issued forth from their tawny bodies as they were struck by thunderbolt-like weapons;
and all five of them were slain in a single moment by those discharged by the commander of the army.
With clusters of reeds bearing trembling fruit, he crushed Babhru’s army;
with tens of millions of arrows scattered here and there by the commanders of the host,
the Nakulas, their limbs shattered, surrounded Nakulī.
Then that voice of Nakulī, the sole mistress of eloquence,
was seized with great wrath due to the reversal of fortune for the Nakulas.
He fixed upon the wielder of the Śārṅga bow a great weapon named Akṣīṇanakula, which faces in all directions and has its tip enveloped in flames of fire.
Then, from that weapon, millions of mongooses were spat forth—
possessing diamond-like bodies, diamond-like hair, diamond-like fangs, and great speed.
Hard as the essence of a diamond, dense, and terrifying with their diamond nets,
they quickly tore open the surface of the earth with their diamond-shaped claws.
They are adorned with eyes that shine like vajra-jewels;
they resemble the falling of a thunderbolt and produce hissing sounds through their nostrils.
They crushed the army of the enemies of the gods with the tips of their tusks;
those sinless ones displayed many kinds of prowess.
Thus, by means of billions of Nakulas, terrible as thunderbolts and possessed of great strength,
the vile Dānavas were destroyed limb by limb and perished.
Thus, when Bala was thwarted by those adamantine circles of weapons, he was brought low.
In that battle involving a hundred akṣauhiṇīs, those leaders of the armies— reduced to only their own mothers due to extreme terror and seized by rage—
drew their bows and waged an even greater conflict.
Engaging in a manifold battle with them, the sovereign lady of Nakula severed the hard head of Karaṅka with her spear.
Tārkṣya, repeatedly swooping down upon his four enemies who were crying out like crows, severed their heads with his sword.
Seeing such agility on the part of Nakulī, Śyāmalāmbikā—
She considered herself a great being who would destroy the wicked asuras;
and Śyāmāmbikā gave her the reality of the deity of her own limb.
When such supramundane qualities are seen, in whom would joy not arise?
Those who remained after being struck down, trembling with fear, have gone for refuge to the Lord of the Mongoose.

The white parasols of the Daityas were eclipsed by the drops of blood flowing from the multitudes of elephants being slain,
which fell upon their heads.
Neither the directions, nor the sky, nor the mountains, nor the earth, nor anything else was seen;
only the dust was visible, thick with the fainting [of all things].
The trees on its banks were revealed by the throngs of dancing headless trunks,
while the river was as tender as sprouts of moss with the thousands of hair-tufts of the Daityas.
Resplendent with a circle of white parasols and white lotuses,
she possesses a succession of feet like tortoises that have severed the hosts of elephants with their wheels.
The great mountain-like masses of the throats of the mighty Daityas were shattered by her spear;
it was covered with severed trunks and fallen, frothing *bala* and *cāmara* fans.
Its banks were made dense by nets of sharp sword-blades,
and it shone with rows of pearls released from the eyes of heroic Daityas.
A river of blood flowed between the two armies as they fought, agitated by hundreds of cranes that were the fragments of the hosts of the Daityas' mounts.
Thus the battle commenced, terrifying even unto death;
on the morning of the fourth day of battle,
it continued for two watches, fierce for both armies alike.
Then the battle between the venerable Goddess Lalitā and Bhaṇḍa took place,
with the horizons made tumultuous by the clash of missiles and counter-missiles.

Extremely terrifying with the twanging of bowstrings and the sounds of "huṃ," he [struck] with fearsome arrows released from the excellent bow drawn from the mouth of his quiver— arrows that were life-taking in battle.
Due to the speed of his manual dexterity, nothing could be discerned regarding the movement of the Great Queen’s lotus-like hands in the discharge of arrows;
O Pot-born One, listen as I shall tell you everything that occurred in that battle.
Upon being joined to the bow it was one; upon its release from the bow it became tenfold;
in the sky it became a hundredfold; upon reaching the army of the Daityas it became a thousandfold;
and upon striking the limbs of the Daityas, the arrows reached the number of ten million.
Creating profound darkness and piercing the two worlds with her arrows,
the Great Queen struck the vital organs of the fierce one with her mighty shafts.
Then that Dānava, Bhaṇḍa, whose eye was red with rising anger,
rained down a great shower of arrows upon Laliteśvarī.
He discharged the great weapon named Andhatāmisraka;
the Great Goddess repelled it with her arrow, Mahātaraṇi.
In the battle, the great hero Bhaṇḍa discharged the weapon of the heretics;
the Mother of the World (Jagadambikā) released the Gāyatrī weapon for his destruction.
Bhaṇḍa discharged the Andhāsra missile, which destroys the vision of the Śakti;
his mother quelled it with the great Cākṣuṣmata missile.
In that great battle, Bhaṇḍa discharged the weapon named Śaktināśa;
however, Viśvāvasu dispelled its pride with his own weapon.
Enraged, the Dānava Bhaṇḍa discharged the Antaka weapon with great force;
he destroyed that army with the Mahāmṛtyuñjaya weapon.
Bhaṇḍa discharged the weapon called Sarvāstrasmṛtināśa;
Cakreśī destroyed its power with the Dhāraṇā weapon.
Bhaṇḍa discharged the Bhayāstra, which strikes terror into the Śaktis,
while the Mother of the Universe released the Abhayāṅkara Aindra-weapon.
The Dānava unleashed the weapon of great diseases upon the armies of Śakti;
from that, diseases such as consumption (rājayakṣmā) and others arose by the thousands.
In order to achieve the warding off of that [obstacle], the supreme goddess Lalitā discharged the great weapon of the great mantra consisting of her three names.
Acyuta, Ananta, and Govinda arose from the arrows;
having burned those diseases with a mere *huṃ* sound, they brought about joy.
And having bowed to that Great Goddess, they returned to their own abodes, commissioned to bring about the alleviation of the disease of her devotees throughout the three worlds.
The Dānava Bhaṇḍa discharged the weapon that destroys life-force,
but the queen released the weapon in the form of Kālasaṃkarṣaṇī.
The Dānava Bhaṇḍa discharged the unrestrained great weapon of the Asuras;
from that, thousands were born, possessing massive bodies and great strength.
Madhu and Kaiṭabha, as well as Mahiṣāsura,
the Daitya Dhūmralocana, Caṇḍa, Muṇḍa, and other such Asuras.
Cikṣubha and Amara, as well as the asura Raktabīja,
and Śumbha and Niśumbha— the mighty Kālakeyas.
And others named Dhūmra arose from that weapon;
all those foremost of Dānavas [attacked] with circles of harsh weapons.
Crushing the army of Śakti and roaring terrifyingly, the Śaktis, being crushed by the Daitya, cried out in distress, "Alas! Alas! (hā-hā).
"Having sought refuge in Lalitā, [they cried out] 'Save us! Save us! in haste.
Then the Goddess, becoming violently enraged, let out a roar of laughter in her wrath."
Then there arose a certain illustrious goddess named Durgā,
fashioned from the splendors of all the deities and possessing a universal form.
The trident was given by Śūlin, the discus was presented by Cakrin,
the conch was given by Varuṇa, and the spear was bestowed by the Fire-god.
In that great battle, he received from Marut a bow and two inexhaustible quivers,
and from Vajrin a thunderbolt bestowed by Caṣaka and Dhanada.
The staff of Time (Kāladaṇḍa), the great staff, the noose bestowed by the Holder of the Noose (Varuṇa),
the water-pot given by Brahmā, and the bell presented by Airāvata.
She bore a sword and shield bestowed by Death, a necklace presented by the Ocean,
and ornaments granted by Viśvakarman.
With their limbs, which possess rays resplendent like the multitude of beams from the thousand-rayed sun,
they illuminate all weapons with great splendors.
Adorned with various equipments given by others,
Nārāyaṇī mounted her lion-vehicle and engaged in battle.
In that manner, those Dānavas who resembled buffaloes were struck down,
just as he had performed his ritual action in the past according to the Caṇḍikāsaptashatī.
In that very same way, she performed the difficult task of crushing the pride of Mahiṣa and the other demons upon the circle of the battlefield; having done so, she prostrated before Lalitā.
The Dānava Mūkāstra, corrupted by wickedness, discharged the weapon named Mahāvāgvādinī against the armies of Śakti; it was a weapon created by the Mother of the World.
In that battle, the arrogant Dānava Bhaṇḍa created thieves of the Veda, which is the embodiment of knowledge— the lowest of Asuras.
Repelled by the nail of the thumb of the Great Queen’s right hand,
the exceedingly brave demon Bhaṇḍa discharged the ocean-weapon in battle.
There, the army of Śakti sank into the surging flood of water; then,
from the nail of the forefinger of the auspicious Lalitā’s right hand,
the Primal Tortoise (Ādikūrma) emerged, measuring a yojana in length and breadth.
Supported by him with his vast, broad-edged vessel of great enjoyment,
the Śaktis were filled with joy and abandoned their fear of the ocean.
The Blessed One drank up that entire ocean water,
while the wicked Dānava discharged the great weapon of Hairaṇyākṣa.
Therefore, thousands were born with golden eyes and maces as weapons;
while the army of the Śaktis was being struck down by them, it became terrified and overwhelmed,
fleeing here and there as their martial efforts slackened.
Then, from the nail of the middle finger on the right hand of Śrī Lalitā,
the Great Boar emerged, white like Mount Kailāsa.
By that boar-like one, who was equal to a thunderbolt,
those crores of Hiraṇyākṣas were torn asunder and, being crushed, went to their destruction.
Then Athabhaṇḍa, out of extreme anger, knit his brows;
from his knitted brows were born crores of golden [beings].
Blazing like the sun, with lamps as their weapons and horses,
they crushed the army of Śakti and also crushed Prahlāda.
He who is Prahlāda, characterized by supreme bliss among the Śaktis,
became that very boy who was oppressed by Hiraṇya.
Having sought refuge with Lalitā, the Queen attained compassion; then, by her power, she protected Prahlāda in the form of Nanda.
The Great Goddess shook the tip of the ring finger of her right hand;
from that shaking, Maheśvara’s mass of matted hair was stirred, and his three eyes blazed forth.
Janārdana has the face of a lion and the form of a man; below his throat he has claws as weapons, possesses the form of Kālarudra, and utters a terrible, loud laugh.
Possessing thousand-fold mighty arms, he was the observer of Lalitā’s command;
he [subdued] all the Hiraṇyakaśipus born from the frowns of Bhaṇḍa.

In an instant, the goddess Lalitā tore apart the most terrible weapon of the lord of the Balis, which destroys all the gods, with her nails as hard as thunderbolts; she hurled it back at the great asura Pratibhaṇḍa.
Then, for the destruction of the mirror of weapons, hundreds of dwarfs of great splendor emerged from the tip of the little finger of the Mahārājñī’s right hand.
Increasing in strength moment by moment, those mighty beings with nooses in their hands bind the powerful lords of the asuras— born from weapons— with the fetters of their snares.
Born from the tip of the little finger of his right hand were the wives of Kāmeśa;
possessing massive bodies and great vigor, they utterly destroyed that weapon.
On the field of battle, the demon Bhaṇḍa discharged the Haihaya weapon;
from it were born thousands of millions of Sahasrārjunas.
Then, struck by the nail of the thumb on the left hand of Śrī Lalitā,
the descendant of Bhṛgu blazed up, filled with wrath and uttering a lion’s roar.
Tearing these apart with the heavy edge of his axe,
he destroyed those numbered as the thousand Arjunas in a mere instant.
Then the Daitya Bhaṇḍa, enraged, uttered a roar of defiance (*huṅkāra*) out of anger;
from that roar was born [a being] bearing a sword as bright as the moon.
Surrounded by a demonic army consisting of a thousand akṣauhiṇīs,
he took his younger brother Kumbhakarṇa and his son Meghanāda,
and crushed that host of Śakti at a great distance.
Then, from the nail of the index finger of the left hand of Śrī Lalitā,
Kodaṇḍarāma appeared, accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa.
Wearing a crown of matted locks, with a quiver bound to his back by a creeper-like strap,
dark as the petal of a blue lotus, he repeatedly drew his bow.
In an instant, he destroyed the Rākṣasa army with divine weapons;
he crushed his own brother Kumbhakarṇa, the son of Pulastya,
and Lakṣmaṇa annihilated the great hero Meghanāda.
The Dānava Bhaṇḍa unleashed the exceedingly terrifying Dvividāstra;
from it were born many monkeys with tawny eyes.
In his extreme fury, he— emitting cruel *kreṅkāra* roars and possessing jaws each as large as Hanumān— utterly destroyed the army of Śakti.
Then, from the nail of the middle finger on the left hand of the illustrious Lalitā,
there emerged Tālāṅka, whose eyes were reddened by the midst of his wrath.
With his limbs clothed in blue garments, as pure as Mount Kailāsa,
he destroyed all the monkeys produced by the weapon of Dvivida.
The one of great strength created a mighty weapon named Rājāsura;
from that weapon, many royal Dānavas were born.
Śiśupāla, Dantavakra, Śālva, the lord of Kāśī,
Paiṇḍraka Vāsudeva, Rukmī, and Ḍimbhaka and Haṃsaka.
Śambara and Pralamba, as well as the Asura Bāṇa,
Kaṃsa, the wrestler Cāṇūra, Muṣṭika, and Utpalaśekhara.
Ariṣṭa, Dhenuka, Keśin, Kāliya, the two Yamalārjunas,
Pūtanā, Śakaṭa, Tṛṇāvarta, and other such asuras.
The great hero named Naraka, an asura in the form of Viṣṇu,
arose along with his many armies, weapons in hand.
To destroy them all, the eternal Vāsudeva was born from the nail of the ring finger of the lotus-hand of the goddess Śrī.
He manifested the fourfold form, and from that he became four;
the second was Vāsudeva, while the other is known as Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Pradyumna and Aniruddha, all of them with their weapons gleaming,
[slew] those entire host of ill-behaved ones who did not follow the path of the Lord of the Earth.
They destroyed the great asuras who were disguised in the attire of kings.
Then, when they had been destroyed, the enraged Dānava Bhaṇḍra released the terrible Kalya weapon, which causes the destruction of dharma.
Then the Andhras and Puṇḍras will arise as kings,
along with Kirātas, Śabaras, Hūṇas, and Yavanas of wicked conduct.
Corrupters of the Vedas, enemies of dharma, destroyers of living beings,
and those who cause confusion among the castes and stages of life— these foul-limbed ones repeatedly crushed the armies of Lalitā’s Śaktis.
Then, from the nail of the little finger of the radiant lotus-hand of Śrī Lalitā, there arose Janārdana named Kalki.
Mounted upon his horse, he whose splendor was blazing let out a loud, mocking laugh;
by that very sound, which resembled the crash of a thunderbolt, all [were struck].
The Kirātas fainted and perished, while the Śaktis were filled with joy;
those Lords of the ten incarnations, having performed this difficult task.
Having paid homage to Lalitā with their palms joined in reverence,
those fish were appointed by Lalitāmbā to protect the Dharma in every kalpa; thus commissioned, they set out for Vaikuṇṭha along with the twice-born.
When all the weapons had thus been destroyed,
the evil-minded one discharged the weapon of great delusion (mahāmoha), by which the Śaktis were rendered unconscious.
Having discharged the Śāmbhava weapon, Ambā destroyed the Mahāmoha weapon.
When this great battle had thus arisen with streams of missiles and counter-missiles,
the youthful Lord of Rays (the Sun) began to set behind the mountain of sunset.
Then, by means of the Nārāyaṇa weapon, that goddess Lalitāmbikā reduced all of his Akṣauhiṇī divisions to ashes in the battle.
Then, with the Pāśupata weapon, which possessed the brilliance of a blazing fire at the end of time,
the Great Queen crushed forty commanders of armies.
Then he [beheld] that wicked Ekaśeṣa, whose kinsmen had been entirely destroyed,
blazing with rage and causing the ruin of the world.
The Supreme Goddess Lalitā deprived of life the great Asura, the great being Bhaṇḍa of fierce prowess, by means of the Mahākāmeśvara weapon, which possesses the radiance of a thousand suns.
Then his city, including its women, children, cattle-pens, wealth, and grain, was overwhelmed by the flames of that weapon and became a void.
The entire area was suddenly consumed by fire until only the bare ground remained;
with the destruction of Bhaṇḍa, the three worlds danced with joy.
Having thus accomplished the work of the gods, she of irreproachable character— the glory that adorns the circle of the chariot of the Sovereign Śrīcakra,
Kāmeśvarī, the mother of the three worlds— shone forth, her majesty radiant and enriched by the splendor of her bowless [state].

When the sun had set, the goddess Śrī, whose power is renowned, brought back to her own camp the entire army, which was exhausted by the labors of battle and scorched by the fierce fire-arrows of the demon Bhaṇḍāsura.

O Lord of those whose wealth is austerity, for him who recites even once this *Lalitāmbā-bhaṇḍadānavavadha* composed [by me], all calamities go to destruction; and for one who has attained the eight supernatural powers (*siddhi*), both worldly enjoyment and liberation indeed remain in the palm of his hand.
Those men who recite this purifying *Lalitāparākrama*, which destroys all sins and bestows every spiritual attainment (*siddhi*), on auspicious days, shall enjoy the highest abundance of fortune.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Slaying of the Asura Bhaṇḍa," in the Lalitopākhyāna of the Hayagrīvāgastyasaṃvāda within the Uttarabhāga of the Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa.
Agastya said:
O horse-faced one of great wisdom, I have heard this most excellent narrative.
The valor of Lalitādevī has been described by you as preeminent.
O horse-faced one, I am well-pleased by the faultless deeds of the Goddess;
I have heard of that great power of the two ministers, Daṇḍin and Nātha.
O Hayānana, what did Ambikā do there after the battle on the night of the fourth day when dawn had broken?
Hayagrīva said:
Listen, O wise one born from a jar, to that deed which was performed afterwards by that Mother of the World after the Dānava Bhaṇḍa had been slain.
He repeatedly gladdened the entire army of the Śaktis— which had been afflicted by hundreds of battles with the Daityas— with his eyes drenched as if in nectar.
Through the stream of nectar from the side-glances of Lalitāparameśānī,
the Śaktis, their minds filled with joy, cast off the exhaustion of battle.
At this juncture, all the gods, led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, arrived to serve him, gratified by the crushing of Bhaṇḍa.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, as well as Śakra and the other gods of the thirty-three;
the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Maruts, and the Sādhyadevatās.
The Siddhas, Kimpuruṣas, Yakṣas, the night-stalkers beginning with Nirṛti,
and the great Daityas beginning with Prahlāda— all these indeed dwell within the cosmic egg.
Having arrived, they praised with affection the Great Sovereign Lady of the Lion Throne.
Brahmā and the others said:
Salutations, salutations to you, the sole Lord of the world; salutations, salutations to the one named Śrī Tripurā!
Salutations, salutations to the slayer of the great asura Bhaṇḍa; let there be salutations to Kāmeśvarī, the Mistress of the Left!

O Cintāmaṇi, skilled in granting what is thought of; O you whose waves and crests have been contemplated for a long time; O you who are variegated garments and the progenitor of the wondrous world; O you who are eternally called "Wonderful" and the bestower of happiness—homage to you!
O Goddess who bestows liberation, whose crest is adorned with the charming moon, whose smile is lovely, who is skilled in the discernment of enchantment,
and who is fond of mudrās in the silver Tantra worshipped by Mudreśvarī— salutations, salutations to You!
O destroyer of the cruel ender, O you of delicate limbs who assume a dark form in times of wrath,
O you whose face is like a boar’s, who have protected the circle of armies and embraced all fear— homage to you!
O Lalitā, who are surrounded by a retinue of goddesses with six limbs, who are praised by Vedic verses endowed with the six limbs,
who abide within the six cakras, who are joined with the six waves, and whose form consists of the six states of being— salutations to you!

Obeisance to you, who are the essence of desire, auspiciousness, and all that is primary and eternal; O lotus-eyed one, seated upon your beloved’s lap; O bestower of desires, O passionate one, O beloved of Kāma and Śambhu, O sovereign of the arts! BndP_3,30.16 //

O Consort of the God of Gods, salutations to you who are endowed with compassion, who possess the form of a multitude of cities beginning with divine herbs, and who shine intensely with the splendor of a thousand suns.

Obeisance, obeisance to you, O Mother of the world, who are to be served by the eightfold powers beginning with *aṇimā*, who dwell upon a throne radiant with the nature of Sadāśiva, who are worthy of the assembly, and whose feet are eternally worshipped.
O you who are served by the hosts of Mothers with faces like Brahmā, O beloved of Brahmā, O friend and protector of the Brahmins,
O stream of the nectar of Brahman, O royal swan among women, O Sovereign of Brahmā— salutations to you, Śrī Lalitā!

O you who are served by all the mudrās headed by Saṃkṣobhiṇī; O destroyer of saṃsāra! O witness to the essence of the playful form of saṃsāra; eternal salutations to you, O Lalitā, O Sovereign Lady, who draws in names with your sixteen digits, and who is to be served by the Pramatha host.
O eternal one, whose manifold display of compassion is free from fear; O you with rows of dark-blue locks of hair, salutations, salutations to you!

You who are incessantly served by the goddesses of Love, exulting with the flowers and other offerings of the bodiless god; you who destroy the unworthy, whose form is a mass of imperishable syllables; O graceful one, salutations to you, who have destroyed the host of enemies!

Salutations to you, who dwell in the pure state and the pure refuge, rich in splendor, brilliantly illuminated by the fourteen primary garlands of flames beginning with Saṃkṣobhiṇī, and who sustain yourself within that which is abounding in grace.

O Śrī Lalitā, who are praised by Śarva, the Siddhas, and others; whose lotus feet are known by the omniscient; who are supreme over all, omnipresent, and the bestower of all accomplishments—salutations to you!
O Goddess whose wheel-stage is resorted to by other goddesses who have become omniscient; O fulfiller of the desires of all immortals; O mother of the entire world—protect us! BndP_3,30.24.
I bow to you, O Sovereign of Speech beginning with Vaśinī, who carry the radiance of the expanding wheel;
O ocean of words, whose hair is dark as a rain-cloud, O granter of boons, O beautiful one, protect the universe! BndP_3,30.25 //
Homage to You, who are the sovereign of all divine weapons such as the *bāṇa*, a forest fire at the edge of the army-forest of the demon Bhaṇḍāsura,
and a sea ablaze with most fierce splendor, being resorted to from every side.
O Mistress of Desire, Mistress of the Vajra, O Thou whose form is the Mistress of the Bhaga; O Daughter, skilled in destroying Time;
O Thou who made the hosts of Daityas insignificant through Thy discourse; O Lotus-eyed One, abiding in the Lord of Desire—salutations to Thee!

Salutations to you, O Lalitā, who abide as the *bindu*, whose singular form is the digit of the *bindu*, whose nature is the *bindu*, and in whom the light of consciousness has expanded; you who possess a necklace swaying upon large breasts, and who are of vast power.
O Goddess who eternally dwells upon the lap of Kāmeśvara, whose nature is Time, who have shown compassion,
O you who arise at the end of the aeon in the form of Kālī, O granter of desires, O wish-fulfilling creeper— salutations to you!
O lady with eyes like a young deer and a face like a lotus, you who are cool as thick nectar under the moon of Varuṇa,
the eternal ground of the essence of all essences, and the sovereign of all branches of knowledge— homage be to you!
By your power, through the wife of the fire of consciousness (cidagni) as revealed by Śrī Śambhunātha,
the fierce Bhaṇḍāsura and others— who had become thorns to the world— were slain in battle.
Having assumed all these fresh forms through floods of the nectar of intense compassion for us,
you have made the entire world live happily, O beautiful one, who is attainable by the virtuous.

He who was detached because of his residence in the hermitage of Sthāṇu, which was produced from the expansion of the second splendor of the noble Śrī Śambhunātha, and whose enjoyments were destroyed by separation from Satī; // BndP_3,30.33 //
Therefore, they set about uniting Umā—who had obtained birth within the lineage of the mountains—with him;
thus did they incite Smara toward him as he remained engaged in formidable asceticism.

Then, consumed by the fire from his forehead produced by that anger which destroyed his passion and asceticism, Madana was reduced to nothing but ashes; from those ashes, indeed, this Bhaṇḍāsura was born.
Thus, the destruction of that evil-minded one, who was intoxicated by the pride of battle, has been accomplished by you.
Now, for our sake, may you quickly become the one who restores Kāma to life once more.
This Rati, distressed by separation from her husband, has attained the most unfortunate state of widowhood;
yet, through the arousal of desire produced by you, she shall once again find a protector in Śrī Lalitā.
But upon seeing her, the Lord whose crest is the moon, though already deluded by the mind-born god of love as before,
will immediately marry that Pārvatī after performing a great and most extensive worship for a long time.
And from the union of those two, a prince shall be born, the leader of the entire host of gods;
by that very hero, having cast down in battle the king of the enemies of the gods named Tāraka— BndP_3,30.39.
If he who is the friend of the evil-minded demon Bhaṇḍa— that comet of destruction for the three worlds—
is slain in battle by the son of Śrīkaṇṭha, then our very life-force shall be established once more.
Therefore, O Mother Tripurā, having brought forth from Rati a son who is the destroyer of the pride of people and the foremost hero among the gods of love,
dispel the sorrow of widowhood for me, whose hair is disheveled.
This helpless woman, her slender frame wasted by the loss of her husband, has sought refuge in you;
she bows before you who are named Tripurā—therefore, show her a measure of your compassion.
Hayagrīva said:
Having thus praised her, Maheśānī and the foremost of the gods, beginning with Brahmā,
showed Rati to them, soiled and emaciated by grief.
With tears streaming down her face, her hair disheveled and grey with dust, she—
having cast off all ornaments due to widowhood— bowed before the Mother of the World.
Then, the Supreme Goddess, moved by compassion arising from that sight, [looked] from her side-glance; thereupon, he whose lotus-face was smiling with happiness was born.
With a great longing for his former body, intoxicated with passion,
he has two arms, is adorned with all ornaments, possesses flower-arrows, and carries a bow of flowers.
Gladdening his beloved Rati from a previous birth with a sidelong glance,
the goddess Rati, in turn, was filled with joy upon seeing her own husband immersed in a vast ocean of bliss.
Gladdening Rati, his beloved from a former birth, with a sidelong glance,
the goddess Rati too, plunging into a vast ocean of bliss,
was filled with joy upon beholding her own husband.
"O Śyāmala, having bathed her and adorned her with garments, girdles,
and other ornaments as before, let her be brought here quickly."
Having received that command upon her head, Śyāmā performed everything accordingly,
according to the marriage rites prescribed by the Brahman-sages, Vasiṣṭha and the others.
He caused the auspicious marriage ceremony of the couple to be performed,
accompanied by all the celestial nymphs with dancing, singing, and other festivities.
Having seen this, Mahendra and the other gods, as well as the sages whose wealth is their asceticism, praised Lalitāmbikā, exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent! and offering hymns of praise.
Showering down a rain of flowers, all of them, with contented minds,
bowed with great devotion to Laliteśvarī.
Having approached her side, they stood with their palms joined in reverence;
then Kandarpavīra, having prostrated before Maheśvarī, addressed these words with a mind overflowing with devotion: BndP_3.30.54.
O Lalitāmbikā, that body of mine which was burnt by the eye of Śiva has been restored once more through the grace of your sidelong glance.
"I am your son, I am your servant; employ me for some task whatsoever.
Thus addressed, the Supreme Sovereign spoke to that Makaradhvaja:
The Goddess said: "O child, come, O mind-born one! You have no fear;
by my grace, go and delude the entire world with your unimpeded arrows."
His composure shattered by the falling of that arrow,
the Lord will soon marry Gaurī, the daughter of the Mountain.
By my grace, thousands of crores of celestial nymphs born from you shall enter the bodies of all [beings] and grant them supreme delight.
By my grace, even though that Lord is enraged, he will not be able to bring about the burning of your body because of his dispassion.

With an invisible form, deluding the existence of all living beings and fearing separation from his own wife, that cowardly-souled one, his mind struck by your arrow, will go forth and offer half of his body.
"From this day forward, O Kandarpa, by virtue of my great favor,
those who shall utter your censure or harbor intentions hostile toward you,
shall inevitably suffer impotence in birth after birth."
"Indeed, those who are most wicked, evil-minded, and hostile toward my devotees—
cast them into intercourse with women who should not be approached, and destroy them."
For those whose minds are devoted to my worship and to my bhaktas,
fulfill all their desired objects of sensual pleasure.
Thus, remembering the command given by the illustrious Goddess Lalitā, Smara,
bearing it upon his head with the words "So be it," departed from there with palms joined in reverence.
From all the pores of that bodiless one (Anaṅga) arose many beautiful-formed Madanas, who delude the entire universe.
Having deluded the entire wheel of the world with them, Manobhava (the Mind-born) returned once more to the hermitage of Sthāṇu, desiring to conquer the Moon-crested Lord.
With Vasanta as his friend, with Śītarocis as his commander-in-chief, with Rāga as his attendant, and with Mandānilaraya as his companion; ||| BndP_3,30.68 |||
He was accompanied by the loud, sweet warbling of male cuckoos;
he was endowed with the sentiments of love and heroism, his body embraced by Rati.
Shaking his victorious bow and leading the foremost of heroes,
he fearlessly stood facing the enemy of Madana.

He struck the moon-crested Lord, who was devoted to asceticism, with arrows. Then, struck by the multitude of Kandarpa’s shafts, the moon-crested Lord cast aside his detachment and abandoned that difficult penance.
Having abandoned all his religious observances and lost his fortitude, Śiva became afflicted by love;
meditating upon that very Pārvatī again and again, he was overcome by passion.
Sighing, his pale cheeks trembling, the solitary Śarva,
tormented by the collapse of his fortitude and shedding tears,
remembered the Daughter of the Mountain again and again as she had been seen before.
For the wielder of the trident, who was being tormented by the fires of the arrows of the bodiless god of love,
neither the crescent moon nor the Gaṅgā was able to alleviate the heat of his body.
On the bed of flowers brought by the circles of attendants headed by Nandi, Bhṛṅgi, and Mahākāla, he rolled about again and again.
Taking Nandin by the hand, he went from one bed of flowers to another,
moving repeatedly from one floral couch to the next.
Neither on a bed of flowers, nor by the nectar trickling from the crescent moon,
nor in the waters of the Himalayan snows did the fever of his body cease.
Seeking to repeatedly extinguish the flames of his body’s heat,
Śiva resorted to slabs of stone that had become like sheets of frozen water;
again, he traced the form of the Mountain’s Daughter with his fingernails upon a painted cloth.
Beholding her, who was drawn by him as she stood bowed with modesty while looking at him with sidelong glances, his passion increased the pain of love that was not yet far off.
He cast that variegated cloth upon his limbs and over the horripilation [caused by her touch];
yet, due to the great attachment of his thoughts and the immense abundance of his passion,
the three-eyed Lord suffered greatly from the intense heat of longing.
Beholding her alone on every side and directing his mind toward her alone,
he conversed in that very manner with the woman who had been possessed by madness.
With his heart fixed solely upon Him, his mind absorbed in Him, and his ultimate refuge in Him,
he spent all his days and nights sustained by the nectar of stories concerning Him.
Delighting in the praise of her character, eager to behold her form,
and possessing a garland of flowers in the form of his mental constructs regarding her beautiful enjoyments,
Śiva attained a state of complete absorption in her and was tormented exceedingly.
Having observed this incurable affliction born of love, that Dhūrjaṭi became intensely intent upon arranging her marriage.
Having thus deluded that god at the command of Lalitā,
Kandarpa then tormented that daughter of the mountain with his swift arrows.
With the petals of his lower lip drying up from the fires of his sighs, which were soiled by the intense flames of separation,
the surface of his cheeks became deeply pale.
He desired no steadfastness in food, nor in lying down, nor in sleep;
he was constantly sprinkled with thousands of libations and cooling treatments.
Though she was tormented again and again and once more became overwhelmed,
she found no relief from her pain, for the fire of Manmatha was all the greater.
Afflicted by the pain of separation, Pārvatī found no sleep;
by the burning of her own body, she increased the distress of her father.
O Śivā, beholding the separation from his daughter— a separation for which there was no remedy—
that lord of mountains fell into great sorrow.
"O blessed lady, having propitiated the god Maheśvara through asceticism, you shall obtain him as your husband"—
thus was she then urged by her father.
On the peak of the Himavat mountain named Gaurīśikhara,
Pārvatī performed difficult austerities for the sake of obtaining her husband.
In the cold seasons she dwelt in the water, and in the summer she stood in the midst of fire;
with her gaze fixed upon the sun, she undertook most terrible ascetic penance.
Pleased by that very asceticism, Śiva granted his presence and accepted her as his wife according to the rites of marriage.
Then he married the lotus-eyed daughter given by the Lord of Mountains,
whom he had previously requested through the gate of the Seven Sages.
And taking his pleasure with her, that Maheśvara dwelt for a long time in the city of Oṣadhīprastha, in the house of his father-in-law.
Returning again to Kailāsa together with all the Pramathas,
he brought Pārvatī to the Lord of the Mountain and brought him joy.
He took delight in her company on Kailāsa and Mandara,
as well as on the Vindhya mountain, the Golden Mountain, Malaya, and Pāriyātraka.
Maheśvara found delight in various places;
then, she was unable to endure his fierce virility, and he discharged it into her.
She, too, cast him upon the earth; he threw him into the fires of the Kṛttikās;
they released him into the waters of the Gaṅgā; and she, in turn, cast him into the Śara forest.
There, the great hero Mahāsena, who has six faces, was born;
he was brought to the vicinity of the Gaṅgā, and Dhūrjaṭi attained growth.
Growing day by day with intense prowess,
he was instructed by his own father and attained all branches of knowledge.
Then, having received permission from his father, the commander of the celestial army slew Tāraka along with all the Dānavas.
Then Guha brought forth Devasenā, who had been given by Śakra, who was filled with satisfaction at the slaying of the Daitya lord Tāraka.
That illustrious daughter of Śakra, named Devasenā, having approached Skanda, her lover,
experienced intense joy.
Thus, having thoroughly deluded the entire circle of the world, the Mind-born One (Kāmadeva),
having successfully accomplished the work of the gods, returned once more to Śrīpura.
He went to that holy city where the supreme goddess Lalitā resides for the prosperity of the worlds, in order to serve her there.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Rebirth of Madana," in the Lalitopākhyāna within the Hayagrīvāgastyasaṃvāda of the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Agastya said: What is this [city] named Śrīpura, and in what form does it exist?
Or by whom was it previously created? Tell me all of that.
O Lord, tell me what its dimensions are and what its color;
you alone are the sun that dries up the mire of all my doubts.

Hayagrīva said: Just as Lalitā, the Supreme Goddess, who is born from the fire of the Great Sacrifice (mahāyāga), having attained the wheel-chariot endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics— BndP_3,31.3.
Having performed the nuptial rites, she was again entreated by Brahmā and the other gods,
and she conquered the asura named Bhaṇḍa, a thorn to the worlds.
Then the gods, headed by Mahendra, experienced great satisfaction;
they were eager to construct a magnificent palace for both Kāmeśvara and Lalitā, intended for all their eternal enjoyments.
The Kumāras— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—
summoned Viśvakarman, the divine architect skilled in the arts of the gods, [to serve as] the carpenter for Lalitādevī.
Having summoned Maya, the architect of the gods and an expert in magic, and having honored him, they spoke by the command of Lalitā: BndP_3,31.7 //
The supervising officials said:
"O Viśvakarman, knower of the arts! O Maya Mahodaya!
You two are masters of all scriptures and experts in the methods of construction."
By mere resolve, you two, who are experts in great craftsmanship and ritual, [should create] for Lalitādevī, the great ocean of eternal knowledge, [the necessary objects].
In the midst of the sixteen sacred fields, there should indeed be established cities adorned with various jewels, equal in number to those fields.
There, the Supreme Goddess Lalitā, divided into sixteen forms,
will perpetually establish her residence for the protection of the universe.
For this is dear to us, and it is dear to the Maruts as well;
since it is dear to all the world, let it be composed under that very name.
Having heard these words of the causal deities, those two, who were composed of Viśvakarman, bowed down and replied, "So be it."
Having bowed again, those two asked those personified causes:
"In which fields should the highly prosperous Śrīnagarīs be constructed?"
Thus questioned by Brahmā and the others, those two artisans spoke again,
arranging the divisions of the sacred fields (kṣetra) as was appropriate.
The causal Puruṣas said:
"First, on the summit of Meru, on the mountain Niṣadha,
on Hemakūṭa, on the Himavat mountain, and fifthly on Gandhamādana."
Nīla, Meṣa, Śṛṅgāra, Mahendra, and the great mountain [Mahāmeru]—
these nine terrestrial fields are indeed known.
Indeed, it is said that there are exactly seven watery oceans in all the rivers:
the salt ocean, the ocean of sugarcane juice, the ocean of wine, and the ocean of clarified butter.
The Dadhisindhu, the Kṣīrasindhu, and the Jalasindhu as the seventh;
these are the nine previously mentioned lords of mountains, followed by the seven oceans.
"Having selected sixteen sites for the construction of Ambā’s Śrīpura,
wherein are the divine mansions of the highly majestic Lalitā,
you two must act as craftsmen, experts in divine engineering."
In those fields where the Goddess, while slaying the great asuras, manifested her forms, they became renowned by the very names of those eternal [manifestations]; of this there is no doubt.
For she, the supreme goddess, by her eternal nature, pervades time; as the very essence of the act of reckoning, she measures the entire universe.
And because the Great Queen is eternal and there is no distinction between her and that which is eternal,
she was therefore celebrated in ancient times as being of the same name as it.
Kāmeśvarīpura, Bhagamālāpura,
and Nityaklinnāpura— these names are indeed widely renowned.
Therefore, on an auspicious and most meritorious day, let them construct a beautiful city according to the principles of great architecture, with names corresponding to its colors.
Thus addressed by the lords of causes— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—
they established those two [liṅgas] in those sacred fields situated within Śrīpurī.
Now, O Lord of Lopāmudrā, having paid heed, I shall describe the extent of Śrīpura and the presiding deities of the city; listen.
Mount Meru, the support of all things, lofty and extending for infinite yojanas,
has a body that pierces through the wheel of the fourteen worlds.
It has four peaks situated in the regions of Śakra, Nairṛta, Vāyu, and the center; their height is now described.
The three previously mentioned peaks are one hundred yojanas in height and one hundred yojanas in breadth; it is held that there are three worlds upon them.
The world of Brahmā, the world of Viṣṇu, and likewise the world of Śiva—
I shall describe the architectural layouts of these in due course.
Listen now to the extent and height of the peak situated in the middle:
it is four hundred yojanas high and likewise wide.
On that very same great peak, O Pot-born One (Agastya), a city named Śrīpura was built by two artisans,
extending for four hundred yojanas in width.
In this regard, this classification is now demonstrated in detail:
the first enclosure is said to be constructed of black iron.
It is sixteen thousand and six hundred yojanas in length and circumference;
it possesses gates on its four sides and rises four yojanas high.
O Lord of the Ocean, the circumference of the base of that Śāla tree is ten thousand yojanas;
at its summit, however, there is a separate window-like opening measuring one gavyūti.
The height of each palace door measures one yojana;
at each door there are two panels, each half a gavyūti in width.
In these two [gates], which are one yojana high and constructed of black iron,
the bolts are likewise half a krośa in length.
Thus has the description of the four gates been proclaimed in equal measure;
now, O Pot-born One, I shall describe the configuration of the gate-tower (gopura).
At the base of the aforementioned Śāla tree, which measures one yojana [in circumference],
two yojanas each were taken on both sides and fashioned [into palaces].
Its width extends for that same distance, with its two sides each measuring two yojanas and the middle of the Śāla tree measuring one yojana, all enclosed within the gateway.
O Sage, it measures five *yojanas* in extent,
and on both sides it is joined by two and a half *krośas*.
Having measured five yojanas in length,
O Sage, a gateway was thus constructed there within the enclosure wall.
Therefore, the circumference at the base of the gateway is twenty yojanas;
it is proclaimed that above each successive level, there is a reduction in size.
The height of the gateway is said to be twenty-five yojanas;
at every yojana there is a beautiful door equipped with panels.
There are also as many terraces, which decrease in size as they go upward;
indeed, the width at the top of the gateway rests upon one yojana.
O Pot-born One, its length is indeed that much, and it is known there as Trimukuṭa;
the width of Mukuṭa, however, is one krośa.
O Sage, it rises to a height of two *krośas* and decreases like a city gate (*gopura*);
within the interior of the crown, the earth is measured at half a *krośa*.
The crown is in the west; at the eastern, southern, and northern gate-towers, there are crowns on the right and left;
and at the western gate-tower, there are likewise crowns on the right and left.
The [deities] at the northern gate are said to be like those at the southern gate;
the arrangement of crowns at the eastern gate is like that at the western gate.
Within the distance of one *yojana* from the hall known as Kālāyasa,
and within the distance of the Kāṃsya hall, there is a gatehouse provided with a gopura, just as before.
The measurement of the *śāla* roots is proclaimed as before;
the bronze hall (*kāṃsya-śāla*) is likewise provided with doors in the directions starting from the east.
At every gate there were gate-towers possessing the characteristics of mountain peaks,
made of black iron and bronze, with openings on all sides.
O Pot-born One, that is called the Great Garden of Various Trees;
everything that exists, beginning with those born from sprouts, is present there.
There were more than a thousand trees that always bore flowers, always bore fruit,
were always rich in the beauty of new shoots, and were always filled with fragrance.
Mango trees, *kaṅkolaka* trees, *lodhra* trees, *bakula* trees, *karṇikāra* trees,
*śiṃśapā* trees, *śirīṣa* trees, *devadāru* trees, and *nameru* trees;
There are *punnāgas*, *nāgabhadras*, *mucukundas*, and *kaṭphalas*;
as well as *elās*, *lavaṅgas*, *takkolas*, and trees bearing camphor.
The *pīlava*, *kākatuṇḍī*, *śālaka*, and *āsana* trees,
as well as *kāñcanāra*, *lakuca*, *panasa*, and *hiṅgula*.
Pāṭala trees, Phalinīs, Jaṭilīs, Jaghanephālās, Gaṇikās, Kuraṇṭas, Bandhujīvas, and pomegranate trees; 3,31.59.
Aśvakarṇas, Hastikarṇas, Āmpeyas, Kanakadrumas,
Yūthikās, Tālaparṇīs, and Tulasis that bear fruit at all times.
Tāla, astamāla, hintāla, and kharjūra trees; śara and barbara;
sugarcane and milky trees; as well as śleṣmātaka and vibhītaka.
There are *harītakī* trees with downward-facing flowers, *ghoṇṭālī* trees, and *svargapuṣpikā* trees;
as well as *bhallātaka*, *khadira*, *śākhoṭa*, and sandalwood trees.
There were black aloe-wood trees, kālaskandha trees,
tamarind trees, as well as udumbara, arjuna, and aśvattha trees, śamī trees, and evergreen trees.
Rucakas, kuṭajas, saptaparṇas, kṛtamālakas,
kapitthas, tintiṇīs, and others of this kind exist there by the thousands.
Filled with various seasons, these excellent trees, which serve as causes for the Goddess's amorous passion,
possess great heights and diverse species of trees.
Seven yojanas within the interior of the bell-metal hall (kāṃsya-śāla),
there is a square copper hall (tāmra-śāla) rising one yojana high on the banks of the Indus.
The space between these two is called Kalpakavāṭikā;
it is filled with fragrant camphor and endowed with beautiful seeds of jewels.
The trees were laden with fruits as beautiful as golden bark;
the coral upon the branches was truly like divine yellow garments.
Nectar shall be their sweet juice, and flowers their ornaments;
many such kalpa-trees are proclaimed to exist there.
This shall be the second enclosure, known by the name Kalpavāpī;
within the space of the Copper Hall (Tāmraśāla), it is proclaimed as the Nāga Hall (Nāgaśāla).
The horizontal extent of both of these should be seven yojanas;
there, a grove of *saṃtāna* trees shall be, resembling the Kalpa-pool.
Between those two, it is said, lies a grove of yellow sandalwood trees on the earth,
resembling the Kalpavāṭī garden and teeming with fruits and flowers.
In all these palaces, the arrangement of doors is as before;
likewise, the arrangement of gate-towers and crowning ornaments is as before.
And at each gate, a gopura was constructed; there was a measurement at every door, and in the intervals between them, at a distance of seven yojanas, were made of brass.
The eastern Śāla tree is made of the five metals and has the same appearance as the [western] Śāla;
between those two, it is said, lies the earth consisting of a grove of Mandāra trees.
At a distance of seven yojanas from within the region of the five metals, the Silver Hall is said to exist,
endowed with the characteristics previously described.
Between those two, it is said, lies the middle earth, a grove of *pārijāta* trees,
filled with divine fragrance and radiant with an abundance of fruits and flowers.
In the interval between the silver hall, a golden hall is described, seven yojanas in extent, adorned with gates as before.
Between those two, it is said, lies a grove of Kadamba trees;
there stand divine Nīpa trees, two yojanas in height.
From them always flows the intoxicating essence, radiant with abundant blossoms,
from which the Yoginī named Kādambarī grants enjoyment.
Those excellent *nīpa* trees, which were always dear to Mantriṇī,
possessed beautiful shade, were leafy, and thick with sprouts;
their interiors were filled with the humming of swarms of bees restless for the fragrance.
Right there, to the northeast of the enclosure of the Kadamba forest, is the most beautiful temple of Mantriṇīnāthā.
Four lofty palaces were constructed by the primordial architect;
the width of each individual palace was five yojanas.
Extending five yojanas in length, it stands with seven enclosures;
likewise, in all other directions, there are everywhere *priyaka* trees.
This is proclaimed to be the city of residence for Śyāmā.
For the sake of the army, there was another city in the region of the Mahāpadma forest;
its palace was located right here, many yojanas away.
The constant service of the Goddess could not be performed by Matriṇī;
therefore, a residence was constructed near the palace of the Cintāmaṇi by Maya,
