the celestial architect, for that illustrious Mistress of Mantras.
Who indeed, even if he possessed a thousand tongues like serpents, could fully describe the many virtues of the temple of the Goddess Mantreśvarī in Śrīpura?
There, the noble daughters of the Mātaṅgas sport, their eyes copper-red from the intoxication of *kādambarī* wine, singing with sweet lutes.
Agastya said: Who is said to be this one named Mātaṅga, and how is it that his daughters,
languid with the intoxication of honey-wine, always serve the mistress of the ministers?
Hayagrīva said:
There was one named Mataṅga, a treasury of asceticism whose wealth was his penance;
he was endowed with great power and was intent upon the creation of the world.

Through the power of his asceticism and with a focused mind, he was an enforcer of commands everywhere. His son, Mātaṅga, being of steadfast intellect, completely fulfilled Mudriṇī, the leader of the mantrins, by means of most formidable austerities.
It was attended for a very long time by Mataṅga, the son of the sage.
"O Mantriṇī, having granted your presence, choose a boon," she commanded.
Then Mātaṅga, the best of all sages and a treasury of asceticism, spoke to that Śyāmalāmbikā who had granted her presence before him: BndP_3,31.93 //
The great sage Mātaṅga said: "O Goddess, by the mere remembrance of you, all my supernatural powers,
beginning with *aṇimā*, as well as all other manifestations of power, have indeed arisen."
"There is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that remains for me to attain;
for one like you, whose memory of past conduct is ever-present, everything has been attained at the proper time."
Moreover, let this presence of yours not be fruitless for us;
thus I pray to you, O Ambikā: fulfill that supreme boon.
Formerly, while intoxicated with play, he had engaged in irreverent jesting and laughter with the Himavat, who was his friend.
He boasted of himself, saying, "I am the preceptor of Gauri";
yet those words did not affect me at all, because my own merit was superior in that regard.
But when the qualities of both friends are equal, yet one possesses a superior quality,
a longing for that other person arises in the first due to that cause.
O Lord of the Mantrinis, although my desires were already fulfilled, I performed austerities for the sake of praising the greatness of Gaurī; therefore, become my daughter.
"Because of this, you will become renowned by my name; of this there is no doubt.
Having heard these words spoken by the great sage Mātaṅga, he said, "So be it," and having vanished from sight, the sage was filled with joy.
Then, in a dream, that great seer Mātaṅga joyfully gave him a single cluster of *tāpiccha* blossoms to serve as an ear-ornament.
By the power of that dream, Mātaṅga’s wife,
Siddhimatī by name, quickly conceived a child in her womb.
Because she was born from that very source, she is celebrated as Mātaṅgī;
she is called Laghuśyāmā because she is the root and bulbous base of Śyāmā.
Millions upon millions of charming Mātaṅga maidens—
light-skinned Śyāmās, dark-skinned Mahāśyāmās, and Mātaṅgīs gathered in throngs—
having attained the power of their own bodies, serve the beloved of Priyaka.
Thus, O Pot-born One, the origin of the Mātaṅga maidens has been told,
as well as the seven enclosures and the halls constructed of iron and other metals.

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Daughter of Mataṅga," in the dialogue between Hayagrīva and Agastya within the Lalitopākhyāna of the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Agastya said: Indeed, there are protectors for each of the seven halls made of iron and other metals.
Proclaim that name, O wise one, by which my doubt may be severed.
Hayagrīva said:
"O Pot-born One, Mahākāla, the devourer of all worlds, whose body is dark-hued, resides in a great garden of various trees."
Wearing a dark-blue tunic and with eyes reddened by intoxication,
he drinks from the goblet of the cosmic egg the elixir of the universe, which fills it to the brim.
Seated upon a lion-throne at the end of the aeon, which is characterized by dissolution, he cast his sidelong glances toward Mahākālī, who was dark as a rain-cloud and moist with passion.
Endowed with the practice of meditating on Lalitā and eager for the worship of Lalitā,
he extended the length of his own life through devotion to Lalitā;
he was even served by the servants headed by Kāla and Mṛtyu.
Mahākālī and Mahākāla, who carry out the command of Lalitā,
sustain the entire universe while dwelling on the first path.
The Kālacakra of Mataṅga has become his very seat;
it is endowed with four enclosures and possesses a beautiful bindu in its center.
A triangle, a pentagon, a sixteen-petaled lotus, and likewise an eight-spoked lotus; thus, Mahākāla is situated in the center.
In the triangle, however, are Mahākālī, Mahāsaṃdhyā, and Mahāniśā;
these three great goddesses are the powers (śaktis) of Mahākāla.
In that very place, at the tip of the five corners, are Pratyūṣa and Pitṛprasū;
the five powers of time are Prāhṇa, Aparāhṇa, and Madhyāhna.
Now, O Sage, hear of the powers (śaktis) residing in the sixteen-petaled lotus:
Dinamiśrā, Tamisrā, Jyotsnī, and Pakṣiṇī.
Pradoṣā, Niśīthā, Pūrṇimā, Praharā, Rākā, Anumati, and likewise Amāvasyikā; // BndP_3,32.12 //
Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Bhadrā, Upalā, and Ṣoḍaśī—
these sixteen powers, abiding in the sixteen measures (mātrās), are traditionally known as the sixteen.
The *kalā*, *kāṣṭhā*, *nimeṣas*, *kṣaṇas*, *lavas*, *truṭis*, *muhūrtas*, *kutapas*, days and nights, and likewise the bright fortnight; 3,32.14.
The dark fortnight, the southern solstice, the equinox, the thirteenth day,
the Saṃvatsara, the Parivatsara, and also the Iḍāvatsara.
These sixteen Śaktis are remembered as dwelling upon the petals of the lotus;
they are Indravatsarā, Induvatsarā, and Vatsarā.
The lunar days, the weekdays, the asterisms, the yogas, and the karaṇas—
these are the powers (śaktis) situated upon the serpent-leaves of the lotus.
Kali, Kalpā, Kalanā, and Kālī—
this quartet attained the status of gatekeepers for the radiant Kālacaṛka.
These Mahākāla goddesses, their faces grinning with intoxication,
hold wine-filled goblets of beautiful reddish luster;
all of them are dark-complexioned women of Time.
Devoted to the worship, meditation, recitation, and hymns of Lalitā,
they serve Mahākāla, who is seated upon the throne of Kālacakra.
Now, O Pot-born One, the protector of Kalpakavati was the Spring season, possessed of great splendor and a servant devoted to Lalita.
Seated upon a throne of flowers, intoxicated by the honey of flowers,
he whose weapon is the flower, who is adorned with flowers, and who is graced by a parasol of flowers.
Madhuśrī and Mādhavaśrī were the two goddesses of that sporting god; they were intoxicated by the wine of flowers and longing for the flower-arrowed one.
The summer season is the gardener of the garden of her life-stream; with its scorching rays, it is ever the servant of Lalitā, carrying out her commands.
Śukraśrī and Śuciśrī are recorded as his two wives;
O Sage, the Haricandana grove remained [there] during the rainy season.
He was the season of rain, possessed of great splendor, with eyes streaked by flashes of lightning;
he resounded with the loud laughter of the thunderbolt and was borne upon intoxicated clouds.
Clad in armor of clouds, bearing a jeweled bow,
he was devoted to the worship, meditation, recitation, and hymns of Lalitā.
O Destroyer of the Vindhya, he dwells there, bestowing joy upon the three worlds;
he is the beauty of the sky and the beauty of the month of Nabhasya, possessing his own essence and his own garland.
Ambā, Dulā, Nirali, Abhrayantī, Meghayantrikā,
Varṣayantī, Cibunikā, and Vāridhārā are the Śaktis.
The twelve [goddesses] who pour down rain are said to have eyes red with passion;
together with those Śaktis, that season of rain [worships] the Supreme Goddess.
Constantly engaged in recitation, he adorned the regions of Lalitā’s devotees with clusters of flowers gathered from his own garden, using his own abundant wealth.
But the arrival of the clouds, O Goddess, constantly acts as a servant to you by afflicting the enemies of those [who favor you] with drought upon the earth.
Dwelling eternally in the Mandārava grove during the autumn season,
the glorious one protects that enclosure, bringing clarity of mind to the world.
Iṣaśrī and Urjaśrī were the presiding goddesses of that season;
with them, he gathered water using clusters of flowers produced from themselves,
and thus worshipped the sovereign queen, the consort of Śrī Kāmeśvara.
The winter season possesses great splendor, its form cooled by frost;
it is always cheerful of countenance and has Lalitā’s dear servant as its attendant.
Worshipping the Supreme Goddess with abundant flowers produced from himself,
the Conqueror of Fire (Agni) guards the grove of the Pārijāta tree.
Saha and Sahasyaśrī were his two auspicious wives;
the protector of the grove of Kadamba forests was Śiśirākṛti.
O best of sages, O Pot-born one, the winter season is now prevailing;
by him, that entire enclosure has everywhere been turned into a snowy landscape.
Then Śyāmā, the deity residing there whose form is cool as ice,
and Tapaḥśrī and Tapasyaśrī— those two most excellent women—
along with them, she worshipped Ambā Lalitā, the purifier of the universe.
Agastya said: "O illustrious one, face of a Gandharva, I have taken refuge with Mahākāla, the first guardian of the garden, who is surrounded by the seven [categories] beginning with various trees."

"The fourfold protective wheel has been proclaimed by you for him; however, we have heard from you that there is a guardianship over the other six seasons in the garden groves of the Kalpa, but the goddesses of the wheels (cakradevīs) have not been heard of."
Therefore, O Blessed One, tell me in due order the deities of the enclosures of the wheels beginning with Vasantā; for you are the Great All-Knowing One.
Hayagrīva said:
Listen, O best of sages, to those deities who reside within each of those wheels.
The Kālacakra was previously described; now the Vāsantacakra is being declared:
the triangle, the pentagon, the eight-petalled lotus, the sixteen-spoked lotus, and again the two sets of ten spokes.
It should be known as quadrangular and endowed with seven enclosures;
in its center resides the spring season of great splendor, situated within the circle of the *bindu*.
When those two, Madhuśrī and Mādhavaśrī, were joined together as one,
they both, with their own hands, [pressed] a single breast of each.
Pressing with the pair of his own hands a fragrant cup filled with flowers, wine, and meat.
In this very way, O destroyer of Vindhya, the meditation on all the seasons is performed; however,
in the meditation on the rainy season, the first two powers should be understood as being situated in the lap,
while the other powers are positioned nearby.
Now listen as I speak of the goddesses situated on the spring wheel:
Madhuśuklaprathamikā and Madhuśukladvitīyikā.
The third day of the bright fortnight of Madhu, the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Madhu,
the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Madhu, and the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Madhu.
The seventh day of the bright fortnight of Madhu, and again the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Madhu,
as well as the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Madhu, and the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Madhu.
The eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Madhu, the twelfth day from the bright fortnight of Madhu,
the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Madhu, and the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Madhu.
The first is the full moon day of the bright fortnight of Madhu; the second is the dark fortnight of Madhu;
the third is the dark fortnight of Madhu; and the fourth is the dark fortnight of Madhu.
The fourth is Madhukṛṣṇā, and the fifth is Madhukṛṣma;
the sixth should be Madhukṛṣṇā, and the seventh is Madhukṛṣmataḥ.
Madhukṛṣṇāṣṭamī, Navamīmadhukṛṣṇa, and Daśamīmadhukṛṣṇā, O destroyer of Vindhyadarpa! BndP_3,32.55.

The eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, the twelfth from the dark fortnight of Māgha, the thirteenth of the dark fortnight of Māgha, and the fourteenth of the dark fortnight of Māgha; // BndP_3.32.56 //
Madhvamā and Ceti are to be known as these thirty Śaktis;
in this very manner, they are situated within that which is called Mādhava.
The thirty other powers beginning with the first day of the bright fortnight (śukla-pratipad),
totaling sixty when combined, are known as the spring powers (vāsanta-śakti).
There, the seven stages of the enclosures of the Vāsanta-cakrarāja are to be worshipped according to the ritual procedure with their respective mantras.
There are sixty deities residing within those sixty grounds;
they should be worshipped by practitioners, having divided them, with their respective mantras.
Likewise, there is the Vāsanta-cakra, and it is the same for the other three;
however, the deities are distinct, according to the divisions of Śukra, Śuci, and so forth.
In the wheel of summer, there are sixty powers of great manifestation;
likewise, in the wheels beginning with that of the year, [one should know] the divisions born from the elements of earth and ether.
Sixty powers are established in each and every wheel;
however, for fear of excessive prolixity, I shall desist from enumerating their specific numbers.
These powers of the seasons grant happiness to the devotees of Lalitā,
provided they are devoted to the worship, meditation, recitation, and praise of Lalitā.
Wandering through the garden-circles of the Kalpa and other realms, languid with intoxication, they gratify Maheśvarī with the honey produced from their own respective flowers.
When added together, they are reckoned as three hundred and sixty;
thus, in the seven halls, there are the *pālikās* who are the deities of the wheels.

Having first described the Nāmakīrtana to you who have questioned me, I shall now speak of the inclusion of other halls as well, for the sake of completion; listen attentively as I explain their extent and their capacity.

Thus, in the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the latter section, within the dialogue between Hayagrīva and Agastya, in the narrative of Lalitā, this is the account titled "The Revelation of the Deities Who Guard the Seven Courtyards of Śrīnagara Tripurā.
Hayagrīva said:
"The characteristics of the seven halls as fashioned by the artisans have been described."
Now, the halls made of jewels are proclaimed; listen attentively.
The delightful space between the golden palace and the one made of topaz is said to be seven yojanas in width.
There, perfected beings and perfected women sport, overwhelmed with intoxication,
by means of elixirs, rejuvenators, swords, and even foot-salves.
Devoted to Lalitā and gratifying great souls,
various people dwell there, drinking the essence of wine.
The arrangements for the doors of the halls made of topaz and other gems are as described before. In those halls of topaz and other gems, the door-panels, bolts,
and gate-towers should be known as being composed of topaz and the like, shining with the intense luster of the moon and the sun.
The moat situated between the golden rampart and the one made of topaz is also said to be composed of topaz.
In all the great halls and courtyards that are about to be described,
there were birds of those same colors, and the lakes there were also of those same colors.
The rivers there have waters the color of that [region], and the jewel-trees are of that same hue;
those perfected beings (siddhas) who, among the classes of Siddhas, worshipped the Goddess through various rites and first cast off their bodies, dwell there together with their consorts.
Those who have recited the mantra of Lalitā and are devoted to the practice of the Lalitākrama—
all of them are those who proclaim the names of the goddess Lalitā.
Within the great hall of Puṣparāga, at a distance of one yojana from the wind-gate,
there is a square hall made of Padmarāga on all sides.
The ground was rich with rubies, and the gate-towers and other structures were likewise composed of them;
there, those residing in the region of Cāraṇa attained perfection after the destruction of their former bodies, becoming servants of the lotus-feet of the Great Queen.
And the women of the bards, with lovely limbs and languid with passion,
sang again and again the melodic compositions of Lalitādevī.
Right there, seated upon platforms situated in the midst of the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa),
they drink sweet honey while accompanied by their husbands.
Within the great hall of Padmarāga, extending for a hundred yojanas,
stands the great hall of Gomedaka, shaped like the eastern hall;
between these two is the exceedingly lofty hall of Hīra, which is the ground of diamonds.
O Pot-born Sage, having worshipped the Goddess there in a previous birth,
the preeminent Gandharvas dwell together with throngs of Apsarases.
Singing of the multitude of virtues of the Great Queen with the sounds of lutes,
they were solely devoted to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures; their bodies resembled those of the god of love,
they were of delicate nature, and they were full of devotion to the Goddess Śrī.
The Gomedaka mountain has a shape resembling a palmyra tree or a *śāla* tree;
within it dwell tens of millions of Yoginīs and Bhairavas,
who there serve the Mother Kālasaṅkarṣaṇī with devotion.
Within the great hall of Gomedaka, at the distance of a yojana from Māruta,
dwell Urvaśī, Menakā, Rambhā, and likewise Alambuṣā.
Mañjughoṣā, Sukeśī, Pūrvacitti, Ghṛtācikā, Kṛtasthalā, Viśvācī, together with Puñjikasthalā.
Tilottamā is the courtesan of the gods; others of her kind likewise [attend them].
Together with the Gandharvas, they enjoy the ever-new flowers of the Kalpa trees.
Drinking [the nectar] of Lalitādevī and meditating upon her again and again,
they recite her mantra for the sake of increasing their own good fortune.
All the Apsarases born from the fourteen sacrificial ladles dwell there with joyful hearts, worshipping the Goddess in their respective stations.
Agastya said: O Lord, O one of great wisdom, O great treasury of all knowledge, please recount the fourteen births of those Apsarases as well.
Hayagrīva said:
"The Brāhmaṇa, desire, death, the earth, and the wind;
the rays of the sun, the rays of the moon, the Vedas, and fire."
Saudāminī, Pīyūṣa, and Dakṣakanyā, as well as Jala—
these the wise declare to be the causes of their birth.
All these women, whose abundant wealth of splendor and good fortune is celebrated by the hosts of gods,
worship the Wielder of the Discus together with the Gandharvas.
O Sage, the Kinnaras along with their women, as well as the Kiṃpuruṣas together with their women,
intoxicated with passion, have taken refuge on the Diamond Plateau (Hīrakasthala).
O Pot-born One, having shaken off all impurities through the recitation of the Mahārājñī mantra,
they remain dancing and singing.
O Sage, on that very land of diamonds flows the river named Vajrā, crowded with diamond-workers and radiant with trees upon its banks.
That purifying river there flows everywhere, with sands consisting solely of vajra-jewels and waters composed of liquid vajra.
O Agastya, those best of men who are devotees of Lalitā-Parameśānī,
having drunk her water, possess bodies with the nature of a vajra;
they become long-lived and free from disease.
When the thunderbolt had been dropped and released by Bhaṇḍāsura, Śatakratu,
possessed of devotion toward Vajreśī, performed austerities on the bank of the Tārā.
Having arisen from that water and given the thunderbolt to the enemy of Bala, the Goddess vanished once more;
he too, his purpose accomplished, went to heaven.
Then, at a distance of one yojana from the Vajra grove,
there is a lofty grove of vaidūrya stones, complete with gate-towers as before;
and there is a pot made of vaidūrya, radiant in appearance.
Whosoever among the inhabitants of Pātāla are practitioners of the worship of the Śrīdevī,
they dwell there in bodies perfected by yoga, flourishing in happiness.
Śeṣa, Karkeṭaka, Mahāpadma, Vāsuki, Śaṅkhaka, Takṣaka, Śaṅkhacūḍa, Mahādanta, and Mahāphaṇa; ||| BndP_3,33.36 |||
Such are the Nāgas there, numbering three times ten million;
and there likewise dwells the host of Daityas who abide in righteousness, headed by Bali and Indra, together with the Nāgas and their wives.
Those who have recited the Lalitā-mantra, those initiated into the Lalitā-scriptures,
and those who constantly worship Lalitā dwell as enjoyers of divine pleasures.
There, in the courtyard of vaidūrya stones, are rivers with cool waters and lakes of pure water adorned with cranes.
The palaces there are divine and adorned with lapis lazuli gems;
within them, those nāgas and asuras sport together with their women.
Within a great hall known as Vaidūrya, at a distance of one yojana from Māruta,
there is a sāl tree made of sapphire, like another circular mountain range.
And the middle courtyard-ground there, O Sage, is composed of sapphire;
therein are sweet rivers, cool lakes,
and various kinds of delightful objects for enjoyment.
Those mortals who have gone to the world of the living and are practitioners of the Lalitā-mantra,
indeed dwell after the end of their bodies in the blue enclosure of Śakra.
There, accompanied by women, they enjoy divine objects,
drinking sweet wine and dancing with hearts overflowing with devotion.
O Pot-born One, in those lakes, on the banks of the rivers, in delightful bowers of creepers, and in magnificent palaces of great splendor; BndP_3,33.45 //
Constantly chanting and reciting the virtues of the Śrīdevī,
those highly fortunate ones dwell surrounded by women.
Upon the exhaustion of their karma, they return once more to the human body in the world of mortals;
endowed with their former latent impressions (*vāsanā*), they worship the Goddess who holds the discus again,
and then go once more to the great site of Śakranīla in the City of Śrī.
O Sage, due to contact with that very place, human beings always remain joined with dark states of being arising from passion and hatred.
But those mortals who possess knowledge, who are free from the pairs of opposites and have their senses restrained—
they, O Sage, filled with wonder, enter into Maheśvarī.
Within the distance of one yojana from the Śāla grove called Indranīla,
there is a Śāla grove made of pearls, complete with gate-towers as before.
O Sage, between those two is a ground that is exceedingly radiant and clear;
it is entirely inlaid with pearls, cool, and most enchanting.
The Tāmraparṇī, the Mahāparṇī, and the Sadāmuktāphalodakā—
such great rivers flow forth upon the great land.
On their banks dwell all those who reside in the worlds of the gods— those who, in their previous births, were practitioners of the mantras of the Śrīdevī.
In the eight directions beginning with the east, the worlds that are the domain of Śakra and the other guardians are joined all around the Muktāśāla grove at the locations of the gates.
In the middle of the two gates of the blue Muktāśāla,
on the eastern side is the world of Śakra, and in its corner is the realm of Agni.
In the southern quarter lies the city of Yama; there dwells the Lord who wields the staff, a reciter of the Lalitā-mantra everywhere, possessed of a fierce nature.
Guha, the upholder of commands, together with the messengers of Yama led by Citragupta, strictly enforces the ordinance of the Goddess Śrī.
Those of wicked conduct, cursed by Guha; those who harbor hatred toward Lalita; fools devoted to hypocritical devotion; and those who are stubborn and exceedingly arrogant.
[One should avoid] those who steal mantras, those with evil spells, those who resort to false sciences,
atheists, those of sinful character, and those who harm living beings in vain.
O Pot-born One, those who hate women, those hated by the world, and those who protect heretics,
go to the Kālasūtra, Raurava, and Kumbhīpāka hells.
In the terrible Asipatravana, in Kṛmibhakṣa, Pratāpana,
Lālākṣepa, Sūcīvedha, and likewise in Aṅgārapātana;
O Pot-born One, by the command of that glorious goddess of great majesty, he casts [them] into such agonizing hells as these.
In the western part of that very place dwells Nirṛti, bearing a sword;
having taken refuge in the world of the Rākṣasas, he exists as a worshiper of Lalitā.
And on its northern side, at the junction of the two gates,
he always dwells in Varuṇa, taking recourse to the world of Varuṇa.
Intoxicated by the tasting of the wine of Varuṇī, white-limbed, and having the fish as his vehicle,
he is always a reciter of the mantra of the goddess Śrī and a practitioner of the Śrīkrama.
Having bound those who hate the vision of the glorious deity with fetters, he leads them down the downward path; yet he is the liberator of his devotees from bondage.
And in its northern corners is the world of Vāyu, of great splendor;
there dwell those whose bodies are air, who are ever-rejoicing and exalted.
There were also perfected ones and divine sages, others devoted to the practice of breath control (pavana),
and other yogins such as Gorakṣa and his peers, who were intent upon yoga.
Together with these, O Agastya, the illustrious Māruteśvara exists there,
manifesting in entirely distinct forms.
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumṇā are his powers;
these three are always languid with the intoxication of honey for the Lord of the Winds.
Holding a banner in his hand, seated upon his great vehicle, the best of deer, he is intent upon the sequence of worship consisting of graceful gestures, offerings, and meditation.
Surrounded by other Śaktis whose limbs are filled with bliss,
that glorious Māruteśvara constantly mutters the Cakriṇī mantra.
At the end of the eon, that being leads the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, to their ultimate dissolution and dispels them in that very instant.
For the sake of that being’s accomplishment, he remained there, adoring and meditating upon that very Laliteśvarī, adorned with all ornaments.
In the world of the Yakṣas situated in the eastern part of that [world],
the glorious and highly effulgent lord of the Yakṣas dwells, positioned between those two gateways.
Accompanied by the ninefold treasures and the powers of supernatural success, growth, and so forth,
he fulfills the devotees of Lalitā with wealth and abundance.
And with charming yakṣīs whose conduct was agreeable,
and with various kinds of honey, she honors the wielder of the discus.
Maṇibhadra, Pūrṇabhadra, Maṇimān, Māṇikandhara—
these and others are indeed the generals of the Yakṣas present there.
To the east of that world is the highly exalted realm of Rudra;
it is inlaid with priceless jewels, and Rudra is its presiding deity.
He was always ablaze with wrath, always with his great quivers fastened,
accompanied by great beings equal to himself who were skilled in carrying out the commands of the world.
Constantly surrounded by skillful faces stationed in sixteen enclosures with strung bows, he muttered the mantra of the auspicious deity.
Perfectly endowed with the meditation on the Goddess Śrī, eager for the worship of the Goddess Śrī,
his flanks were adorned by hosts of many millions of Rudrāṇīs.
And all of them had their limbs ablaze with passion, were proud of their fresh youth,
were intent on graceful meditation, and were always languid from the intoxication of wine.
And together with them, that glorious Mahārudra, the bearer of the trident,
was attended by Hiraṇyabāhu and other Rudras.

Having pierced with the tip of his trident those who had fallen away from the sight of Lalitā, those who were arrogant, and those who had insulted their gurus, he [consumed them] with the bitter fires arising from his eyes.
He torments their wives and servants and destroys even their offspring;
he is the great hero who upholds commands and the protector of Lalitā’s orders.
O Pot-born Sage, he dwells in the exceedingly radiant world of Rudra;
the Pramathas are the attendants of that great Rudra.
Who indeed would be capable of describing those Rudras who are beyond counting—
those Rudras who exist upon the earth by the thousands of thousands?
And even in heaven they exist by the thousands upon thousands,
for whom food is their sacrificial oblation, and for whom the winds are their arrows.
And those of great power, whose arrows are blazing for a year, who have tawny eyes,
and who move upon the ocean and in the atmosphere;
Those with matted locks, honey-colored, blue-necked, and deep red;
those who are the sovereign lords of all beings, arrow-less and wearing their hair in braided coils.
Those Rudras who pierce people as they drink from various vessels, those who are chariot-makers on the roads, and those who dwell at sacred fords; ||| BndP_3,33.92 |||
And those other thousands of Rudras, armed with spears and carrying quivers, who carry out Lalitā’s commands, have stationed themselves throughout the directions.
All those great-souled ones, who in an instant traverse the three worlds,
were seated in meditation upon the Śrī Devī and reciting the mantra of the Śrī Devī.
And the compassionate devotees of the Śrī-devatā protect the sixteen-fold wheel within the circle of the pearl enclosure.
Having taken refuge in the great and highly prosperous Mahārudra, all those Rudras,
headed by Hiraṇyabāhu, worship Jvalanmanyu.

Thus, in the glorious *Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa*, in the latter section, within the dialogue between Hayagrīva and Agastya, in the narrative of Lalitā, the thirty-third chapter titled "The Description of the Seven Inner Courtyards, Beginning with the Puṣparāga and Ending with the Mine of Jewels," Agastya said:
"What is that sixteen-fold enclosure-cakra, and what is its presiding deity, Rudra?"
And who are those Rudras stationed there, and by what names are they proclaimed?
In which reflection-frames of the obstructions do they dwell, and what are their names?
O treasury of compassion, tell me their names according to their functional and fierce characteristics.
Hayagrīva said:
Therein, the dissolution of Rudra is proclaimed, fashioned from a lattice of pearls;
it is five yojanas in width and adorned with a length of that same measure.
Endowed with sixteen enclosures and captivating with its central pedestal,
Mahārudra dwells upon that central pedestal, blazing with fury and possessing three eyes.
O Sage, the hand holding the bow of truth always remains;
O Pot-born One, it is said that there are exactly three Rudras in the triangle.
Hiraṇyabāhu was another general and lord of the quarters.
Vṛkṣa, Harikeśa, as well as the supreme Paśupati, Śaṣpiñjara, Tviṣīmant, and Pathīnāmpati; // BndP_3,34.7 //
These six are situated in the hexagon; furthermore, Babhruśās is in the octagon, as well as Vivyādhi, Anapati, Harikeśa, and Upavītī.
Puṣṭānāmpati, Anya, Bhava, and Heti likewise;
in the tenth petal of the enclosure, the first is Jagatāmpati.
Rudra, Ātāpin, Kṣetrapati, Sūta, and another; I am yet another, Vanapati, Rohita, and Sthapati.
There was also another, the lord of trees; and these [others] had their bows strung:
the minister, the merchant, and likewise the other, the lord of the forest.
Bhava shall be the fourth, and Vāri thereafter the fifth;
O Pot-born one, the Lord of Herbs (Oṣadhīpati) shall be the sixth.
Likewise, the Lord of husbands cried out with a loud voice,
and the Lord of beings ran about, completely stripped of his garments.
These twelve, situated upon the petals, reside in the fifth enclosure:
Sahamāna, Nirvyādhi, and likewise Avyādhinām-pati.
Kakubha, Niṣaṅgin, the Lord of Thieves (Stenānāṃ pati), and Niceru—
these are to be known as the deities of the sixth enclosure.

Furthermore, O Pot-born One, there are the attendants of the underworld, the forest-dwellers, and the lords of those who carry poisoned darts; they are the masters of those who wish to kill and those who steal.
O Sage, there are Asīmanta, Suprājña, Naktamcara,
Prakṛtīnāmpati, Uṣṇīṣin, and Gireścara.
O Pot-born one, the lord of the Kuluñcas was Iṣumān;
they were skilled with bows, unyielding, and ever placing [their weapons] before them.
These sixteen, who dwell upon the sixteen spokes, were drawing back, releasing, shooting, and piercing Sindhu as well.
Whether sitting or lying down, walking or even waking,
standing still or running, those present in the assembly are indeed masters of meditative absorption.
Aśva, Aśvapati, Avyādhin, Gaṇādhyakṣa, Bṛhanta, and Vindhyamardana—these are the leaders of the hosts. Bṛhat-Parāśara Purāṇa 3.34.21.
In the eighth enclosure, there are eighteen kinds of deities known as the Gṛtsas;
then there are the lords of the Gṛtsas, the Vrātas, and likewise the lords of the Vrātas.
There were hosts and leaders of hosts, possessing universal forms and diverse shapes;
some were great and others small, and some were chariot-warriors while others were without chariots.
Chariots, those called chariot-warriors and infantry, as well as army commanders, stewards, charioteers, carpenters, and wheelwrights; 3,34.24.
And the potters—these are the Rudras, the deities of the ninth enclosure;
as well as the smiths, the Puñjiṣṭhas, the Niṣādas, and the groups of arrow-makers.
O Pot-born One, Bhava is Rudra; he is the makers of bows, the hunters, the dog-leaders, the dogs themselves, the horses, and the lords of horses.
Śarva, Paśupati, Nīlagrīva, Śitikaṇṭhaka, Kapardin, Vyuptakeśa, and another, Sahasrākṣa.
Śatadhanvan, Giriśa, Śipiviṣṭa, and Mīḍhuṣṭama— O Kumbhaja, these are declared to be the ten Rudras residing on the Śāla tree.
Then there were those stationed in the eleventh wheel:
Iṣumān, Hrasva, Vāmana, Bṛhan, Varṣīyān, and Vṛddha, together with Samṛddhi.
Agrya, prathama, āśu, ajiranya, śīghra, śībhyaka,
urmyāvasvan, arudra, srotasya, and divya are the names of the rivers.
O Pot-born One, there are the eldest and the youngest, as well as the elder and the younger,
the middle, the one to be understood, and the lowest.
These twenty-four Rudras of great power have been described; furthermore, there are Budhnya, Somyarudra, Pratisarpaka, and Yāmyaka.
Then Kṣemya, Vokṣalya,
Ślokya, Avāsānya, Vanya, Kakṣya, Śrava, and then another, Pratiśrava.
Āśuṣeṇa, Āśuratha, Śūra, O storehouse of asceticism,
Avabhinda, Varmin, and Varūthin, together with Bilmin.
Kavacin, Śruta, Sena, Dundubhi,
Āhananya, and Dhṛṣṇu— these six are remembered as the twenty-six [attendants].
Standing in the twelve enclosures, they possess massive bodies and great strength.
There were also scouts and messengers sent forth, as well as bowmen;
one carried a quiver, while another likewise held sharpened arrows for the battle.
O Pot-born One, Svāyudha, Sudhanvan, Stutya, Pathya, Kāpya, Anāḍhya, Sūdha, Sarasīya, and Vindhyamardana; BndP_3.34.37.
Then there is another, the Nādhamāna, the Veśanta,
the Kupya, the Avadhavarṣya, the Avarṣya, the Medhya, and the Vidyutya.
Idhryātapyau, as well as Vātyau, and another, Reṣmya;
Vāstavya, Vāstupa, and Soma—these are the ones of great strength.
O Sage, hear now of those Rudras who reside in the thirteenth enclosure:
Rudra, Tāmrāruṇa, Śaṅkha, and likewise Paśupati, O Sage.
The fierce one, the terrible one, likewise the slayer in front and the slayer from afar;
the destroyer, the one most worthy of being slain, the bull, and the one with golden hair.
O Sage, he is Tāra, Śambhu, Mayobhū, Śaṅkara, and Mayaskara; he is Śiva, Śivatara, Tīrthya, Kulya, as well as Pārya, Apārya, Prataraṇa, and Uttaraṇa.
Ātarya, likewise Labhya, and similarly Ṣaṣṭha and Phenya—
these Rudra deities are said to reside in the fourteenth enclosure.
O treasure of asceticism, there are also Sikatya, Pravāhya, likewise Iriṇya,
Prapathya, Kiṃśila, and immediately after that, Kṣayaṇa.
Kapardin, Pulastya, Goṣṭhya, Gṛhya, Talpya, Gehya, Kāṭya, Gahvareṣṭha, and Urudīpaka.
O Sage, one should also protect *niveṣṭya*, *pāntavya*, *rathanya*, and *śukya*; likewise, *harīti*, *alotha*, *lopyāḥ*, *urya*, and *sūrmyai*.
Payeya, Parṇaśa, as well as Vaguramāṇaka, Abhighnanāśi, Prakhidana, and Kirika likewise; BndP_3,34.47.
O wise one, the heart of the gods and the thirty-two deities of the Rudras remain there,
equipped with their weapons, during the fifteen-fold enclosure.
In the sixteenth enclosure, however, there are those situated at the eastern and other gates,
known as Vikṣiṇatkas, Avicinvatkas, and Nirhatas.
And those who speak of diseases, having been purified by fire, worship Mahārudra;
thus, there are thousands of Rudras stationed within the sixteen halls.
But Mahārudra, the promoter of Lalitā’s command, having been served,
abides for the prosperity of the worlds in the corner of Muktāśāleśa.
These Rudras, numbering one hundred and known as the Śatarudriya, possess great strength;
they protect those endowed with devotion to Lalitā day and night,
while they subject non-devotees of the goddess Lalitā to obstacles.
In this manner, Śakra and the other guardians of the directions, having taken refuge in the Suktāśāla grove,
perform only the service of the supreme sovereign Lalitā.
Then, within the Māruta-yojana of the forest known as Muktākhya,
there is a forest called Mārakata, which rises four yojanas high.
As before, it is beautifully adorned with gate-towers (gopura) and other structures;
there, the [temples] of Śrī Daṇḍanāthā and others are situated in the directions starting from the southeast.
Four abodes have been proclaimed as the expansions of the Mantriṇī-dwelling,
which rest upon the joints of the great chariot of the Gīticakra.
In the great battle with the demon Bhaṇḍāsura, those goddesses remained awake there;
all the grounds were auspicious, inlaid with rows of emeralds.
Abounding in forests of red sandalwood and filled with all kinds of objects,
there all the goddesses reside, possessing a splendor equal to that of the Lord of the Staff (Yama).
Countless palm trees, variegated with fresh gold, move about even as they carry plows, harrows, and pestles.
Their trunks extend for a yojana and are provided with broad leaves;
they have golden bark, are exceedingly smooth, possess beautiful luster, and are bent down by their fruit.
Hanging from root to tip and filled with jars of wine, these palm trees,
fashioned by artisans for the pleasure of Daṇḍanāthā, stand there.
And having drunk again and again that filling of palm-juice,
the wheel-deities beginning with Jṛmbhiṇī became agitated with intoxication, as did the Bhairavas beginning with Hetuka.
And the seven goddesses of suppression dance, overwhelmed by intoxication,
in the four intermediate directions wherever Daṇḍinī, she of the great vision, is present.
There, in the eastern direction and other quarters, are those with splendor equal to that of the Goddess:
Unmattabhairavī, Svapneśī, and [the others] in every direction.
The residence of Daṇḍanāthā is merely nominal;
her actual seat of service is another place in the region of the Great Lotus Forest (Mahāpadmāṭavī).
Because that [former] location is so very distant from its precincts, her house is situated there for the purpose of service.
Furthermore, in that *śāla* grove, which is seven *yojanas* in extent and has the appearance of emerald,
there is a rampart with the luster of coral, as rosy as the sun at dawn.
There, all the dry land was composed entirely of coral;
likewise, Brahmā, who resembles coral, has a lotus as his seat.
Having come from the world of Brahmā together with all the lords of sages,
he remains ever vigilant for the purpose of serving the illustrious Goddess Lalitā.
O Lord of the Ocean, that [knowledge] exists together with the progenitors such as Marīci and others,
as well as the fourteen sciences and their thousands of subsidiary branches.
And the sixty-four arts themselves, embodied and most exalted,
reside within the rampart that has the appearance of coral, situated in the world of Brahmā;
by the command of the Goddess, they abide there for the prosperity of the worlds, being full of grace.
Then, within the distance of a *māruta-yojana* from the coral palace,
in the location of the ruby pavilion,
the realm of Viṣṇu exists, surrounded on all sides and eager for the service of Lalitā.
In that world of Viṣṇu, the eternal Viṣṇu himself,
Mādhava, constantly exists there with his forms perpetually divided fourfold, tenfold, and likewise twelvefold.
Furthermore, those ten deities who are the incarnations born from the nails of Śrī Devī during the great battle with the asura Bhaṇḍa are also present in the ruby pavilion.
But compared to the previous inner courtyards, in that particular courtyard,
there was specifically a covering above made of masses of rubies.
There, in that inner courtyard, the Lord, bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
and divided into twelve forms, protects the directions beginning with the east from the demons.
In the eastern direction is Keśava, the wielder of the discus, with the luster of Jāmbūnada gold;
behind him is Nārāyaṇa, the wielder of the conch, resembling a dark blue cloud.
Madhava, dark as the petal of a blue lotus and rich in honey, protects;
on the right side is the great Govinda, the wielder of the bow, with the luster of the moon.
In the north is Viṣṇu, the wielder of the plow, resembling the filaments of a lotus;
in the southeast is Madhusūdana, the wielder of the mace, with the luster of a white lotus.
Trivikrama, with sword in hand, is in the southwest, radiant as fire;
Vāmana, the wielder of the thunderbolt, possessing the brilliance of the rising sun, is in the northwest.
In the northeast is Śrīdhara, with the luster of a white lotus, armed with a paṭṭiśa;
Hṛṣīkeśa, radiant as lightning, is in the southern direction, bearing a mallet.
Padmanābha, holding the Śārṅga bow and possessing a splendor equal to a thousand suns,
circumambulates the location of the ruby pavilion in a clockwise direction.
Possessing all weapons, all powers, all-knowing, and facing in every direction;
resembling an indragopaka insect, holding a noose in his hand, he is unconquered.
But Dāmodara, the soul of all, overflowing with tender devotion,
circumambulates the location of the ruby pavilion in reverse order.
Thus, with twelve bodies, the lotus-eyed Lord shines resplendent in the world of Viṣṇu, seated within a pavilion of rubies.
Then, within a hall of various jewels, at a distance of one yojana from Māruta, was a most enchanting pavilion named Sahasrastambhaka.
Inlaid with various jewels and adorned with various jewels,
a lofty śāla tree made of various jewels stands there.
A single row extends across a thousand pillars;
indeed, there are many such rows of pillars in all four directions.
And the upper covering is likewise made of precious wood as described before;
there, the great world of Śiva remains awake, radiant with shimmering splendor.
There, twenty-eight Śaiva Āgamas are recorded as being personified;
among them, Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, Mahākāla, and others are considered the foremost.
And the deities of the twenty-six principles, with the faces of elephants by the thousands,
were present in that supreme world of Śiva within the pavilion of a thousand pillars.
The Lord of all sciences, the moon-crested one,
the protector of Lalitā’s command and the promulgator of Lalitā’s command.
Constantly reciting the Lalitā mantra with a mind full of bliss,
she regards her own devotees with a Śiva-like vision for the sake of their accomplishment in the Lalitā mantra.
Manifesting that power of intelligence (*medhā-śakti*), which is of the nature of great light and is capable of shattering the mass of darkness both within and without; BndP 3.34.93.
The omniscient and omnipotent Mahādeva, overflowing with devotion for the Goddess, remains in the pavilion of a thousand pillars; meanwhile,
the pot-born Agastya dwells, taking refuge in various halls.

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Regions from the Guardians of the Quarters up to the World of Śiva," in the Lalitopākhyāna of the Hayagrīvāgastya-saṃvāda within the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Hayagrīva said: Now, we shall describe the various divisions of the enclosures (kakṣyā) for the ponds, temples, and other features.
Merely by hearing these, great prosperity is born.
Within a distance of one yojana from the hall with its thousand pillars,
there is a great *śāla* tree named Mana, adorned with all kinds of jewels.
As before, it is provided with gate-towers, doors, panels, and bolts;
the middle courtyard section therein consists entirely of nectar-pools.
Having drunk that, yogins become perfected beings with vajra-bodies and great strength;
indeed, that alone is the elixir for wise men.
In that pond consisting of nectar, he exists having attained the state of water;
by the mere smelling of its fragrance, one becomes the lord of the beautiful women of the Siddhas.
O enemy of Vindhya, even without touching it, a man whose impurities are exhausted [attains liberation] on both sides of the two Śāl trees, on the two banks of the Sudhāvatī pool.
All the other ponds are one krośa in length and breadth;
however, the bottom of that [central pond] extends four yojanas into the water.
Her staircases were encircled and variegated with various jewels;
they were golden-hued and jewel-colored, and upon them were swans and cranes.
The two shores are struck by gently undulating waves;
birds drink that water, which is like a fresh elixir of life.
O destroyer of the Vindhya mountains, there the birds known as kāraṇḍavas have attained freedom from old age and death, being constantly marked by their warbling.
They chant the most exalted mantra of the goddess Lalitā,
surrounding it extensively with a circle of lotus ponds.
There is no path to go there except by means of a boat;
only by the command of the Mantrī and the Daṇḍanātha does the great power named Tārā, the mistress of the gateway, exist there.
There, many female attendants of Tārā, dark as blue lotuses,
sported in the waters of the lake upon thousands of jewel-adorned boats.
They go from this shore to the further shore, and again return to the further bank,
playing repeatedly on lutes, flutes, drums, and other instruments.
There, millions of Tārā’s boatwomen, in the prime of their youth,
repeatedly sing and dance the most meritorious fame of the Goddess.
Some with oars in their hands, and some with ladles and water-vessels in their hands,
they move about upon hundreds of ships, drinking that nectar-like water.
Among those boat-pulling female deities of dark luster,
Tārāmbā was the foremost, capable of subduing the surging flood of waters.
Without the command of those two, Tārā and Mantriṇīdaṇḍadhāra,
she did not grant even the Three-eyed Lord passage across the waters of the lake.
As the great queen moved along with her singing attendants on boats beautiful with jewels,
she displayed magnificent generosity at every step.
In that enchanting palace of jewels, they dwell upon every boat, drinking copiously from the interiors of ruby goblets.
The assembly of the powers of Tārā and Taraṇī is exceedingly beautiful;
O Sage, some of the boats are richly adorned with gold, while others are fashioned from jewels.
Some had assumed the form of crocodiles, some were boats with the faces of deer, some were ships with lion-thrones, and some had the faces of elephants.
Thus surrounded by ships of various forms,
Tārāmbā shines forth, having boarded a magnificent vessel.
Constantly moving through this enclosure like a female crane creating ripples in the water of a pond by swimming both forward and backward, Tārā indeed protects this [enclosure].
At a distance of seven yojanas from the interior of Manaśāla,
there is the one known as Buddhiśāla, which rises four yojanas high.
In the middle courtyard of that [palace] lies the entire Ānandavāpikā;
there, divine great wine, thick with the fragrance of *bakula* flowers and possessing the luster of molten gold, exists as its water.
The Ānandavāpikās are proclaimed to be as deep as before;
likewise, the sequence of stairs and so forth for the birds there is as it was previously.
There, standing on the banks, the Śaktis— flushed with intoxication— sport, drinking again and again the wine that is the water of that place, maddened by their own passion.
And there, the goddess Vāruṇī herself is the mistress of the ships;
she whom they call Sudhāmālinī and whom they call Amṛteśvarī.
There, stationed upon her jeweled ship and surrounded by an army of Śaktis,
she bestows pride upon the three worlds by her mere slight appearance.
Resembling the rising sun, with cheeks flushed red with intoxication,
her hair was adorned and entwined with a garland of *pārijāta* flowers.
She carries a goblet filled with intoxicating liquor and a swaying blue lotus,
as well as a piece of cooked flesh in a jeweled vessel and another in yet another.
There shines the mistress of the row of boats for crossing the Vāruṇī river;
by the command alone of both the Minister and the Lord of Punishment,
she grants the crossing of the pond even to the Three-eyed One, and not otherwise.
Then, at a distance of one yojana from the great hall of Buddhi,
there is the great hall of Ahaṃkāra, likewise endowed with gate-towers as before.
O Sage, between those two Śāl trees, the entire ground of the courtyard is known as Vimarśavāpikā, which consists of the nectar of the Suṣumṇā.
Within the inner mind of those great yogins, the supreme nectar awakens, filled with the vital wind within the hollow of the channel of Suṣumṇā.
O ascetic, that very water of her pond remains as it was before;
indeed, those banks, stairs, birds, and boats are remembered just as they were.
There dwells the goddess Naukeśvarī, renowned as Klarukullā;
she has a form dark like the tamāla tree and wears a dark-blue bodice.
She is surrounded by other ship-mistresses who are her equals,
who constantly hold jewels and oars in their hands, and who are overflowing with radiant joy.
O Sage, the pond, which was previously described as having water deep as the ocean, now revolves all around with those who have boarded jeweled boats.
Within the Śāla grove of Ahaṅkāra, at the junction of the winds,
stands the great Śāla tree of Sūryabimba, four yojanas in height.
The rising of Aruṇa was a great event even for the Sun;
the earth within that middle zone was inlaid with rubies.
There, in the emergence of the morning sun's heat, the supreme goddess Lalitā performed exceedingly intense austerities, and the Sun-god obtained that splendor.
All the hosts of planets and zodiac signs, as well as the lunar mansions and stars,
have indeed attained their status as illuminators of the world by performing penance right here.
There, O Sage, Mārtaṇḍabhairava is divided twelvefold,
accompanied by millions of radiant Śaktis;
he is the embodiment of great light, with eyes as red as wine.
He who dwells absorbed in that state, ever eager for the flavor of play amidst groves of *kaṅkolita* trees on the far shore of the Vindhya's pride, remains there.
There exists a great power called Mahāprakāśanā;
his other, most exalted power is Cakṣuṣmatī, known as the goddess Chāyā.
Thus surrounded by these three protective powers (iṣṭāḥ śaktayaḥ),
one should always recite the Vidyā of the Great Goddess Lalitā with the Heart-mantra.
Illuminating the radiant senses of His devotees,
He utterly crushes the web of darkness, both external and internal, along with its very roots.
There, within the great hall of the solar orb at a distance of one yojana, the terrifying Bhairava Mārtaṇḍa shines amidst the rising rays of the morning sun.
The Śāla tree, consisting of the lunar orb, rises four yojanas high;
it is equipped with gate-towers, doors, panels, and bolts, just as described before.
The entire ground in the middle of that is called the gateway of the moonlight (candrikādvāra).
Having performed most severe penance at that very gateway of Candrikā,
the Moon, born from the eye of Atri, attained his splendor.
Here resides the god named Śrīsomanātha, of stainless form,
who destroys the darkness of the three worlds and brings an end to the cycle of worldly existence.
And drinking the stainless nectar of moonlight, which was filled with the six [flavors],
he was surrounded by the powers of the twenty-seven lunar mansions.
The Blessed Moon, whose own form is eternally full and stainless, exists right there at the gateway of the moonlight, possessing his natural appearance.
There, the Moon, joined by the Aśvinī and other stars, passes his time through the recitation and meditation upon Lalitā, as well as through hundreds of hymns and worship services.
And there are thousands of other powers named Tārā who remain in his very presence; that court is filled with them.
Now, within the Śāla grove of Candra, at the distance of a Māruta-yojana,
there is a Śāla tree named Śṛṅgāra, which rises four yojanas high.
Constructed as if from jewels of love in the form of beautiful mansions, like *kaustubha* gems,
the entire earth lies within it, surrounded by a moat of great passion.
In that moat, which is filled with the sentiment of erotic love (śṛṅgārarasa),
there dwell the powers of erotic love, resplendent with various ornaments.
There, moving about upon a thousand boats, those women, arrogant with passion, constantly attend upon that being who stands upon his boat like the god of the flower-weaponed one.
But he, who is subservient to the command of Lalitā, deludes the entire universe with his arrows, such as the Sammohana, bringing all the worlds under his power.

Deluded by its power, those dressed in pure attire and filled with intense, graceful devotion proceed with attentive minds toward the region of the Great Lotus Forest (*mahāpadmāṭavī*) to worship it. (Bṛhadbrahmāṇḍapurāṇa 3.35.64)
Neither the gods, the siddhas, nor human beings are able to go there;
yet Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, whose minds are pure by their very nature,
proceed to that supreme region of the Mahāpadma forest at his command.
And those wandering in saṃsāra are blinded by passion and filled with manifold conceptual constructions;
even men of noble lineage are soiled by the knowledge of their own discursive thoughts.
Those who are dense with abundant passion are not wise enough to cross over the great moat of erotic sentiment, which bestows mature delusion.
For Smara dwells there, possessing invincible beauty that deludes the people of the three worlds,
and holding the office of the great moat of erotic passion.
Having transcended all of that, which deludes even the great,
no one at all is capable of proceeding to the Great Lotus Forest.
Then, at a distance of seven yojanas within the Śṛṅgāraśāla,
there was the great abode of the Cakrarāja, named Cintāmaṇigṛha.
The entire ground in its center is adorned all around with jewels;
it is named the Great Lotus Forest (Mahāpadmāṭavī), which bestows all auspicious fortune.
O Sage, the gate extending as far as the great Kāla known as Śṛṅgāra is situated in this very manner;
such is the arrangement of the gates in all four directions.
O Sage, in all directions there are one hundred gates as described;
the auspicious halls are said to be twenty-five in number.
The base of all these halls measures one yojana;
O Sage, listen attentively as I describe the site of the Lotus Forest.
In that place, which is inlaid with all kinds of jewels and extends for six yojanas,
there are indeed great-stalked lotuses covering the ground on every side.
The trunks, however, are a yojana in length and covered with soft thorns;
their leaves indeed have a span of about ten palm trees.
The filaments of the lotuses are five tālas in length,
and the pericarps are proclaimed to be ten tālas in height.
There are many lotuses, even by the millions upon millions, that are exceedingly delicate, always in full bloom, heart-stealing with their fresh fragrance, and possessed of broad petals.
O Pot-born One, in the eastern part of the enclosure of the Mahāpadma forest,
there stands a form of fire, one krośa in height, circular in shape.
O Agastya, the great vessel for the arghya-offering, which is ten kalās wide, extends for half a yojana.
Surrounding that support,
the ten digits of the fire-god, beginning with Dhūmrārcis, shine forth, their forms ablaze with power.
Possessing the splendor of radiant youth and adorned with various ornaments,
languid with passion, they embrace the Lord, the eater of oblations, who is the glorious substratum of all forms, and remain encircling him on every side.
Dhūmrārcis, Uṣṇā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī,
Suśrī, Surūpā, Kapilā, Havyavāhinī, and Kavyavāhinī—
these are declared to be the ten kalās of Agni, who is the form of the foundation.
There, the Lord resides upon the support, taking the form of the vessel;
he is the Sun, whose rising is renowned for utterly destroying the darkness of the three worlds.
That vessel, consisting of the sun, is one and a half yojanas in height,
one yojana in length and breadth, and illuminated by a great light.
Twelve digits (kalās), possessing exceedingly brilliant luster, exist around that vessel like dolls with bodies clinging to it.
Tapinī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvalinī, Ruci,
Suṣumṇā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā.
In that vessel is the supreme nectar, the cause of ultimate bliss,
rich with the essence of all medicinal herbs and endowed with a heart-pleasing fragrance.
It was always made fragrant with blue lotuses and white water-lilies that were unfading and exceedingly sweet-scented; it was pleasing to the heart, cool, light, and pure.
Magnificent with hundreds of moving waves, worthy of worship with graceful offerings,
and always resonant with sound, it shines as the cause of worship.
That [nectar] is declared to be the arghya-offering, consisting of the digits of the moon;
within it reside the subtle *nauṅkā* goddesses, fashioned like jewels. These lovely digits of the moon, possessing fresh youth, sport there.
Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣṇā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭī, Rati, Dhṛti,
Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, and Aṅgadā.
Pūrṇā and Pūrṇāmṛtā are the digits (kalās) of the Moon;
they are full of fresh youth and always have smiling faces.
Nourishment, prosperity, stability, intelligence, beauty, fortune, splendor, fortitude,
old age, and accomplishment— these are said to be the playful manifestations of Brahmā’s digits.
Sthiti, Pālinī, Śānti, Īśvarī, Tātikāmikā,
Varadā, Āhlādinī, Prīti, and Dīrghā are the portions (kalās) of Hari.
Tīkṣṇā, Raudrī, Bhayā, Nidrā, Tandrā, Kṣutkrodhinī, Trapā,
Utkārī, and Mṛtyu— these obstructive times (kāla) are situated there.
The portions of Īśvara are said to be yellow, white, reddish, and bright;
indeed, these four are declared to be the portions of Śaṅkara.
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidya, and likewise Śānti;
Indirā, Dīpikā, Recikā, and Mocikā.
Parā, Sūkṣmā, Vindhyāre, as well as Sūkṣmāmṛtā, Kalā,
Jñānāmṛtā, Vyādhinī, Vyāpinī, and Vyomarūpikā—
these sixteen are proclaimed; therein the Śaktis sport.
Then, mounted upon the boat of Rudra,
thousands of Vidyās, restless here and there, sport there in the form of Śaktis.
Prepared by the Supreme Lord for the purpose of purifying the *arghya* offering,
the Śaktis always rejoice after drinking that *arghya*, which is nectar.
Though dwelling in the great lotus forest and situated upon the great wheel,
[they experience] ever-new [pleasures] again and again, and repeatedly that which possesses unfettered fragrance.
Having repeatedly filled it with thousands of jewel-jars and ten million golden vases,
that great nectar of worship was constantly replenished.
Those who dwell in houses made of wish-fulfilling gems,
intoxicated with pride, offer their services as attendants to those possessing powers such as *aṇimā*.
The arrangement of the central shrine in the eastern sector of the Mahāpadma forest enclosure has thus been described;
hereafter, other matters therein shall also be told.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Offering of Arghya in the Great Lotus Forest," within the Lalitopākhyāna of the Hayagrīva-Agastya Saṃvāda in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Hayagrīva said:
To the south-east of the Cintāmaṇi house is the Kundamānaka.
It was one yojana in length and breadth, and one yojana in height.
There the fire of consciousness blazes, honored by hundreds of streams of nectar;
it generates supreme sovereignty and is purifying by the command of Lalitā.
There the flame of consciousness blazes, without fuel yet possessing a great radiance; its form is satiated by nectar, and it has the hue of the sprouts of the kaṅkolī plant.
Therein, the Great Goddess is the Hotrī and the supreme Kāmeśvara is the Hotā;
both of them, as the eternal Hotṛs, protect the entire world.
The unsurpassed Lalitā, who is independent of others, has been set in motion;
and Kāma, impelled by Lalitā, was set in motion by Śaṅkara.
In the forest of lotuses, within the portion belonging to the Rākṣasas of the great palace of the wish-fulfilling gem.
The king of chariots, the best of vehicles, stands with its lofty form;
it is composed of nine sections and possesses a structure made entirely of all kinds of jewels.
Four yojanas in width and ten yojanas in height, it decreases in size as one moves northward; it is massive and resplendent with its pole-socket.
The great wheel of the four Vedas, with the goals of human life as its magnificent horses,
was adorned by the waving chowries of the attendant principles.
Endowed with the characteristics previously described and adorned by a pearl umbrella,
he performed acts of daring in the great battle against the demon Bhaṇḍāsura.
The foremost of chariots proceeds at the head of the wind-path in the forest of lotuses within the great palace of the wish-fulfilling gem, which is carved out from the seat of the Goddess Śrī.
The sovereign chariot-wheel of Geyacakra stands at the edge of Mantriṇī,
within the forest of lotuses in the Rudra-sector of the great palace of Cintāmaṇi.
Vallabha, the great chariot-warrior (mahāratha), is in the Kiricakra of Daṇḍanāthā;
these three chariots are to be known as identical in all the series of Śrīpuras within the entire field, just like the deities stationed in their respective limbs.
The fiery pit situated in the southeast, which is always blazing—that is indeed the heated Gāyatrī; it is heated and terrifying.
After that is the sun, the radiant one; then the temple of Oṃkāra;
and the goddess Turīyagāyatrī, who is also Cakṣuṣmatī, O ascetic.
Then the king of the Gandharvas, as well as Rudra and his assembly,
and the blessed goddess Tārāmbikā, stood behind him.
Residing in the portion of the Rākṣasas within the supreme palace of the wish-fulfilling gem,
the Blessed Lord Hari is to be invoked by the mantra consisting of his three names.
Mahāgaṇapati has his banner situated to its north;
he is expressed by the five-syllabled mantra, and to his north is Śiva.
Then Mṛtyuñjayeśa is [worshipped] by means of the three-syllabled mantra to be recited;
Sarasvatī, known as Dhāraṇā, indeed dwells above him.
O Destroyer of Vindhya, to the north of that Mātṛkā is the temple of her form, which consists of the letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa'.
In the north are indeed Sampadeśī and likewise Kālasaṃkarṣaṇī;
and Śrī Mahāśambhunātha is the cause for the manifestation of the Goddess.
Śrī, Parāmbā, and Viśadajyotsnā of pure form—
these deities, having made their abodes, [reside] one after another.
Bālā, Annapūrṇā, and likewise Hayārūḍhā—
these four Śrīpādukās have their respective temples situated one after the other.
Starting from the northwestern ground of the great palace of the wish-fulfilling gem,
there is another forest of great lotuses where other deities have made their dwellings.
Unmattabhairavī, the supreme Svapnavārāhikā,
Tiraskaraṇikāmbā, and another supreme fifth [goddess].
Just as before, these goddesses of great prosperity have established their abodes:
the great goddess Śrīpūrti and also Śrīmahāpādukā.
Just as previously established in the two houses, those same supreme deities were propounded by Śaṅkara within the ocean of the six Āmnāyas;
and all those vidyās likewise reside in the region of the Great Lotus Forest (Mahāpadmāṭavī).
Thus, O ascetic, the houses in the glorious Raśmimālā city were constructed of jewels,
with lofty flagstaffs, high halls, and provided with staircases.
O Samudra, at the eastern gate of the great palace of the wish-fulfilling gem,
on the southern side, stands the great residence of the Lord of Mantrins.
On the left side is the palace of Daṇḍanātha, constructed of jewels;
to the east of it is the place of honor for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa.
Illuminating the entire circle of directions with rays of light from their jewels,
all these deities, overflowing with devotion for Lalitā and engaged in the recitation of Lalitā’s mantra, worship the Śrī Devī.
The previously mentioned place for the arghya and the previously mentioned preparation of the arghya are prescribed to be the same for all [deities], beginning with those at the southern gate.
Now I shall describe the Cintāmaṇi palace; listen, O great sage!
It is situated in the middle of that illustrious city, extending for two yojanas.
Its walls were made of wish-fulfilling gems (cintāmaṇi) and its interior was very spacious;
likewise, it was covered above by ceilings made of wish-fulfilling gemstones.
Enclosed by a deceptive form, rising high here and there,
the wall of the house was thus uplifted to a measurement of four yojanas.
The ground rising up from it is said to be twenty yojanas;
above that, it is joined with a gradual decrease, shining with the three crowns of its thickness.
And those crowns, O Sage, consisting of will, action, and knowledge,
are ever resplendent and composed of wish-fulfilling gems.
The entire Cintāmaṇigṛha is said to consist of wish-fulfilling gems;
it has four doors, each measuring half a krośa in width.
O Sage, the width of the gates is said to be half of a half-krośa;
furthermore, within all the gates are houses made of wish-fulfilling gems.

O great sage, the river Pihitā is graced by the Goddess Lalitā; it is like a stream of molten red iron, possessing the brilliance of a thousand rising suns yet cool as the moon, flowing forth repeatedly in the form of a current.
The eastern gate is proclaimed as consisting of the Eastern Tradition (pūrvāmnāya),
while the region of the southern gate is characterized by the Southern Tradition (dakṣiṇāmnāya).
The region of the western door is characterized by the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya),
and the region of the northern door shall be characterized by the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya).
Within the interior of that king of houses,
radiant jewel-lamps with inlaid handles, possessing a brilliance like ten million suns,
are situated all around the walls, illuminating the interior of the residence.
In the vast central space of this wish-fulfilling jewel palace,
upon an exceedingly high platform, is the most sublime Bindu-cakra.
The middle ground of the Bindu, from the high wall of the Cintāmaṇi palace,
is declared to be three *krośas* in extent, excluding one *krośa* for the wall itself.
In that place spanning three *krośas*, by means of the radiance of the self consisting of *aṇimā* and the other powers,
that entire area of three *krośas*— calculated according to the method of measuring with hands—
is said to be measured by twenty-four thousand hands.
From the Bindu-pīṭha up to the Lord [of the pīṭhas], there are fourteen divisions;
when these internal divisions have been distinguished, the number of hands is now stated by me.
O Sage, from the site of the Lotus Forest to the interior of the Cintāmaṇi palace, the height is twenty cubits; there reside the powers beginning with aṇimā.
The internal breadth of an *aṇima* is four *nalvas*;
four hundred *kiṣkus* are declared to be one *nalva*, and four *nalvas* are one *kiṣku*, which is also called a *hasta*.
In that interval, however, [the powers] beginning with *aṇimā* have their abodes established in the east and other directions:
*aṇimā*, *mahimā*, *laghimā*, and likewise *garimā*.
Lordship, mastery, the power to have one's will fulfilled, liberation itself,
the attainment of desire, and the fulfillment of all wishes— these are the supreme accomplishments (siddhis).
The accomplishment of alchemy (rasasiddhi), the accomplishment of liberation (mokṣasiddhi), and likewise the accomplishment of strength (balasiddhi);
the accomplishment of the sword (khaḍgasiddhi), the accomplishment of the sandals (pādukāsiddhi), and the accomplishment of the collyrium (añjanasiddhi).
Mastery of speech, mastery of the world, and immediately thereafter, mastery of the body—
these are the eight accomplishments (siddhis), though many others are recognized by yogis.
In that interval, O Sage, millions of *siddhis*, beginning with *aṇimā* and ending with *paramaiśvarya*, attend upon the Supreme Goddess on all sides within that [space].
Filled with the splendor of their youth, their lotus-like faces smiling,
holding blazing cintāmaṇi jewels in their hands, sixteen years of age,
and of exceedingly noble nature, they sport about, overwhelmed by intoxication.
Above that, extending to the limit of the powers such as *aṇimā*, there was a most enchanting region,
twenty cubits high and four *nalvas* in width.
And in the four directions, with rows of stairs, it shall be most beautiful;
there is the celestial abode of Brahmā and the others—listen now to those goddesses stationed therein.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
Vārāhī, Māhendrī, and Cāmuṇḍā as the seventh,
and Mahālakṣmī as the eighth— these [goddesses] have established their abodes there.
Abounding in various kinds of weapons and equipped with various powers and attendants,
they have established their abodes starting from the eastern direction and proceeding in a clockwise manner.
Then, O Pot-born One, above that [city] lies the Brahmāntara region,
twenty cubits high and four *nalvas* in extent;
it is called Mudrāntara, and there the *mudrās* have established their dwellings in three divisions.
Saṃkṣobhaṇī, Drāvaṇī, Ākarṣiṇī, Vaśyā, Unmādinī, Mahāṅkuśā,
Khecarī, Bījā, Yonī, and again the tenth is Trikhaṇḍā.
Beginning from the eastern direction, these mudrās are established;
they possess exceedingly beautiful forms and are overwhelmed with fresh youth.
Filling the interior of their homes with lovely splendors,
O tiger among sages, they serve the Goddess Lalitāparameśvarī.
This triad of intermediate cakras is the "Deluder of the Three Worlds" (Trailokyamohana).
Within this [system], those powers (śaktis) that reside in them have been declared by the name "Manifest" (Prakaṭa).
The presiding deity over these is Tripurā, the mistress of the wheels (cakras);
she is the protector of that wheel, whose nature is the agitation of the mudrās.
Now, above the other mudrā, the Nityākalātara is proclaimed;
it is twenty cubits high and four nalvas in width,
and it is intended that there be a mountain and a staircase rising higher and higher.

Within that eternal *akalā*, there are sixteen [deities] consisting of the digits of the moon (*indukalā*), who have established their positions all around and derive bliss from the attraction of desires.
Satisfying the circle of the directions with their very cool streams of nectar—
O Pot-born one, learn their names from me.
The eternal Kāmākarṣiṇī, the other, Buddhyākarṣaṇikā, the eternal Rasākarṣiṇī, and the digit (kalā) Gandhākarṣaṇikā. BndP_3,36.69.
The art of attracting the mind is eternal; the art of attracting fortitude is a craft; the art of attracting mindfulness is eternal; the art of attracting names is a craft.
The power that eternally attracts seeds, the art that attracts wealth,
another that attracts nectar, and the art that attracts the body.
These are the Guptayoginīs; Tripureśī is the wielder of the wheel (Cakriṇī), known as Sarvāśāpūrikā, the presiding deity of the wheel.
In this wheel, however, is the *pālikā* mudrā, known as *drāviṇikā*;
it is eternal, situated above the end of the *kalā*, and is an exceedingly beautiful abode.
Twenty-five cubits in height and four nalvas in width,
it is provided with steps as before and is named Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa.
There, eight powerful Śaktis, with eyes red with intoxication and possessing the fresh bloom of youth, serve the Supreme Goddess.
Kusumā, Mekhalā, Madanā, Madanāturā,
Rekhā, Veginī, Aṅkuśā, and Mālinī— these eight are the Śaktis.
With a retinue of ten million, possessing powers preceded by the bodiless one (Anaṅga), this wheel is the agitator of all; its presiding deity is [the goddess].
She should be known by the name Sundarī, though she is extremely secret;
she is remembered as the one who protects that wheel and as the attractor of the mudrās.
O Pot-born Sage (Agastya), above the power of Anaṅga,
there is an intermediate space twenty cubits high and four *nalvas* wide,
which bestows all good fortune and contains the powers beginning with Saṃkṣobhiṇī.
There dwell fourteen powerful Śaktis, headed by Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī; hear their names from me.
The power that agitates all, as well as the one that subdues all;
the power that attracts all, and likewise the one that gladdens all.
The power that deludes all, the power that paralyzes all,
the power that causes all to yawn, and likewise the power that brings all under control.
She is the power that colors all, the power that intoxicates all;
she is the power that accomplishes all aims and fulfills all prosperity.
She is the power consisting of all mantras, the destroyer of all dualities;
these [goddesses] are known as the oral traditions (saṃpradāya), residing in the city of Cakriṇī.
The mudrās known as "all-subduing" (sarvavaśyā) are considered the protectors of that wheel;
there, crores of Śaktis are present, and their handmaidens (kiṅkarīs) have been extracted from among them.
O Agastya, above the innermost [court] of Saṃkṣobhiṇī and the others,
there is a temple said to be twenty cubits high and four nalvas in extent;
it is called Viṣṭi, the abode of all the Siddhas and other [beings].
She is the bestower of all accomplishments and likewise the bestower of all prosperity;
she is the goddess who makes all dear and who brings about all auspiciousness.
The Goddess is the bestower of all desires, the liberator from all suffering,
the pacifier of all death, and the warder-off of all obstacles.
The goddess Sarvāṅgasundarī is the bestower of all good fortune;
these goddesses, carved out by the *kalās*, are known by name as the Yoginīs.
Śrī Cakriṇī is to be known as the one who accomplishes all aims;
she is the wheel that protects the circle and the mudrās that intoxicate everyone.
O Kumbhasambhava, above the limit of all attainments and the like,
it rises twenty cubits high and extends four nalvas in width.
That which is between Sarvajña and the others is known by name as Sarvarakṣākara;
it is the most excellent divine wheel, and Sarvajña and the others are proclaimed [as its spokes].
The Goddess is all-knowing, all-powerful, and the bestower of all sovereignty;
she consists of all knowledge and is the destroyer of all diseases.
She is the very nature of the support of all, likewise the remover of all sins;
she is the Goddess consisting of all bliss, whose very form is the protection of all.
These sovereign yoginīs bestow all that is desired and are free from pride.
The Mālinī is said to be the Cakriṇī mudrā, the great goad for all;
thus it is within the Cintāmaṇi house, from Sarvajñā onwards.
O Sage, listen as some other wheels are also described.

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Interior of the Cintāmaṇi Palace," in the Lalitopākhyāna of the Hayagrīva-Agastya Saṃvāda within the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Hayagrīva said: O Pot-born Sage (Agastya), above the interior of the All-Knowing One (Viṣṇu)...
It was twenty-five cubits high and four nalvas in width.
Between Vaśinī and the others, there is to be known the temple of stairs as before;
that wheel is renowned by the name Sarvarogahara (the Remover of All Diseases).
There, the goddesses beginning with Vaśinī are situated in order according to the directions starting from the east;
there, the first is Vaśinīśvarī, devoid of vowels.
The Vāgbhavī [seed-syllable] associated with the Ka-group is called Kāmeśvarī;
the third [Vidyā], Modinī, is Vāgīśī, joined with the Ca-group.
The goddess Sarasvatī, known as Vimalā, is adorned with the *ṭa*-group of consonants;
likewise, when endowed with the *ta*-group, she is the fifth, the sustainer of speech.
The sixth [vowel], however, is considered victorious when expanded by the labial class (pavarga);
it consists of all sovereignty and the like, and is composed of speech within the four corners of the letters beginning with ya.
Kaulinī is considered the eighth [goddess] with slightly more than six syllables;
these goddesses are devoted to recitation and are adorned with ornaments of pearls.
O Agastya, they are considered to be constantly caressed by waves of shimmering prose and verse; through sweet poems and plays that captivate the ear,
they entertain the illustrious goddess.
O Vātāpitāpana, these are renowned by their secret names;
this leader of her own circle is proclaimed by the name Siddhā.
O Subduer of Vindhya, Khecarī is considered the protectress of this wheel, situated above the space between Vaśinī and the others.
The weapon known as the discus (cakra) should be understood to be twenty-two cubits in height and four nalvas in width; therein reside the deities such as Bāṇa and others.
The five goddesses of Bāṇeśvarī and the five arrows of Kāmeśvara are the two blazing goads belonging to the first couple, both male and female.
O Agastya, two bows are arranged on the enemy of Vindhya (Mount Mahendra), nine on Puṇḍra,
two nooses of blazing luster, and four missiles.
Of Kāmeśvarī there are four [weapons], and of the illustrious Maheśitṛ there are four;
thus, making eight weapons in total, they blaze and shine forth.
In the great battle with the asura Bhaṇḍa, having drunk the blood of the wicked dānavas,
the divine weapons become exceedingly satisfied and remain fully alert.
Furthermore, for each of these weapons, there are abundant secondary weapons;
they exist within those other missiles there by the tens of millions.
The vajra-śakti, the śataghnī, the bhuśuṇḍī, as well as the mallet (musala),
the sword, the paṭṭiśa, the mallet (mudgara), and the bhindipālaka.
Thus, thousands upon thousands of such weapons,
along with the great spears of the eight armaments, attend upon him, overwhelmed by intoxication.
Now, above the interval between the weapons,
there is a hearth (*dhiṣṇya*) twenty cubits high and four *nalvas* wide;
it is considered the place for the three goddesses who preside over the seasons.
The goddesses there are Kāmeśā and the others; three are [named], while the fourth is distinct.
She alone is Laliteśvarī, the progenitor of the entire universe without exception.
Listen to the names of the three: Kāmeśī is considered the first;
Vajreśī and Bhagamālā are the others, and they are served by thousands.
And all those various goddesses who are remembered in all the philosophical systems (darśanas),
they all serve there, along with Kāmeśā and the other great deities.
In the context of these [practices], and in the constant engagement with them,
Śrī Devī, whose nature is fulfillment, resides within the Cakriṇīs and Yoginīs.
Lalitāmbikā, who reclines upon the lap of the god Kāmeśvara,
is considered the fourteenth [deity] beginning with Kāmeśī and the sixteenth among the Nityās.
The ninth [deity] is proclaimed as the Yoginī of the Cakradevīs;
she is Samayeśī, situated above the intermediate space, ending at Ilvala.
