The other sanctuary (nāthāntara) is said to be twenty cubits in height and four nalvas in width, adorned with staircases as described previously.
There, the great goddess Nāthāmahādevī was the promoter of the Yogaśāstra for all,
the preceptor of mantras for all, and a great ocean of all branches of knowledge.
And four lords of sacrifice were created here by the god who is a portion of Kāma for the protection of the worlds; hear their names from me.
Mitrī, Śoḍiśa, and Caryākhya, O Pot-born One (Agastya)—
by them were created many [beings] consisting of sandals for the sake of protecting the worlds.
The divine sciences, the multitudes of humans, the multitudes of siddhas,
and the celestial ascetics have attained the perfections such as sālokya, sārūpya, and sāyujya.
The great ones serve those gurus, and they in turn serve many gurus; then, above the interval between the lords, there is indeed the supreme abode.
It is twenty-five cubits in height and four *nalvas* in width;
this is declared to be the "eternal interior," for indeed, fifteen eternal goddesses reside here.
Then there are Kāmeśvarī Nityā, Bhagamālinī Nityā, as well as Nityaklinnā, Bheruṇḍā, and Vahnivāsinī.
Mahāvajreśvarī, Dūtī, Tvaritā, Kulasundarī,
Nityā, Nīlapatākā, Vijayā, and Sarvamaṅgalā.
Jvālāmālinikā and Citrā—these fifteen have been proclaimed;
they are the very forms of the goddesses, possessing great strength and prowess.
The first [day] has attained the status of the primary lunar day (mukhyatithi), pervading the three worlds;
it takes the form of the three times and is expert in swallowing time.
By the command of the Goddess, all beings beginning with Brahmā, who had existed for a long time, remained in the form of having a lifespan of one hundred years according to their respective times.
Ever-striving and boundless, born from the limbs of Śrī Parā,
they serve Lalitā, whose nature is consciousness, for the prosperity of the worlds.
Having attained the state of those [energies], the fifteen radiant lords reside in the wheel of emission and the bindu; however, the abode of the sixteenth is considered to be within that very wheel.
Then, O Agastya, above the space between the two eternal ones,
the intermediate region of Aṅgadevī is said to be twenty cubits in height.
O Sage, in that temple of stairs, which measures four *nalvas* in width as described before,
there indeed reside the powers (*śaktis*) beginning with the Goddess of the Heart.
The goddess of the heart, the goddess of the head, and likewise the goddess of the crest;
the goddess of armor, the goddess of sight, and the goddess of weapons—these six are proclaimed.
Those beautiful-browed ladies of Śrī Kāmeśvara stood very close by;
their limbs were filled with fresh loveliness, and they remained vigilant, bearing their weapons.
Moving about on all sides upon the seat of the Bindu, they possess haughty forms; they carry out the command of Lalitā and abide upon the seats of those who have attained mastery.
Then, above the inner Aṅgadevī,
there is a circular-shaped great seat (mahāpīṭha) consisting of Bindu and Nāda, ten cubits in height.
This Bindupīṭha, which extends for eight nalvas and resembles the rising sun, should be known; it is also considered a Śrīpīṭha.
It should be known as the Great Seat (Mahāpīṭha), it is also desired as the Seat of Knowledge (Vidyāpīṭha), and likewise as the Seat of Bliss (Ānandapīṭha); it assumes the form of fifty seats.
There, within the great [palace] consisting of the five Brahmans of the illustrious Goddess Lalitā, the jewel-throne Mañcaratna remains awake, which is the root of the three worlds.
The four legs of that couch are proclaimed to be ten cubits in height and three cubits in width.
Through the constant yoga of meditation on Śrī, they have attained the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and Īśvara, and have reached the state of Śakti.
One, however, has five feet and resembles the hibiscus flower;
he is to be known as having Brahman as his essence, and he is situated in the direction of fire (the southeast).
The fourth bed-leg, however, is made of the essence of *karṇikāra* wood;
it should be known as the self of Īśvara, situated in the direction of Īśa (the northeast).
All these, equipped with weapons and adorned with every ornament,
have the form of pillars above and below, while in the middle they have the form of persons.
With eyes closed in auspicious meditation and limbs rendered motionless by that very meditation,
Sadāśiva was upon the plank of their couch.
Having the luster of a blooming pomegranate flower, four *nalvas* in width and six *nalvas* in length,
he possesses a form that is eternally radiant.
O ascetic, from the inner space of the Aṅga-deities up to the planks of the bed,
the limbs are composed of wish-fulfilling gems and consist of the nature of the Tattvas.
The stairs shine forth with thirty-six dwellings;
we shall now describe these stairs according to the sequence of the ascent.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space;
as well as smell, taste, form, sound, the organ of generation, the anus, and the feet.
The hands, speech, nose, tongue, skin, eyes, and ears,
as well as ego, intellect, mind, primordial nature (prakṛti), and the individual soul (puruṣa).
Niyati, Kāla, Rāga, Kalā, and Vidya [arise] from Māyā; then Śuddhavidyā, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, Śakti, and Śiva. (Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-purāṇa 3.37.60)
These thirty-six are declared to be the rows of steps of the ladder of reality;
the row of steps belonging to Pūṣan rests toward the eastern direction of the couch.
Then, above the couch, there was a bed with a downy swan-feather mattress,
one cubit in height and four nalvas in extent.
It was adorned with foot-rests and head-rests, graced by pairs [of pillars],
beautified by sixty-four *gaḍḍukas*, and possessed the luster of the *pāṭala* flower.
Above that,
an upper covering was prepared from pure, soft safflower-colored cloth, radiant with the luster of rubies.
Dwelling upon that [mountain], facing the eastern direction, he is endowed with compassion,
always sixteen years of age, and beautiful in his attire of amorous grace.
Resembling the orb of the rising sun, with four arms and three eyes,
he is adorned with necklaces, armlets, a crown, bracelets, and other ornaments.
The Blessed One, the primordial God, Śiva, the Lord of Desire, remains awake— he whose cheeks are filled with the moonlight of his lovely smile.
Seated upon his lap was she who was as rosy as the morning sun,
eternally sixteen years of age and proud of her fresh youth.

The splendor of her feet, bearing a crimson hue like polished rubies, surpasses the beauty of sandalwood paste, lotuses, and streaks on the nails; it possesses a luster of lac-dye that flows forth regardless of all else.
She is enchanting with anklets and falling bracelets that produce a sweet sound;
her shapely calves destroy the pride of the excellent quiver of the Bodiless One (Kāmadeva).
Her thighs were as beautiful as the stalks of a plantain tree, resembling the trunk of an elephant;
her ample hips were adorned with a very fine, soft, and reddish silk garment,
and she shone with the full expanse of her loins.
Her lower garment is knotted at the waist and adorned with a jeweled girdle; her deep navel is like a great whirlpool, and the three folds of her belly shine like waves upon a river.
Her body was draped with hundreds of pearl necklaces swaying upon her bud-like breasts,
and her waist was made slender by the weight of her exceedingly full bosom.
His four arms possess the luster of petals as soft as a garland of śirīṣa flowers.
Wearing on her fingers rows of armlets and bracelets adorned with gems,
she bore a neck as beautiful as a conch shell kissed by her husband.
With a chin as round as a mirror for her face, and lips as rosy as the *pāṭala* flower,
she displayed moonlight with her teeth— pure, perfectly aligned, radiant with the splendor of knowledge, and possessing the beauty of jasmine buds.
She shone with various ornaments bound with large pearls;
her hips were covered by the inner petals of a *ketaka* flower, and her eyes were exceedingly long.
Her forehead is graced by a crescent moon, with masses of curls artfully arranged;
her ears are adorned with pālīvata ornaments and earrings set with rubies.
Her mouth was sweetened by a betel-roll perpetually fragrant with fresh camphor and musk,
and her face was as lovely as the orb of the moon shining in autumn.
Her beautiful crown was fashioned from the essence of wish-fulfilling gems,
and she was resplendent with a forehead marked by a central eye that shone like a glittering tilaka-jewel.
Her mass of hair was thick and sparse with deep darkness,
radiant with rows of *kunkuma* applied at the parting of her hair.
Her crest was adorned with a throbbing digit of the moon, her tremulous eyes were intoxicated with passion,
she was enriched with every erotic attire, and she was decorated with all ornaments.
She is the mother of all the worlds, the eternal increaser of bliss,
and the source of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Īśa, and Sadāśiva.
Satiated by the cascades of compassion dancing from the corners of her eyes,
that Blessed Lady Lalitāmbikā shines forth, the destroyer of all sins.
They know that the fruit of the worship of all other deities is obtained through her worship;
indeed, they declare that the very act of worshipping her yields that same fruit.
And how could I possibly describe that Goddess Lalitā? Even in a thousand million years, not even a single portion of her can be described.

For how can there be any access for words, which by nature consist of non-primordial forms, when describing that [reality], since words turn back along with the mind, failing to reach it? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.37.87)
What is the use of saying more here? Listen to this which is the very truth:
it is spoken by me neither out of partiality, nor out of affection, nor out of delusion.

Having offered libations according to the prescribed rule to the classes of gods, sages, and ancestors, and having performed the worship of the Sun and of the Goddess who resides within the solar orb; BndP_3,38.25.

Seated upon a soft seat, one should meditate upon the great Śrīnagara,

Pure within and without, one should meditate upon the divine Śrīnagara;

One who recites this mantra is indeed freed from all sins;
possessing a form as beautiful as the three worlds, he causes even the God of Love to be deluded.
Endowed with all perfections, omniscient, and honored by all,

yet by his physical form, he could cause agitation in villages, hamlets, cities, and the like in an instant.
By a mere slight contraction of his eyebrows, he is the paralyzer and likewise the one who causes yawning;
he is the expeller, the deluder, and the slayer of those with wicked minds.
Though previously angry, he becomes gracious by force when delighted by the sight of him;
he attains firm mastery in the eighteen branches of knowledge.
His speech was as sweet as the flood of the Mandākinī;
there was nothing unknown to him among all the scriptures, O Pot-born One.
He is capable of refuting all philosophical systems;
he knows the entire reality and attains omniscience.
His heart was always moist with compassion toward all living beings;
the three worlds were not capable of becoming the object of the fire of his wrath.
At the moment of his appearance, their waist-knots became loose,

Their forms were adorned with rows of pearl-like drops of perspiration,

The rows of jeweled bracelets on their lotus-like hands were slipping down;

With their abodes of love melting away and adorned with the sprouts of horripilation,
they seemed as if they had assumed another form through the Mind-born One.
They seemed to be ablaze with masses of flames from unrestrained passion,

Tormented by longing, distressed by the heat of their bodies,

One's family, caste, moral conduct, sense of shame, and retinue;
fear of the world, fear of kinsmen, and likewise fear of the next world.

O sages, know this [universe] to be composed of the twenty-five principles and the five veils of Māyā,

Śiva, Śakti, and Īśvara, as well as Śuddhabodha and Sadāśiva—

Having worshipped this supreme deity, Kāmākṣī, in the worlds according to the rules with devotion, many have attained all their desires in their entirety.
Even today, O Sage, the devoted still obtain the fruit;
and many more shall come to be within the compassionate gaze of Kāmākṣī.
Who indeed is capable of describing the majesty of this Śrī Devī?
Neither I, nor Śambhu, nor Brahmā, nor Viṣṇu; how much less others?
Thus, I have related to you something of the radiant character of Kāmākṣī;
it is remembered as removing all sins for those who hear or read it.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter in the Lalitopākhyāna of the Hayagrīvāgastyasaṃvāda in the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Agastya said:
"What kind of yantra does she have, or what kind of mantra? And what is her boon?"
And what kind of teacher should he be, or what kind of disciple is traditionally taught?
O Hayagrīva, you are omniscient, the manifest Supreme Person;
O Lord, out of your compassionate gaze toward me, please explain all of this.
Hayagrīva said:
"The mantra of her mouth is indeed the Śrīcakra; she is Tripurāmbikā, and she alone is Mahālakṣmī, who formerly manifested from her own self."
Then he beheld a wheel expanding with the nature of light;
indeed, the majesty of this wheel is truly beyond comprehension.
In reality, that very Mahālakṣmī is the Śrīcakra;
having worshipped it, the lotus-eyed Mahāviṣṇu assumed a form that deludes all the worlds and infatuates with desire.
Having worshipped Him, the Lord became the sovereign of all knowledge;
by worshipping Him with special devotion, Brahmā became the creator of the cosmic egg,
and Smara became the one who deludes the sages through his service to Him.
Having placed a wheel made of gold, silver, or other materials before the Śrīdevī and having worshipped it with scents using the sixteen-syllable vidyā, [one should proceed].
Every day, possessing an auspicious form, he should worship with thousands of pure *tulasī* leaves while reciting the root mantra, joined with meditation upon the Goddess Śrī.
And having worshipped with auspicious honey, clarified butter, sugar,
and milk-rice porridge, as well as with faultless food offerings consisting of charming bean cakes, [he should proceed].
The Supreme Goddess bestows her presence upon that wise man who propitiates Mahālakṣmī within the three mandalas, by means of his splendor.
Whatever is desired by the mind, she fulfills when pleased;
one should worship her with white flowers according to the procedure for the *cakramukta*.
On the tip of its tongue, Bhāratī dances eternally.
He who worships the Cakra with pale-red flowers (*pāṭala*) according to the prescribed method shall bring even a sovereign emperor under his control like a servant.
Whoever worships as before with auspicious flowers of yellow color, in his chest Śrī herself dwells eternally; this is certain.
One should not worship with flowers that are foul-smelling, odorless, or even those that are golden-colored;
rather, one should worship with fragrant flowers and blossoms.
Kāmākṣī herself is Mahālakṣmī; the Cakra is indeed the Śrīcakra.
She is Śrīvidyā, the supreme Vidyā, the Mistress, and the Mistress of Gurus.
O ascetic, the king of mantras for this [goddess] is indeed Śrīvidyā itself;
it is joined with the Śrī-bīja at the end of the mantra ending in Kāmarāja.
This sixteen-syllable vidyā is proclaimed as Śrīvidyā;
thus has the secret been declared, which must be guarded with great effort.
This Vidyā is said to be the power (śakti) of all three forms;
among all mantras, this Vidyā is their very life-breath.
This knowledge, which liberates from bondage, has been known through tradition;
when recollected, it removes sin and destroys old age and death.
When worshipped, she destroys suffering, misfortune, disease, and poverty;
when praised, she pacifies the flood of obstacles; and when meditated upon, she bestows the accomplishment of all goals.
He who knows the reality of the specific mudrās, whose impurities have been destroyed by initiation,
and who worships the Supreme Sovereign Goddess, shall obtain his desired fruit.
Clad in white garments and dwelling in a white abode,
a man devoted to celibacy should worship her with white flowers.
One should worship the Supreme Goddess with white food offerings, such as curds, milk, and cooked rice, or even with offerings that are pure through the purity of one's intention.
With a pure mind, one should worship that sixteen-syllable vidyā, in which the syllables *Śrī*, *Vā*, *La*, *Ntrya*, *Kṣī*, and *Bī* are joined respectively to the [six] segments.
Reciting with the syllables of the mātrikā in both forward and reverse order.
O ascetic, while meditating before the gods upon the illustrious goddess in the form of a lamp— whether mentally, in a whisper, or even by recitation— BndP_3,41.26.
Accompanied by the Śrīdevī-nyāsa and having assumed the form of Śrīdevī,
one is liberated from great sins by merely reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.
O divine sage, by two hundred thousand [recitations], that supreme power (parā kalā) indeed destroys even the sins committed over seven lifetimes for the practitioner.
O Sage, by reciting the mantra three hundred thousand times, one is liberated from the sins of a thousand births; of this there is no doubt, for one becomes utterly stainless.
By sixteen hundred thousand recitations in sequence, one shall attain the presence of the Goddess.
Daily worship performed at the three times of day, as well as recitation, libations,
fire-offerings, and feeding Brahmins— this is called *puraścaraṇa*.
One should use "svāhā" at the end of the mantra for the fire-oblation (homa) and the satiation (tarpaṇa), and "namaḥ" for the ritual placement (nyāsa) and worship (pūjana);
one should worship the Goddess at the conclusion of the mantra during the time of recitation as is appropriate.
O Destroyer of the Vindhyas, the fire-oblation (homa) should be one-tenth of the recitation (japa), the libation (tarpaṇa) one-tenth of that,
and the feeding of Brahmins one-tenth of that.
But if, due to defects in place or time, any part [of the rite] is omitted,
one should complete the *puraścaryā* by reciting that [part] twice its number of times.
Then, for the purpose of performing rites for specific desires (*kāmyaprayoga*), one should again recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times,
remaining observant of vows, free from agitation, and devoted to worship at the three times of day;
thereafter, by performing rites such as subjugation (*vaśya*) and others, one will attain success (*siddhi*).

When the practitioner, situated in the center of the wheel after having performed worship, contemplates everything as himself, ruddy, and the person to be accomplished (sādhya) likewise rendered ruddy; // BndP_3,41.35 //
Then, O enemy of Vindhya, one becomes beautiful with all auspiciousness;
beloved by all people, one shall bring them under control—of this there is no doubt.
A wise person, having recited the mantra one hundred and eight times, should apply a tilaka made from equal parts of rocanā, saffron, and sandalwood.
Then, whatever one looks at, speaks of, touches, or thinks of,
that person comes under one's control like a servant by means of half of one's body.
Likewise, O ascetic, if one recites [the mantra] one hundred and eight times over flowers, fruit, incense, drink, or clothing, and offers them to a woman with whom one desires intimacy, she—
her heart being utterly infatuated— is instantly drawn toward him.
One should draw an image with yellow pigment (rocanā) on the surface of the earth in a secluded place—
beautiful in form and adorned with the attire and ornaments of a woman in love.

Having joined the Great Knowledge-mantra (mahāvidyā) of one's birth-name with the word "aṅkuśa" [as an internal interlocking], it should be applied to the forehead, throat, heart, navel, and the circle of the knees.
Having inscribed with the letters of passion (madanākṣara) [the name] dissolved into all the joints of his limbs,
he should face the direction of that [deity], having made his own body the triple city (tripurī).
Having bound the Kṣobhiṇī mudrā, one should recite the vidyā one hundred and eight times,
having joined it within the chamber of fire, which is filled with the radiance of the moon and sun.
Then she, whose outer corners of the eyes were agitated, who was tormented by the arrows of the Bodiless One,
and whose hips throbbed with the awakening of a blazing passion;
She whose lotus-eyes were wide, who had cast far away her excellent conduct, and who was swallowed by the swirling rays shining from the wheel of power (śakticakra).
Her eyes were drawn away, her fortitude lost, and her modesty dissolved;
she was bound by the shackles of mantras, yantras, medicinal herbs, and great mudrās;
her virtuous conduct cast far aside, she whose lotus-like large eyes were now distraught.
She whose silken garment was snatched away by those reciting great mantras with intense mental concentration appeared wonderful—
like one who is utterly bewildered, agitated, or scorched.
She was as if painted, as if unconscious, as if crushed,
as if hidden away, as if motionless, and as if she had entered into another state.
One should meditate upon the woman as whirling in the sky, having the form of a bamboo leaf tossed by the wind of the revolving mantra, even from a distance of a hundred yojanas.
Then, one should contemplate the earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves, extending to the limits of the four oceans, situated in the center of the wheel and blazing with light.
Through the practice of yoga for six months, one becomes like the god of love;
merely by being seen, he attracts the world, and merely by being seen, he brings it under his control.
Upon seeing her, one may agitate a woman; by merely seeing her, one removes poison;
by seeing her, one becomes a master of speech; by seeing her, one may delude everyone;
and by seeing her, one destroys quartan fevers and the like in an instant.
One should secretly wear a wheel drawn with yellow pigment;
it quickly effects the paralysis of speech for disputants—of this there is no doubt.
One should also write the name of the enemy joined with [the syllable] preceded by "śatru" using the juice of *mahānīlī*;
having burned it in the fire while facing south, one slays the enemies.
A wheel inscribed with the names [of the enemies], made from buffalo dung, horse dung, and cow urine, and placed in sour gruel (āranāla), causes hatred among one's foes.
Having applied the name with *rocana* and a crow’s wing-feather in the middle, it hangs down in that shape; this is the supreme means for causing expulsion (*uccāṭana*).
Having drawn a wheel with milk, lac, yellow pigment (rocanā), and the juice of mahānīlī, one who wears it shall bring the four castes under his control.
If one should cast it into the midst of water according to this very procedure,
there is no doubt that he will obtain incomparable good fortune through bathing and drinking.
O Sage, one should constantly visualize a region situated in the center of the wheel, or a city, or a beautiful woman, as blazing; within seven days, one shall cause agitation.
Having written this wheel in yellow color,
if one performs it while facing the eastern direction, one shall paralyze all disputants.
One should worship that which is written in the color of vermilion while facing north;
when this is done, the world comes under one's own control, and not otherwise.
Having drawn the wheel with red chalk, one should worship it while facing west;
whoever does so shall become the attractor, subjugator, and agitator of all women.
One who wanders alone in secret on the mountain at the end of the pride of the Vindhya range should perform worship;
the practitioner of mantra attains freedom from old age and death—of this there is no doubt.
O great sage, this secret has been told; it must be kept hidden.
Through concealment, all success shall be attained; through disclosure, there will surely be ruin.
O Sage, he who performs ritual action without having first completed the preliminary practice (puraścaryā) incurs the curse of the deity and does not attain success.
To pacify defects in the performance, the wise man should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times again;
he should also perform worship according to the rules, and thus the person shall once more become fit.
He who, free from desire, constantly worships the deity with overflowing devotion;
Meditating upon that very same [deity], he remains there, reciting the mantra according to his ability.
She alone shall bear his burden in this world and accomplish his liberation;
always remaining near him, she shall tell him everything.
Just as a cow, filled with maternal affection, follows after her calf,
so does that Goddess follow her own devotee who has come to her for refuge.
Agastya said: "O horse, tell me, what is the meaning of the word *śaraṇāgata* (one who has come for refuge),
after which Gaurī runs as she would after a calf running away?"
Hayagrīva said:
That person who, having cast the entire burden consisting of this world and the next upon the Goddess, always keeps his mind fixed on her; ||| BndP_3,41.72 |||
Favorable toward all and entirely free from hostility,
having sought refuge in none other, he fervently entreated Gaurī for protection.
The conviction that "He will protect me," which has service to Him as its sole purpose and is intent upon worship— this alone is taking refuge.

Whenever praise or blame occurs—whether people revile him or the world praises him—the wise one who has taken refuge, having examined this true nature, should not succumb to despondency or weariness. (BndP 3.41.75)
The resolve for what is favorable, the avoidance of what is unfavorable, the conviction that [He] will protect, and likewise the choosing of Him as the Protector; BndP_3,41.76 //
The surrender of oneself in a state of wretchedness constitutes the sixfold taking of refuge.
Having accepted the surrender of oneself, one should offer the five limbs;
for there is indeed no means equal to this for the attainment of enjoyment and liberation.
Humility, freedom from hypocrisy, non-violence, patience, straightforwardness,
service to the teacher, purity, steadfastness, and self-restraint.
Detachment from the objects of the senses, as well as the absence of egoism; the perception of the defects of birth, death, old age, disease, and suffering;
lack of attachment, and freedom from possessiveness toward children, wife, home, and so forth.
And there must be constant equanimity of mind amidst the occurrence of both the desirable and the undesirable,
as well as unwavering devotion toward me with undivided intent.

One should constantly practice these means for attaining knowledge: dwelling in seclusion, a distaste for the assembly of people, constancy in the knowledge of the inner self, and the vision of the goal of the knowledge of reality. (Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa 3.41.81)
He who performs that action, who is devoted to that as the supreme goal, who is its devotee, who is free from attachment,
and who is without enmity toward all beings— he attains the highest glory.
The wise Guru, renowned as the subduer of Vātāpi, is like me;
and the disciple is said to be like you, a teacher of the secret tradition.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter in the Lalitopākhyāna, within the Hayagrīva-Agastya Saṃvāda of the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Agastya said:
"O horse-faced one, explain the method for forming the mudrās."
When these [verses] are composed, the illustrious Goddess becomes well-pleased.
Hayagrīva said: The great mudrā known as Āvāhanī is proclaimed to be Trikhaṇḍā;
having rotated the hands, one should clearly bring the two thumbs together.
Having placed the two index fingers in a curved shape within the ring fingers, O ascetic, one should apply the two little fingers to their own positions;
now listen as I describe the mudrā called Saṃkṣobhiṇī.

Having placed the two middle fingers together in the center, with the little fingers and thumbs held back, and having made the two index fingers like a staff above the middle fingers, [one forms the seal]. BndP 3.42.4.
If the middle fingers of this very same mudrā are made straight,
it becomes the Vidrāviṇī mudrā, which shatters the pride of the Vindhya mountains.
O Kalaśodbhava, when the middle and index fingers are joined together in the form of a hook, with the little and ring fingers placed between them,
this is the Ākarṣiṇī mudrā, capable of attracting the three worlds.
Having formed the hands into the *puṭākāra* gesture, the two index fingers are shaped like hooks; by means of the sequence of rotation, the two middle fingers are positioned below them.
By this sequence, O celestial sage, when the little finger is positioned in the middle,
the ring finger is straight, and the two index fingers are outside of it.
Then, with the two thumbs shaped like staffs and the two middle fingers positioned at the region of the navel—
this mudrā is known by the name Unmādinī, which destroys the offspring of Vātāpi.
Having placed the pair of ring fingers below in the shape of a goad,
one should likewise apply the two index fingers in that same order.
This is the Mahāṅkuśā mudrā, which accomplishes all purposes and goals.

O divine sage, having placed the left arm in the right region and the right arm in the left region, and having crossed the two hands over one another in this sequence, O ascetic, the little fingers and ring fingers should be joined.
The two index fingers press down upon both middle fingers from above.
One should cause both thumbs to touch the base of the little fingers;
this is the mudrā named Khecarī, the most excellent of all.
By the mere knowledge of this, one becomes dear to the Yoginīs. (Bṛhad-yogiyājñavalkyasmṛti 3.42.14)
Having turned the two hands over so that they touch in the shape of a half-moon,
one should then join the pair of index fingers and thumbs simultaneously.
One should place the two middle fingers, pressed down by the little fingers below; then,
having joined these two [middle fingers] in a curved shape at the very bottom of the ring fingers—
this is the Seed Mudrā, which swiftly sets all accomplishments in motion.
With the tips of the middle fingers curved and positioned above the index fingers,
the ring fingers and little fingers should likewise be placed in the middle.
Joining all [the fingers] together in one place and pressing them with the thumbs—
this is the first mudrā, known by the name Yonimudrā.
O divine sage, these mudrās are the causes of the Śrīdevī’s delight;
they should be employed at the time of worship according to their sequential application.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter in the Lalitopākhyāna of the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Hayagrīva and Agastya.
Agastya said:
O horse-faced one of great wisdom, ocean of the nectar of compassion!
Tell me what kind of initiation there is for the vision of the Śrīdevī.
Hayagrīva said:
"If you desire that divine state by which the mire of one's sins is washed away, then we shall explain here that initiation (dīkṣā) for men."
Having visualized Śivapura in his hand, he should recite the Mūla- and Aṅga-mālinī;
the Guru should then touch the body of the disciple—this is declared to be the initiation by touch (sparśadīkṣā).
Closing his eyes and meditating upon Śrī Kāmākṣī with a serene mind, the Guru should look clearly at the disciple; this is called the initiation by sight (dṛgdīkṣā).
Knowledge arises immediately through the mere sight of the Guru, through his speech, or even through his touch; that initiation is considered Śāmbhavī.
Just as the body of the Goddess has been described, so too is the body of the Guru;
by his grace, even the disciple shines forth as having that very same form.
When the Lord of Teachers has been properly satisfied by long and faithful service, he should silently resolve upon the disciple; that is considered the mental initiation (mānasī dīkṣā).
Of all initiations (*dīkṣā*), this alone is the most excellent;
one should first perform the initiation by ritual action (*kriyādīkṣā*), and its procedure shall now be explained.
On an auspicious day during the bright fortnight, having purified his mind and cleansed the impurities of his tongue and mouth, he should bathe according to the prescribed rite.
Having completed the twilight rites and then remembering the supreme body of the Guru,
the illustrious one should dwell in solitude, observing silence and restricting his food.
The Guru, having become such [as described], should enter the temple of worship,
performing the placement of the Vidyā (vidyā-nyāsa) together with the Mothers, accompanied by the Devīsūkta.

Having performed [the worship] with the Puruṣasūkta and the sixteen types of offerings— namely, invocation, the seat, water for the feet, the arghya offering, and likewise water for sipping— BndP_3.43.12.
Bathing, clothing, ornaments, fragrance, and likewise flowers;
incense and lamps, food offerings, betel, and circumambulation.
And with these well-known [verses] beginning with "praṇāmaḥ," one should please the Mother of the Three Cities (Tripurāmbikā).
Then, one should offer a handful of flowers with the thousand-syllable vidyā.

Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ. Oṃ, salutations, O Tripurasundarī! O Goddess of the Heart, O Goddess of the Head, O Goddess of the Crest-lock, O Goddess of the Armor, O Goddess of the Eyes, O Goddess of the Mouth! O Kāmeśvarī, O Bhagamālinī, O Nityaklinnā, O Bhairuṇḍā, O Vahnivāsinī, O Mahāvajreśvarī, O Vidyeśvarī, O Paraśivadūtī, O Tvaritā, O Kulasundarī, O Nityā, O Nīlapatākā, O Vijayā!

O you who are all-auspicious, garlanded with flames, wondrous, eternally great, Supreme Goddess; O you who consist of Mantreśa, who consist of Ṣaṣṭhīśa, who consist of Udyāna, who consist of Lopāmudrā, who consist of Agastya, who consist of Kālatāpana, who consist of Dharmācāra, who consist of Muktakeśīśvara, who consist of Dīpakalānātha, who consist of Viṣṇudeva, who consist of Prabhākaradeva, who consist of Tejodeva, who consist of Manojadeva; O you who possess the siddhi of aṇimā, O you who possess the siddhi of mahimā!

O Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumāri, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, Mahālakṣmī! O you who possess the perfection of greatness, the perfection of lightness, the perfection of lordship, the perfection of mastery, the perfection of attainment, the perfection of irresistible will, the perfection of taste, and the perfection of liberation!
O you who agitate all, who cause all to flee, who attract all, who bring all under control, who madden all, and who are the great goad for all!

O you who move through all the sky, O you who are the seed of all, O you who are the womb of all, O destroyer of all weapons! O enchantress of the three worlds, O Mistress of the Wheel, O Prāṭayoginī, O you whose body is the Buddhist philosophy! O attractor of desire, attractor of intellect, attractor of ego, attractor of sound, attractor of touch, attractor of form, attractor of taste, attractor of smell, attractor of mind, attractor of fortitude, attractor of memory, attractor of name!
O you who attract the seed-syllables, O you who attract the self, O you who attract the nectar, O you who attract the body, O Guptayoginī! O Mistress of the Wheel that fulfills all hopes;

O Anaṅgakusumā, O Anaṅgamekhalā, O Anaṅgamādinī, O Anaṅgamadanāturā, O Anaṅgarekhā, O Anaṅgaveginī, O Anaṅgāṅkuśā, O Anaṅgamālinī! O most secret Yoginī, whose limbs are the Vedic vision; O Mistress of the Wheel that causes universal agitation!
O presiding deity of the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya), whose form is emanation, O you who agitate all, who cause all to dissolve, who attract all, who gladden all,
who delude all, who paralyze all, who cause all to yawn, who bring all under control, who delight all, who intoxicate all,
who accomplish all goals, who fulfill all prosperity, who consist of all mantras, who destroy all dualities, O Yoginī of the lineage!
O you whose limbs are the sight of the Sun; O Mistress of the Wheel that bestows all good fortune; O bestower of all perfections; O bestower of all prosperity; O maker of all dear;

O performer of all auspiciousness; O bestower of all desires; O liberator from all suffering; O pacifier of all death; O remover of all obstacles; O beautiful in every limb; O bestower of all good fortune; O Yoginī who has transcended the Kula; O Mistress of the Wheel that accomplishes all aims; O Omniscient One!

O Thou of all power, O Bestower of the fruit of all sovereignty, O Thou consisting of all knowledge, O Warder-off of all diseases, O Thou whose nature is the support of all, O Remover of all sins, O Thou consisting of all bliss, O Thou whose nature is the protection of all, O Bestower of the fruits of all desires, O Sovereign, O Thou whose body is the Vaiṣṇava vision, O Thou stationed in the wheel that protects all, O Mistress of the Dakṣiṇāmnāya, O Thou whose form is stability, O Vaśinī, Kāmeśī, Modinī, Vimalā, Aruṇā!

Victorious One, Sovereign of All, Kaulinī, Yoginī of Secrets, Enjoyer of Secrets, Guardian of Secrets, whose limbs are the Śākta vision, Mistress of the Wheel that removes all diseases; O Goddess of the Bow, Arrow, Noose, and Goad in the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya); Kāmeśī, Vajreśī, Phagamālinī, Yoginī of the Ultimate Secret, whose limbs are the Śaiva vision, Mistress of the Wheel that bestows all accomplishments, Sovereign of the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya), you who are the form of withdrawal (saṃhāra).
O Śuddhaparā, who has reached the seat of the *bindu*, O Great Tripurasundarī, O Yoginī of the supreme secret of the higher and the lower, O you whose limbs are the vision of Śambhu,

O Mistress of the wheel consisting of all bliss, O Tripurasundarī, dweller in Tripura, glory of Tripura, garland of Tripura, Siddhā of Tripura, Mother of Tripura, abiding in all wheels, whose essential nature is called the Unsurpassed Tradition (*anuttarāmnāya*), O Mahātripurabhairavī, whose form consists of the fourfold qualities!

O Kulākula, O Mahākaulinī, O Supreme One, O You whose limbs are all philosophical systems, O You who abide in the nine seats, O You of nine syllables, O You formed as the nine couples; O You whose essence is the knowledge of Maheśa, Mādhava, Vidhātṛ, Manmatha, Skanda, Nandin, Indra, Anu, Candra, Kubera, Agastya, Durvāsas, and Krodhabhaṭṭāraka;
O You whose form is the three auspicious principles, O You whose nature is Śiva and Śivā; O Power of Brahmā, O Great Supreme Goddess, O Great Tripurasundarī!
I worship Your venerable sandals; obeisance!
*ka eṃ īla hrīṃ hasa kahala hrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ sauḥ klīṃ aiṃ śrīṃ*.
One should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to the Goddess with this thousand-syllable mantra (*sahasrākṣaravidyā*).
The proponents of the Veda say that if it were not so, that worship would be in vain.
Then, on a ground smeared with cow dung,
he should construct there a new [altar] using one *droṇa* of pure rice grains and excellent straw.
A pitcher filled with water from the Droṇa lake and joined with five new jewels [should be placed] beneath branches of the Nyagrodha,
Aśvattha, Mākanda, Jambu, and Udumbara trees.
And having placed bark and sprouts that have been consecrated with incense,
one should set down a ripe and auspicious coconut fruit before the water-pot.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should present incense, lamps, and the like;
then, one should recite the Śrī-Cintāmaṇi mantra while mentally repeating the Mātṛkā in the heart.
Touching the water-pot, which has assumed a physical form for the attainment of prosperity and desires,
one should again present a lamp when one hundred and eight [recitations] have been completed.
Having summoned the disciple to a secluded place and caused his eyes to be bound with a cloth,
the Guru [should receive] three prostrations performed with all eight limbs.
Having placed flowers in her hand, one should cause her to form a handful of blossoms [with the words]:
"O Śrīnātha, mass of compassion! O Sovereign Lady consisting of the supreme light! (BndP 3.43.22).
This handful of flowers is offered by me at your lotus feet;
you are my supreme abode, the supreme Brahman, and the highest deity.
"From this day forward, protect my sons and me who have come to you for refuge.
Having spoken thus, the disciple should place the lotus-feet of the Guru upon his head.

The merit of deeds performed in previous births would be realized when the sandals are placed upon the head by the Guru— those sandals obtained through service to the Lotus-seated Lord, the Lord of the chest, and the Lord of the city.
Having spoken thus, filled with devotion and peaceful, he should rise again and stand on the left side of the Guru, humble and endowed with discipline.
Then, having sprinkled [the disciple] with water from a gourd (tuṃbī), he should present him on his left side;
having released the blindfold, he should show him the sequence of worship.
One should prescribe that sugar, honey, ghee, plantains, and milk-rice constitute the food offering for Mahātripurasundarī.
He should softly recite the sixteen-syllable mantra into his left ear;
then, having gone outside, he should seat the pure man upon a wooden seat.
Having seated the disciple there, facing eastward upon a cloth spread with silk, one should sprinkle him with the waters from the auspicious jar while reciting the mantras.
Having bathed again with pure water and put on two garments,
one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times and then enter into sleep.
When an auspicious dream is seen, then the highest merit should be applied;
but in the case of a bad dream, one should perform the recitation (japa) one thousand and eight times.
One should perform the worship of Tripurāmbā according to the path of liberation;
however, when not even a dream is seen, then accomplishment will come only after a long time.
If the Goddess should accept [the offering] with supreme devotion— even if it exceeds the remaining portion—
that disciple shall immediately become a purifier of those who purify the assembly.
One should offer one's body, wealth, and life to that venerable Guru;
remaining dependent upon him, one should always act accordingly and never disregard his word.
One should recognize as rare that Guru who, when pleased, bestows the glory of liberation in half a moment— he who delivers one from the cycle of existence.
The syllable *gu* has the meaning of darkness, and the syllable *ru* is its suppressor;
because it suppresses darkness, it is designated as *guru*.
Having obtained a Guru who is the embodiment of consciousness, one should not seek another teacher;
one should contemplate even the harsh words spoken by the Guru as a blessing.
One should acquire knowledge from him— whether it be worldly, Vedic, or even pertaining to the inner self— and one should first pay homage to him.
Having thus performed the three initiations, one should again awaken the disciple to his duty:
devotion to the guru, virtuous conduct, and that hostility toward him is a sin.
The remembrance of that state is liberation; this process continues as long as the body exists.
Whatever sin one incurs by speaking untruth in the presence of the Guru [is incurred by failing to remember it].
Even after committing the slaughter of a cow or a Brahmin, one should not take refuge in that sin;
for from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, my lineage is my guru.
"Who on the surface of the earth would not be worthy of worship by me, who am worthy of worship by all?"—
he who is thus well-disposed toward everything is proclaimed to be a true disciple.
One who cultivates the many stainless qualities such as ethical conduct and the like,
and who abides by the instructions of the guru, is called a "disciple" (śiṣya).
When weary from recitation, one should meditate again; when weary from meditation, one should recite again.
For one engaged in recitation, meditation, and the like, the mantra is swiftly accomplished.
Just as even a worm becomes a bee through the power of meditation,
so too a human being becomes one with Brahman through the power of samādhi.
Just as when it is dissolved in time, the manifold world is no longer seen, even so one should close the eyes; this indeed is the characteristic of meditation.
But when the supreme reality— transcending all letters and indeed changeless— is known,
the mantras, together with the lords of mantras, become its servants.
For one who is established in the state of identity with the Self, whatever activity he performs is indeed vision;
that is yoga, that is austerity, that is his mantra, and that very act of beholding is his wealth.
When identification with the body has dissolved and the Supreme Self is realized,
wherever the mind goes, there are states of meditative absorption.
For one who perceives the all-pervading, peaceful, non-dual Self whose nature is bliss,
nothing remains to be attained or known.
A hymn of praise is equal to ten million acts of worship; recitation is equal to ten million hymns of praise;
meditation is equal to ten million recitations; and absorption is equal to ten million meditations.
The body is declared to be the temple, and the individual soul (jīva) is indeed Maheśvara;
one should discard the discarded offering of ignorance and unite with Him through the realization of "I am He."
Rice remains rice when bound by its husk, but in the absence of the husk, it is simply grain;
likewise, the individual soul (jīva) is known as such when bound by fetters, but when freed from the fetters, it is Maheśvara.
Just as the movement of birds in the sky or of aquatic creatures in the waters cannot be perceived, so too the great conduct of the high-souled ones is not seen.

One should perform the daily worship during the day and the occasional worship at night; the performance of rites for specific desires may occur at either time—this is the settled conclusion of the scriptures.
Compared to ten million times ten million great gifts, compared to ten million times ten million great vows,
and compared to ten million times ten million great sacrifices, the remembrance of the Śrīpādukā is superior.
Whether through knowledge or even through ignorance, as long as the body is sustained,
the conduct of one's caste and stage of life must be observed for the sake of liberation from karma.
Whatever has emerged from the mouth of the guru is called the entire scripture;
one should perform even that which is prohibited, for one must never transgress the command of the guru.
Whether he is distinguished by birth, learning, or wealth, upon seeing his guru from afar,
he should joyfully perform three circumambulations, keeping him at the distance of a staff's length.

One should bow to everything with the thought that it is the Guru, even if it be merely a blade of grass; however, one should prostrate before an image made of metal or clay with the thought that it is the deity itself.
Having reviled their guru with shouts of "huṃ" and "tuṃ," and having defeated a Brahmin through mere arguments,
and having exposed secret scriptures, they become Brahma-rākṣasas.
One should always contemplate non-duality, not non-duality with the Guru;
one should not disparage other systems, such as the Vedas, Shastras, Agamas, and so forth.
A disciple residing in the same village should prostrate to the guru at the three junctions of the day;
one residing within a distance of one *krośa* should bow to the guru every day with devotion.
A disciple who intends to travel for the sake of [pilgrimage] should prostrate at five joints [of the body],
beginning from one *yojana* and extending up to twelve *yojanas*.
During the months corresponding to the number of *yojanas* [between himself and the guru], the disciple should prostrate to the guru;
when he is situated at a great distance, he should go [to him] whenever the desire arises.
One should not approach a king, a deity, or a guru with empty hands;
one should offer fruits, flowers, garments, and the like according to one's ability.
Paraśiva himself, bound by human skin,
wanders secretly upon the earth for the sake of bestowing grace upon worthy disciples.
For the sake of protecting true devotees, Śiva— the storehouse of compassion— though formless, assumes a form and acts in the world like an ordinary transmigrating being. Indeed,
Śiva possesses three eyes, while Acyuta possesses four arms.
The venerable Guru is proclaimed to be Brahmā with four faces.
Those devoid of fortune do not behold the glorious Guru, who is known as the Supreme Reality and stands before their very eyes, just as the blind do not see the risen sun.
Reflection on reality is the highest; reflection on recitation is middling;
reflection on the scriptures is low; and reflection on worldly affairs is the lowest of the low.
There is no reality superior to the Guru; there is no happiness superior to knowledge;
there is no worship superior to devotion; indeed, there is no fruit superior to liberation.
In all the Vedas and Śāstras, and in the accounts of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others,
she who is beyond the supreme is described there in various places by these words as the illustrious Kāmākṣī.
Śacī and Indra, Svāhā and Agni, Prabhā and Ravi, Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, Vāṇī and Dhātṛ, and Girijā and Śiva.
Agni and Soma are the bindu and nāda; likewise, they are Prakṛti and Puruṣa, as well as those named the support and the supported, and similarly, enjoyment and liberation.
Inhalation and exhalation, word and meaning, as well as injunction and prohibition,
and whatever dualities such as pleasure and pain are seen or even heard— [all these are likewise].
In all the worlds, all that is undoubtedly the Supreme Brahman;
they know that supreme light which has transcended [all else] as the one named Kāmākṣī.
"Whatever Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others constantly meditate upon— indeed,
such is this path of Power (Śaktimārga) in which a man here abides."
The ground of grace belonging to the Goddess Śrī is the vessel for both worldly enjoyment and liberation for those who worship Kāmākṣī,
whether with or without mantras.
Women, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras indeed attain the supreme goal;
how much more so the Kṣatriyas and Brāhmaṇas who perform sacrifices preceded by mantras?
Even those who wander in saṃsāra are surely liberated; of this there is no doubt.
[The offerings consist of] white rice, honey, clarified butter, plantains, and milk-rice.
One should always offer the food oblation (naivedya) on the five festival days;
even if one is capable, he who does not worship [on these days] shall incur the curse of the Goddess.
If one is unable [to perform elaborate rites], one should always worship Ambikā with meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) and ritual substances;
a householder, moreover, should worship the Great Goddess while endowed with auspicious conduct.
Accompanied by a favorable wife, one should worship Mahālakṣmī;
O Agastya, the preceptor should explain the ritual conduct three times.
If a disciple does not accept [the teaching], the fault does not belong to the guru;
for Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, Vāṇī and Dhātṛ, and Girijā and Śiva [are likewise].
One should indeed contemplate the glorious Guru and the Guru’s wife as one's own parents with the mind;
thus, O Pot-born One, everything has been declared by me in brief.
By attending to this much, one becomes wise and omniscient.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter in the Lalitopākhyāna of the Uttara-bhāga of the glorious Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa.
Hayagrīva said:
Having entered the place for recitation, he brought her to his own seat.
Having sprinkled [the site] according to rule with mantras, following the sequence and application taught by the Guru.
Meditating upon his own self as the form of the deity without distinction therein,
facing the east, he should firmly assume the lotus posture with one-pointed mind.
Having paid homage to the guru and others, one should bind the *trikhaṇḍā* [mudrā],
placing the doubled seed-syllables of the Child (Bāla) on the middle finger and the other fingers in succession.
Having also placed [the mudrās] on the two palms, preceded by the purification of the hands,
the knower of mantras should perform [the protection] up to the perimeter of the fire-walls with his own weapon-mantra.
Having superimposed the pervader [of the alphabet] starting from *ka* in direct order and from the feet (*pāda*) onwards in reverse order,
one should cause it to pervade by means of the Vāgbhava and other seed-syllables.
One should fashion the subtle and gross bodies from the manifest [elements];
then, one should place the seed-syllables of the Child (Bāla) at the navel, the heart, and between the eyebrows.
One should place the Mātṛkā, encircled by the root-mantra, in sequence starting from the navel;
then one should place those very same seed-syllables of Bālā by repeating them twice.
It should not be otherwise on the fingers of the middle and other parts, nor on the palms;
having then placed [the mantras] on the navel and so forth, one should then place them on the two feet.
In the knees, thighs, buttocks, private parts, base of the navel, heart, and head, respectively, are the nine seats:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and likewise Īśvara.
Having installed Sadāśiva, Pūṣan, Tūlikā, Prakāśaka,
and Vidyāsana, one should then show [the seat] in the heart.
Having formed the mudrā known as the three-petaled lotus-yoni with the lips,
and having filled the breath with the syllables *huṃ huṃ huṃ*, one should awaken Kuṇḍalī.
Having raised [the consciousness] by the power of the mantra to the dvādaśānta and contemplated its unity with Śiva, one should then settle it once more in its own place.
One should place the seed-syllables beginning with Vāgbhava at the root, the heart, and the two arms;
and the entire [mantra] on the head, the roots of the arms, the middle of the arms, and the tips of the arms, respectively.
Having placed the two hands upon the limbs from the tips of the thumbs to the palms,
and having performed the placement on the heart and other parts, one should perform the saffron-placement (kuṅkuma-nyāsa).
Furthermore, one should place the pure Mātṛkā encased by the third seed-syllable;
having placed the first two seed-syllables, one should then place the final seed-syllable.
One should perform the arrangement of the *punarbhūta* [syllables] without being overly prolix;
one should place the eight groups at the base, the navel, the heart, and the throat.
One should first place [the syllables] *ā*, *dhā*, *ai*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ān* upon the root, the heart, and the head;
one should then place them upon the armpits, the hips, the shoulders, the left shoulder-blade, the waist, and the heart.
One should place the six limbs below the abundant [syllable] using the groups of consonants beginning with *da*;
the seer of this Śabdabrahman is considered to be Bhūtalipi, and its meter is the same.
The venerable Mūlaprakṛti is said to be the deity of this Manu;
she holds a rosary and a book in her upper hands, and a flower-arrow and a bow.
With her lotus-like hands she holds the boon-granting gesture and the gesture of fearlessness; she bears the incomparable rosary made of *rakṣa* seeds around her neck.
Adorned with heroic ornaments covered by necklaces, armlets, and bracelets,
she was decorated with jeweled earrings and smeared with divine unguents.
Beneath the Kalpa-tree of scripts, one should meditate upon Bhairavī, who is fond of her devotees, who dwells within the lotus of form, and who is manifestly composed of the scripts themselves.
Having thus meditated upon her as being adorned on all sides by many millions of female messengers, one should again inscribe the syllables in sequence upon the ground.

Then one should place the eight groups [of consonants] from the base (mūla) up to the Ājñā center; having placed śa, ṣa, and sa upon the head, one should assign the vowels to those very same locations.
[One should perform the ritual] with the *hādi* [mantras] on the five [limbs] beginning with the head, at the tips and the bases, and in the middle;
as well as on the roots of the fingers, the wrists, the two elbows, and the two feet.
One should assign the letters beginning with *va*—namely *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *sa*—to the stomach, the right and left sides, the navel and the back, as well as to the root, the heart, and the head.
Alternatively, one may assign those beginning with *la*.

Then there are five short vowels, followed by the four diphthongs; *ha*, *ya*, and *ra* are at the beginning of the *vala* (semivowels); *a* and *ka* are at the beginning of the *khaga* (sibilants), and *na* and *ga* are at the beginning of the remaining group (*gaṇa*). This is the sequence for the remaining classes.
These are known as the *śaṣasa* [groups], consisting of forty-two syllables;
the first group has five syllables, and the second has four syllables.
The five-syllabled [mantra] consists of six groups; the ninth is considered to have three syllables.
They correspond respectively to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Kubera, Indra, and Yama.
Varuṇa and Soma—these nine are declared to be the lords of the castes (varṇas) and the three powers (śaktis); this is the sequence of the letters on the earth.
Thus, in the process of emanation, the sequence is reversed; in the process of withdrawal, it is as follows:
the points of articulation (sthānas) are to be joined with the visarga and bindu at the end of the phonemes.
Then, preceded by meditation, the wise one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of Rati and the others;
they resemble the japā flower and have bodies as red as saffron.
They should be meditated upon as holding a bow and arrows, with Kāma mounted upon the left thigh of Rati;
Kāma, joined by Rati and Prīti, is desired by his beloved.
Possessing beauty and endowed with the limbs of desire joined with delusion, he follows after one who is fond of quarreling, accompanied by amorous gestures and acting according to his own will.
Kāma is joined with Kalpalatā; Kāmuka is with Śyāmavarṇā;
Kāma is accompanied by Śucismitā; and Bandhaka is united with Vismṛtā.
Ramaṇa was gazed upon by the wide-eyed woman with her tongue flickering, and this Rama,
the lord of Rati who is fond of Rati, was adorned with the directions as his garments.
Ratinātha is joined with Vāmā and Kubjā; he is united with Dhara, the beloved of Ramā, worshipped by Ramā, and the night-stalker who delights in pleasure.
Kalyāṇa, Mohinīnātha, Nandaka endowed with the supreme,
Nandī enriched by the best of gods, and furthermore Nandana, the one who causes joy.
Endowed with great beauty, the five-arrowed one, the lord of the treasures of youth, accompanied by his beloved who delights in strife, and likewise the friend of Rati; ||| BndP_3,44.39 |||
Ekākṣi, Puṣpadhanvan, Sumukheśa, Mahādhanus,
Nīli, Jaḍilya, Bhramaṇa, and Kramaśaḥpālinīpati.
Wandering about, beloved by Śivā, he is the delusion (bhrama) who is deluded by the charming one;
the bewilderer (bhrāmaka) who has attained delight through Rāmā, he is considered the bee (bhṛṅga) who is made to wander.
Bhrāntācāra is accompanied by Locanā, while Bhramāvaha is again joined by Dīrghajihvikā; Mohana, however, is united with Ratipriyā.
But Mohaka is desired in the housewife Palāśākṣī;
Vikaṭeśa is the bearer of delusion (mohadhara), and this one, joined with the earth (dharā), is to be increased.
Madanātha is Anūpama; Manmatha is accompanied by Malayā;
Mādaka is joined with Ohlādinī; and Samicchan is Viśvatomukhī.
The leader (nāyaka) is preceded by Bhṛṅga; the singer (gāyaka) is joined with Nandinī;
the calculator (gaṇaka) is to be known as being with Anāmaya; and the dancer (nartaka) is desired to be with Kālī.
Kṣvellaka is endowed with Kālakarṇī; Kandarpa is considered intoxicated; Nartaka has Śyāmalā as his beloved; and Vilāsī is accompanied by Jhaṣā.
Having approached the Unmattā, he who increases desire rejoices;
thereafter, preceded by meditation, he should perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) of Śrīkaṇṭha and the others.
Having meditated upon Ardhanārīśvara— whose two halves are like vermilion and gold respectively, who bears the emblems of both the Daughter of the Mountain and the Lord of the Mountains,
and whose hands hold a noose, a rosary, and a lotus— one should assign him to the syllables of the script for the sake of one's desired object.
Śrīkaṇṭha, Ananta, Sūkṣma, Trimūrti, Amareśvara, Urvīśa, Bhārabhūti, Atithīśa, Sthāṇuka, and Hara.
Caṇḍīśa, Bhautika, Sadyojāta, Anugraheśvara,
Akrūra, and Mahāsena— these are the forms of the Bestower of Boons (Varamūrti).
Then [there were] Krodheśa and Caṇḍīśa, Pañcāntaka and Śivottama,
as well as Ekarudra, Kūrma, and Ekanetra, together with Caturātana.
Ajeśa, Śarva, Someśa, Hara, Lāgalin, Dāruka,
Ardhanārīśvara, Umākānta, Cāpāḍhya, and Daṇḍin.
Atri, Mīna, Meṣa, Lohita, and likewise Śikhin;
Khaḍga, Daṇḍa, and Dvidaṇḍa; and the very great Mahākāla and Vyālin.
Bhujaṅgeśa, Pinākī, Khaḍgeśa, and Bakas,
as well as Śveta, Abhra, Lakulīśiva, and Saṃvarttaka.
Pūrṇodarī, Virajā, and the third, Śālmalī; Lolākṣī, Vartulākṣī, and likewise Dīrghaghoṇā.
The two chief ones with very long faces, the ninth with a long tongue,
Kuñjarī, Urdhvakeśā, Dvimukhī, and Vikṛtānanā.
The primary powers of the [Supreme] Sound (svara-śakti) are Satyalīlā, Kalā, Vidyā, and others;
as well as Mahākālī and Sarasvatī, who are endowed with all supernatural accomplishments (sarva-siddhi).
Gaurī, Trailokyavidyā, as well as Mantrātmaśaktikā,
Lambodarī, Bhūtamatā, Drāviṇī, and likewise Nāgarī.
Khecarī, Mañjarī, Rūpiṇī, and likewise Vīriṇī;
Koṭarā, Pūtanā, Bhadrā, Kālī, and Yoginī as well.
Śaṅkhinī, Garjinī, Kālarātri, and Kūrdinī; likewise Kapardinī, Vajrā, Jayā, and Sumukheśvarī.
Revatī, Mādhavī, Vāruṇī, and likewise Vāyavī;
another is Rakṣāvadhāriṇī, as well as the one named Sahajā.
And Lakṣmī, O Vyāpinīmāyā, are enumerated as the powers of the phonemes;
having then formed the colored design with the phonemes of the twice-spoken Bālā, both individually and collectively.
One should perform the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhā-nyāsa) for the sake of attaining the nature of the deity;
first, one should place Vighneśa and the others there, preceded by meditation.
Resembling the young morning sun, with elephant faces and three eyes,
they hold nooses, goads, gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in their hands, and are accompanied by their Śaktis.
Vighneśa, Vighnarāja, Vināyaka, Śivottama, Vighnakṛt, Vighnahantṛ, Vighnarāj, and Gaṇanāyaka.
He who has one tusk and two tusks, the elephant-faced one, the stainless one;
he with matted locks, the long-faced one, the spike-eared one, whose banner bears the bull.
The Lord of the Gaṇas, with the face of a lordly elephant, with ears like winnowing baskets and three eyes;
pot-bellied, of great roar, the fourfold form, the eternally auspicious one.
Āmoda, Durmada, Sumukha, Pramodaka,
Ekapāda, Dvipāda, Śūra, Vīra, and Ṣaṇmukha.
The god named Varada, Vakratuṇḍa, Dvidantaka,
Senānī, Grāmaṇī, Matta, and he whose vehicle is a rutting mouse.
Jaṭī, Muṇḍī, Khaḍgī, Vareṇya, Vṛṣaketana,
Bhaṅgyapriya, Gaṇeśa, Meghanāda, and Gaṇeśvara.
These are the Gaṇeśas of the fifty-one letters in their respective order:
Śrī, Hrī, Puṣṭi, Śānti, Tuṣṭi, and Sarasvatī.
Rati, Medhā, Kānti, Kāminī, Mohinī, Tīvrā, Jvālinī, Nandā, Suyaśas, and Kāmarūpiṇī.
Ugrā, Tejovatī, Satyā, Vighneśānī, Svarūpiṇī,
Kāmārttā, Madajihvā, Vikaṭā, and Ghūrṇitānanā.
She is Bhūti, Bhūmi, Dviramyā, Amārūpā, Makaradhvajā,
Vikarṇabhrukuṭī, Lajjā, Dīrghaghoṇā, and Dhanurdharī.
Likewise, the night is *yāminī*, *rātri*, *candrakāntā*, and *śaśiprabhā*;
it is *lolākṣī*, *capalā*, *ṛjvī*, *durbhagā*, *subhagā*, and *śivā*.
Durgā, Guhapriyā, Kālī, and Kālajihvā are the Śaktis;
then, with a concentrated mind and preceded by meditation, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) upon the internal organs (graha).
Their hands are endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, their bodies embraced by Śaktis,
and they are [colored] by saffron, milk, blood, jasmine, and golden water.
One should contemplate the sun and other planets as being like smoke, clouds, and darkness;
having placed the sun below the heart, one should place the moon on the head and Mars in the eyes.
One should place Śukra in the heart, Budha in the center of the chest, Bṛhaspati in the throat,
Śanaiścara in the navel, Rāhu in the mouth, and Ketu in both feet.
Then, while meditating, one should place the Tārās, who resemble the blazing fire of time (Kālānala), who grant boons and fearlessness with their hands, and who are adorned with all ornaments.
On the forehead, the two eyes, the two ears, the two nostrils, the throat, the two shoulders, and then on the two elbows and the two wrists; // BndP_3,44.81 //

One should perform the placement of the Yoginīs on the two breasts, the navel, the hips, the thighs, the knees, the shanks, and the pair of feet; likewise, being doubly purified, one should place them in the heart.
In the navel, at the root of the svādhiṣṭhāna, between the eyebrows, and in the head, respectively—
in the center of the lotus and its moon-pedicel, and then upon the petals— [one should place] the phonemes and their powers.
One should place all of them upon the tips of the petals at the head of the lotus:
Amṛtā, Nandinī, Indrāṇī, Īśānī, and likewise Atyumā.
She whose hair stands erect, she who knows the Ṛgveda, likewise she who consists of the syllable *ḷ*,
she who bestows sovereignty through her single-footed nature, and she whose essence is medicinal herbs.
Then Ambikā, Rakṣātmikā, and so forth—these are the sixteen Śaktis:
Kālikā, Khecarī, Gāyatrī, and likewise Ghaṇṭādhāriṇī.
And Nādātmikā, Cāmuṇḍā, Chatrikā, and likewise Jayā;
Jhaṅkāriṇī, Saṃjñā, and thereafter Ṭaṅkahastā.
And the twelve Śaktis are to be known in sequence as Ḍaṅkārī,
Ṭaṅkāriṇī, Ṇāminī, and likewise Tāmasī.
Thaṅkāriṇī, Dayā, Dhātrī, Nādinī, Pārvatī,
and Phaṭkāriṇī are to be known as the Śaktis who possess two serpents.
Vardhinī, Bhadrā, Majjā, Yaśasvinī,
Ramā, and Lāminī— these six are the Śaktis in their respective order.
Nārada, Śrī, as well as Ṣaṇḍhā and Śaśvatī—these four are likewise Śaktis; and similarly, there are two others: Hākinī and Kṣamā.
Then, one should assign the zodiac signs beginning with Aries to the right foot, the penis, the belly, the heart, the arms, and the head,
ending at the left foot.
Then one should place the fifty-one seats and the single wheel in the mind:
Vārāṇasī, Kāmarūpa, Nepāla, and Pauṇḍravardhana.
Varasthira, Kānyakubja, Pūrṇaśaila, as well as Arbuda,
Āmrātakeśvara, Ekāmra, Trisrotas, and Kāmakoṣṭhaka.
Kailāsa, Bhṛgunagara, Kedāra, Candrapuṣkara,
Śrīpīṭha, Ekavīrā, Jālandhra, and likewise Mālava.
Kulānna, Devikoṭa, Gokarṇa, Māruteśvara,
Aṭṭahāsa, Viraja, Rājaveśma, and Mahāpatha.
Kolāpura, Kailāpura, Kāleśvara, Jayantikā, Ujjayinī, Citrā, Kṣīraka, and Hastināpura.
Uḍīrā, Prayāga, and likewise Ṣaṣṭimāyāpura;
Gaurīśa along with Laya, Śrīśaila, and Maru as well.
Furthermore, behind Girivara is Mahendra and the Vāmana mountain;
behind that is Hiraṇyapura, and likewise Mahālakṣmīpura.
The wise say that the front garden is likewise a field of shade;
one should place those [deities] associated with the sequence of writing within the locations for writing.

In other places where [the mantras] are stated differently, I have explained the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhā-nyāsa) as it is joined through the transmission of the script; this was spoken directly by the Lord himself.
Having thus disposed the body, one becomes the embodiment of the deity;
then, having performed the sixfold preliminary rite, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Śrīcakra.
One should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) with the mantras beginning with Aṃśa and ending with Ānandāmūrti;
one should place the Cakreśvarī and the mantras for the offering to the wheels (cakra) within the heart.
One should assign Gaṇapati and the others to the various locations as previously described;
one should assign them all in sequence, beginning with the left thigh, equal to the right.
First, Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapāla, Yoginī, and likewise Baṭuka,
as well as Indra and the others, are to be assigned to the tips of the two big toes.
Then, in the sides of the knees, the shoulders, the head, the face, the sides, the knees, the crown of the head,
and the *mūlādhāra*, there is the group of ten supernatural powers (*siddhis*), beginning with *aṇimā*.
They should be placed respectively on the shoulders, arms, back, chest, the two forefeet, the buttocks, the regions of the arms and the back, and the head and the pair of feet.
Aṇimā, laghimā, and thirdly mahimā; likewise īśitva, vaśitva, prākāmya, and prāpti;
icchāsiddhi, rasasiddhi, and mokṣasiddhi—these are traditionally recorded.
Then, O wise brahmin, one should sequentially assign the group of eight Mothers:
on the pair of big toes, on the right side, on the head, and on the left side.
On the left knee, on the right knee, and likewise on the right and left shoulders.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, and Cāmuṇḍā as the seventh.
And Mahālakṣmī should also be known; indeed, the Mothers are to be placed by the wise in due order.
One should assign the eight Mudrā goddesses to these very [locations], and those two again [to the others].
Furthermore, there are the mudrās for the head and the mouth: namely, the Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī, then the Sarvavidrāviṇī, and likewise the Sarvārthākarṣaṇī.
The first of all is the Subduer; the first of all is the Doer of Pleasure;
the first of all is the Great Goad; likewise, the first of all is the Sky-Goer.
The three-part [mudrā], which contains all seeds and is the seal that expands everything, is to be known as the Yoni-mudrā; one should place the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśvarī) therein.
Having offered the Trailokyamohana-cakra and pervaded the body,
one should then sequentially place the sixteen Nityās of the Kalās.
She is the form that attracts desires and the form that attracts sounds;
she is the attractor of the ego-sense and the form that attracts sounds.
She has the form of attracting touch and possesses the form of attracting form;
she has the form of attracting taste and possesses the form of attracting fragrance.
She is the form that draws in the mind, she is the form that draws in fortitude,
she is the form that draws in mindfulness, and she is the form that draws in the heart.
She is indeed of the nature of attracting faith, and she has the form of attracting the self;
she is declared to be the attractor of nectar, and likewise the attractor of the body.
The locations are the right ear, the back, the shoulder, the elbow, the back of the palm of the right hand, its buttock, and the two knees. (Bṛhad-yogiyājñavalkya-purāṇa 3.44.21)
Having placed the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśī) upon the calves and forefeet in reverse order, beginning from the left forefoot, and having worshipped the wheel and pervaded the body; BndP_3,44.22.
Then one should place the eight goddesses beginning with Anaṅgakusumā upon the left conch-shell,
the collarbone, the thigh, and the shank, in reverse order.
Then Anaṅgakusumā, then the second, Anaṅgamekhalā;
then Anaṅgamadanā, and finally Anaṅgamadanāturā.
After her was Anaṅgarekhā, preceded by Vegā;
after her was Anaṅgāṅkuśā, and then Anaṅgādhāramālinī.
Having installed Cakreśī and having offered the wheel, and having pervaded the body,
one should then install the goddesses of power, beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī.
On the forehead, the cheeks, the base of the arms, and the knees;
above and below the shanks, and likewise on the left side in reverse order.
The power that agitates all, likewise the power that subdues all;
the power that attracts all, likewise the power that gladdens all.
The power that deludes all, the primordial one, as well as the paralyzing; the power that causes yawning, the primordial one, and the power that brings all under control, the primordial one.
The power Sarvādyā is Rañjinī, and likewise Sarvādyonmādinī;
the power Sarvārthasādhinī, and likewise Sarvāśāpūriṇī.
The power consisting of all mantras, which brings about the destruction of all dualities,
having placed the Mistress of the Wheel and offered the wheel, pervades the body.
Then one should also place the ten [syllables] beginning with *sarvasiddhiprada* on the right nostril,
the root of the teeth, and likewise on the right breast.
One should place [the mudrās] on the left elbow and wrist in reverse order;
they are the perpetual bestower of all accomplishments and likewise the bestower of all prosperity.
The Goddess who makes all dear, the maker of all auspiciousness,
the power that releases from all evil, and the liberator from all suffering.
She who pacifies all death, she who destroys all obstacles,
she who is beautiful in every limb, and she who bestows all good fortune.
Having installed Cakreśī and having offered the wheel, and having pervaded the body,
one should then install Sarvajñā and the others on the chest and on the surfaces of the teeth.
The Goddess is omniscient, omnipotent, and likewise the bestower of all knowledge;
she consists of all knowledge and is the destroyer of all diseases.
She is the nature of the support of all, likewise the remover of all sins;
she is the goddess consisting of all bliss, whose very form is the protection of all. She should be known as the tenth [digit], the bestower of the fruits of all desires.
Having placed the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśī) and offered the wheel, and having pervaded the body,
the wise one should then place the deities beginning with Prāgvāmā and those beginning with Pakṣiṇī.
On the right side, at the chin, the throat, the breast, the navel, and the two flanks,
the Vidyās are considered to be Vāmā, Vinodinī, Vaśitā, and Kāmikī.
Kāmeśvarī is to be known as the supreme (parā), and likewise Mohinī and Vimalā;
Aruṇā, Jayinī, and thereafter Sarveśvarī are considered [the others]. These are the names of them as proclaimed by the wise as Kaulinī.
Having offered the wheel and pervaded the body, one should place Cakreśvarī;
having visualized a triangle in the heart, [one should place her] in the directions starting from the east in due order.
Outside of that, the wise one should place the four weapons;
he should place the four seats in the corners starting from the southeast and in the center.
Having inscribed the middle circle, one should then inscribe the sixteen Nityās:
Kāmeśvarī-nityā, as well as Nityā, and Bhagamālinī-nityā.
Likewise, Nityaklinnā is eternal, as is the eternal Bheruṇḍinī;
Vahnivāsinikā is eternal, and likewise Mahāvajreśvarī.
The eternal Dūtī, and thereafter the eternal Tvaritā;
the eternal Kulasundarikā, and thereafter the eternal Kulyā.
Nityā and Nīlapatākā, and the supreme Vijayā who is eternal;
after her, Maṅgalā is indeed declared to be preceded by Nityā.
Prabhāmālinikā, Nityā, and likewise Citrā—
these one should place within the triangle, starting from the feet up to the heart.
Nityā, Pramodinī, and Nityā Tripurasundarī—
one should place the Goddess, whose nature is the indivisible universe, in their midst.
Having placed Cakreśvarī in the heart and having raised the wheel,
one should display the mudrā called the Yoni and recite the mantra of Universal Bliss (Sarvānanda).
Thus, for this wheel of the self, there shall be a goddess of the wheel.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter in the Lalitopākhyāna, within the Hayagrīvāgastyasaṃvāda of the Uttarabhāga of the glorious Brahmāṇḍamahāpurāṇa; the Lalitopākhyāna is complete.
This [manuscript] belongs to the one residing in the city named Śrīrāmapūrvaka-Ḍha, situated within the illustrious Pratāpagaḍha fortress.
May this *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, which has been entirely purified of all ancient corruptions, be for the delight of the learned;
yet whatever here remains unpurified,
even though it was edited with care, should be forgiven in its entirety out of compassion.
Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One Vāsudeva;
salutations to Rāma.
This Brahmāṇḍa Mahāpurāṇa is hereby completed.
